excerpts: Ezekiel 43: glory from the east, roar of waters, land radiant, like Kebar, fell face down, glory entered the east gate, filled the temple. 1 Samuel 4: ark captured, Eli, Ichabod. Ezekiel saw God leave; twenty years later he returns through the same gate. Acts 1: this same Jesus will come back the same way. Skip the measurements.

Four views. One: future literal millennial temple, Revelation 20, blueprints. Josh does not hold it; loves those who do. Called a heretic on a Sunday morning. Two: post-captivity ideal guiding Zerubbabel then Herod; measurements theological. Three: christological—temple fulfilled in Christ and the church. Not replacement; promise to the seed, Galatians 3. Are you in Christ by faith? Future for Israel through the gospel. 1 Corinthians 3 you are God’s temple. Ezekiel 47 river and Revelation 22. Why return to animal sacrifices? Four: new-earth view. Jehovah Shammah, Revelation 21 no temple because the Lord and the Lamb are the temple. Affection over agreement. Unity over uniformity. Secret things belong to the Lord. Jesus is coming back. Are you ready?

documents.excerpt: He did not know how to close: glory, judgment, bones, shepherds, measured temple. Then the river. Ezekiel 47: water from under the threshold, trickle, Arizona two-sprinkles. Keep walking. Ankle, knee, waist, then a river you cannot cross. Gospel flows like this. Get in a life group, show up, walk away from temptation. Immeasurably more. Flows to the Dead Sea: dead marriages, churches, sinners live. Presence unleashed into the world. New hearts, new shepherd, new covenant, new temples, new river.

excerpts: Seahawks green and Patriots colors: keep the unity of the Spirit. Series recap: throne room, canal with weeping exiles, hole in the wall at Jerusalem, now a valley of dry bones. Looking to the end of the age and a dead nation raised. Resurrection before they had the name.

He reads Ezekiel 37:1-14. Can these bones live? Sovereign Lord, you alone know. Object lesson on bodily resurrection. Shrek layers: the vision is Israel’s return, God bringing dead people to life nationally, spiritually, eternally. Then, now, future. Bones likely slain soldiers, humiliating unburied Jewish death. Deuteronomy 28 carcass curse. Though we are unfaithful, he remains faithful.

Not fresh bones. Netflix true-crime dry. Prophesy: breath, tendons, flesh, skin. Rattling, bone to bone, no breath. Prophesy to the breath from the four winds. A vast army. These bones are the whole house of Israel: hope gone, cut off. I will open your graves, put my Spirit in you, settle you in your land.

Historical: they feel nationally dead, not spiritually. Return under Zerubbabel, Ezra, Nehemiah. Also a bigger exile: Adam and Eve from Eden. Tree of life in the middle. We were not created to die. Romans 5: sin entered, death through sin. Trace the tree: Genesis 2 sanctuary, Genesis 3 cherubim, menorah, Jesus hung on a tree, veil torn, firstfruits, Eucharist as fruit of the true tree, Revelation 22 both sides of the river. Begins, ends, and is connected by a tree at Golgotha, place of the skull.

Valley of bones to place of the skull. Four winds into the lungs of Jesus. Lazarus rule: he would die again. Return from exile still left them spiritually dead. John 3 wind; Ephesians 2 dead, but God made us alive. Ruach. John 20: he breathed, receive the Holy Spirit. Death becomes a doorman. Lion King theology is wrong. Sister died before 40.

documents.excerpt: Picture bleached silent bones. Can these bones live hangs over every cemetery and ICU. You alone know. Watch my greatest wonder. He does not inspire bones. He raises them. John 5: the dead will hear and live; all in the graves will come out. Virgin-born Son of Man, three days cold, breath entered, he walked out. Why look for the living among the dead? Dead in Christ rise first. Lowly bodies like his. Last enemy destroyed. Death swallowed up in victory. If this is not true, nothing matters. If it is, everything matters. Some feel like these bones. Same voice speaking now. Revival cannot be programmed. Wake up, sleeper. He has spoken and will make good. Pray: last chance to sing, eat, praise.

documents.excerpt: Josh prays the sheep would hear, wanderers come home, stubbornness laid down. He is simple-minded, not a big goal-setter. A 500-adult goal could miss the brokenhearted widow at 490. He wants to be a faithful steward, light a fire to love God and others, a shepherd heaven can rejoice in. When you think of him: sincere love for Christ. You may disagree with his eschatology, be frustrated that he is not a Calvinist, or think his preaching style is weird; you will not argue what God has done. Souls, not seats. No book. Fallen world at war with God. You deserve death; he defeated it. Without Jesus, condemned, stuck like Rahab needing covenant with Yeshua.

Corruption hates criticism. John Wycliffe called out clergy wealth; decades after death they dug up bones, burned them, scattered ashes. Refuse to stay quiet. If you are a victim of spiritual abuse—false words, manipulation, sexual or emotional abuse, silence—Josh offers himself. Sorry. Sometimes the way to heal from a bad shepherd is a good one. Paul’s instruction to the young pastor: two or three witnesses, then rebuke before all.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · February 2, 2026 · Ezekiel : A New Heart
documents.excerpt: I am against the shepherds. Leadership is stewardship, not ownership. When bad shepherds fail, God does not abandon the flock. I myself will search, rescue, gather, pasture, bind, strengthen, destroy the sleek, shepherd with justice. Jeremiah and Isaiah too. I will place over them one shepherd, my servant David. David died about 970 BC; Ezekiel begins 593; David dead about 375 years. Promise alive. Forever king. Matthew’s genealogy: son of David is Jesus.
excerpts: I am against the shepherds. Leadership is stewardship, not ownership. When bad shepherds fail, God does not abandon the flock. I myself will search, rescue, gather, pasture, bind, strengthen, destroy the sleek, shepherd with justice. Jeremiah and Isaiah too. I will place over them one shepherd, my servant David. David died about 970 BC; Ezekiel begins 593; David dead about 375 years. Promise alive. Forever king. Matthew’s genealogy: son of David is Jesus.

In John’s gospel Jesus claims fulfillment of Ezekiel and David; Josh reads the whole section: I am the gate, the good shepherd, I lay down my life, other sheep, one flock. He is not offering comfort. He is announcing identity: I am Yahweh. Hired hands run. Ezekiel: bad shepherds take. Jesus: good shepherd gives. Mark 10: not so with you; servant of all; ransom for many.

Four ways leadership goes sideways: power without love; position without presence; vision without sacrifice; followers without responsibility. Passive sheep damage too. Hebrews 13: submit so their work is joy. You need the church. Sometimes someone must tie your legs and carry you home. Distance in sin is the devil’s shame tool. Come to the throne of grace. Jehovah Shammah: the Lord is there. What Ezekiel saw in promise, John sees in glory. The gate is open. Help us be good shepherds.

1 Peter 4: use whatever gift to serve others. Speak as God’s words; serve with God’s strength. Teaching, preaching, prophecy, wisdom, faith, healing, miracles, tongues biblically, leadership, shepherding, evangelism, giving as if handing it to God. Elders want to equip you to help, not watch. Do not be prideful: gifts exist because of rebirth. Temples of the Spirit. Also offer natural skills. Every part from nursery to Silver Bells. Hospitality, encouragement, listening, needs, forgiveness. Most ministry is unseen. Heaven sees when you walk out and when you are alone. That is the unseen church.

Romans 12: in view of mercy, living sacrifice, true worship. Corporate and personal. We watered true worship by letting style beat unity. Traditional, charismatic, Baptist, contemporary—he could worship with all. Independent not because they cannot make friends but because they value unity. Back-row Baptist Chris with dancing Tom from Bethel. A 70-year-old in Lululemon: Victory in Jesus then Praise. Be comfortable in spirit and truth—and keep worship in truth when you leave, or what you do here is a lie.

documents.excerpt: Ezekiel 8:1. Sixth year, sixth month, fifth day. Elders of Judah sitting before him. Fourteen months after chapter 1. High-level: Israel and nations had temples and priests; only Israel had the glory dwelling. Exodus 40 glory moved in; 1 Samuel 4 departed; 1 Kings 8 filled Solomon’s temple; Ezekiel watched glory leave and begin with glory on the move. Without presence, they are like any people.
excerpts: Ezekiel 8:1. Sixth year, sixth month, fifth day. Elders of Judah sitting before him. Fourteen months after chapter 1. High-level: Israel and nations had temples and priests; only Israel had the glory dwelling. Exodus 40 glory moved in; 1 Samuel 4 departed; 1 Kings 8 filled Solomon’s temple; Ezekiel watched glory leave and begin with glory on the move. Without presence, they are like any people.

Vision runs chapters 8–11. Goal is not to get through the text but the text through you. True worship implies false. He reads 8:2-4: figure like fire and glowing metal, grabbed by the hair, north gate, idol that provokes jealousy, glory of Israel as in the plain.

One would imagine Ezekiel settling in Babylon as Jeremiah said. Christians sing God is always on time then complain he is late. Christianity is not a series of dramatic visions. It is fourteen months of faithfulness. Sometimes quiet; sometimes dragged by the hair. He is not physically in Jerusalem. Fix your eyes on Jesus. Same chariot-throne, likely pre-incarnate Christ. Greatest need is not always a new vision; sometimes he renews an old call because you wandered.

Leaders mixed Jehovah with pagan worship. Demoted him to one of many. Fury without pity is still a way back. Marvel at mercy. excerpts: Josh loves the song and wants to lay a foundation. Last week they approached the likeness of the throne. This entire series is about God changing hearts for his glory. Today we see his glory in the face of Christ. Prophets of old were covenant enforcement mediators, not innovators: certified spokesmen calling people back to Sinai. God remained faithful when they were not.

Marriage analogy: you cannot fully prepare for covenant with a flawed human. They talked faith, family, finances; nobody warned about pillows and the thermostat. Many marry to be happier; God uses it to make them holier. Israel’s covenant differed: clear blessings and curses in Deuteronomy 27–29. Prophets called a prostituted people back. They could announce judgment but not remove guilt, call repentance but not change hearts, enforce but not fulfill.

Jesus is the final prophet and true mediator of a better covenant. Peter in Acts 3: you killed the author of life; God raised him; repent so sins may be wiped out. Moses promised a prophet like me. Jesus bears the curses himself. Galatians 3: cursed is everyone hung on a tree so Abraham’s blessing might come to the Gentiles. Prophets called for obedience; Christ calls for faith. Obedience comes as overflow from a new heart.

excerpts: Unique title in chapter 3: watchman. All offer gifts; there will always be special watchmen set apart to warn. Listen long enough and you become one. Every watchman must know: Christ left equality with God, died, rose, is coming again.

Son of man—humility of Christ taking a man’s title. Stand up; the Spirit raises him. You cannot teach what you have not been taught. Train the tongue by filling the ear. Last week he fell face down; we are dust; God never forgets. Humility first, then stand and take orders. Transfiguration: tents on the mountain, then come down. You cannot merely be educated in the faith; you must be altered by it.

Sent to a rebellious, obstinate house. Thank God he runs after rebels and does not rely on us for outcomes. Whether they listen or not, they will know a prophet has been among them. Isaiah 55: my word will not return empty. Some convinced, many refuse. John 3: light has come; people love darkness. God is not shocked. Do not be afraid of briars, thorns, scorpions. Josh’s family shuts down over a hallway scorpion. Fear drives him to God who drives fear out. If Ezekiel needed three reminders in one verse, how many more do we? Matthew 10: do not fear those who kill the body.

Why fear not? Not sent to obscure speech; if sent to them they would have listened. Israel will not listen because they will not listen to me. I will make your forehead harder than flint. As hard as they are toward disobedience, you will be harder toward obedience. The church has grown soft; one rebuke and they claim church hurt. Spurgeon: bold-hearted men are always called mean-spirited by cowards. Tozer: familiarity breeds complacency. Matthew 11: if Sodom had seen Capernaum’s miracles it would have remained. Do not chase desires with stubbornness. The Christians you call mean might be God’s watchmen.

Truth-tellers, do not grill the lobby. Skilled watchman: Spirit lifted him; he went in bitterness and anger, then sat among the exiles at Tel Aviv seven days, deeply distressed. Sat, felt, wept before he spoke. Find a church whose pastor walks with the people, not only a screen. Weep with those who weep. Romans 9: Paul could wish himself cursed for Israel. Love one another as I have loved you.

documents.excerpt: I have made you a watchman. Warn the wicked or their blood is on your hands. Warn and they refuse: you saved yourself. Righteous who turn to evil without warning die; blood on you. Sit under the weight. Performance is heavy. Wages of sin is death. Enjoy this side of Calvary. Do not ignore the Old Testament; it stirs praise. It is for freedom Christ set us free. External law-righteousness versus internal faith-righteousness. Romans 9: Gentiles obtained righteousness by faith; Israel stumbled over the stone. The law exposed sin; it could not cure. Christ is the culmination of the law.

Ezekiel stood where blood guilt rested on the watchman. We stand under a better covenant. Jesus is the faithful watchman: he warned, wept, obeyed, took the curse. We warn not to earn life but because life has been given. Speak because Christ saved us. Live not under fear of death but in freedom.

excerpts: One of the most significant moments of Josh’s life. Church brat, three generations of preachers in his family; he swore he would never do it. Pew, piano, hypocrisy. He held rebellion until 23. Nothing the world offers comes close to what God made known in Christ.

2 Corinthians 4: God who said let light shine out of darkness made his light shine in our hearts. Knowledge of glory had been jammed into his mind—sermons, studies, baptism, songs—until light shone in the heart. Unshakable thirst to spread that knowledge. Gymnasium at Fort Lewis College in Durango. Man can shape or discourage; only God sets a heart on fire. If man convinced him into ministry, man would have convinced him out.

The call is not the microphone, authorship, or notoriety. He will tell you what he thinks. He wants to handle the Word passionately and walk with humble transparency that comes with a new heart. Jesus washed the past, gives joy in the present, hope for the future. Subpar speaker who studies like a madman. Called to preach Christ crucified, holes in his body, walking out of a borrowed tomb. Restless for those who do not know the risen Christ reigns and will judge. Glorified wedding planner getting the bride ready.

excerpts: He reads Ezekiel 1:1-3. Thirtieth year, fourth month, fifth day, among the exiles by the Kebar. Heavens opened, visions of God. Fifth year of Jehoiachin’s exile. Word came to Ezekiel the priest, son of Buzi. The hand of the Lord was on him.

Author of Ezekiel? Ezekiel. Like Jeremiah and Zechariah, a priest. Name means God will strengthen or harden. Those three the only prophet-priests, spokesmen to exiles in Babylon. Rebuke sin, expose idolatry, reveal glorious future. Called at thirty from priest to prophet.

Brad last week got him thinking of men who marked him: Joe, Dan, Bob, preachers like John or Voddie. Ezekiel born 622 BC, grew up listening to Jeremiah. Daniel and Ezekiel likely knew each other before exile.

Jeremiah said seventy years. Settle, raise families, plant gardens. False prophets shaved years off. Changing minds is hard. Parable of the sower: pull weeds before planting. 2 Corinthians 10: demolish arguments. Twofold ministry: judgment on defiant Judah and nations, then encouragement that God would restore his people and the glory of his kingdom.

Millennial who ran Ezekiel 1 through an AI image creator, twenty prompts, none fully honored the text. That is the point. Nothing can represent what Ezekiel saw.

documents.excerpt: Exile mindset in Psalm 74: why have you rejected us? Remember Abraham. Were they still chosen? Did he not punch Pharaoh? Jerusalem under enemy control, temple robbed. First lesson: no matter how bad, God is still on the throne. He has never failed a promise.
excerpts: Exile mindset in Psalm 74: why have you rejected us? Remember Abraham. Were they still chosen? Did he not punch Pharaoh? Jerusalem under enemy control, temple robbed. First lesson: no matter how bad, God is still on the throne. He has never failed a promise.

Where is God in the darkest moments? On his throne. At least twenty-five times Ezekiel says like and likeness. Glory is unpaintable. Kavod means weight. Eyes on the wheels: omniscience. Pair with omnipresence. If you want a God you can figure out, you will have to make one up. Ocean in a flask.

Ezekiel fell face down, then heard. Humble, surrendered, worship. If God works anything good it starts face down. Isaiah: woe is me. Jacob’s limp, Moses’ veil, Daniel fainted, Paul’s thorn. You have seen glory if you have been knocked down a peg.

Before glory: what have you done for me lately. Churches full of people who want the gift, not him. After: pray because they love to talk, read to be taught, obey to please. God glorifies God through you. Gethsemane: your will be done. Greatest command: love God, love neighbor.

excerpts: Luke 4: Jesus led into the wilderness, tempted three times—bread, kingdoms, temple. He answered from Deuteronomy, Moses reminding Israel who God is. Returned to Galilee, taught, praised. In Nazareth he took Isaiah’s scroll and declared himself anointed.

He reads Luke 4:18-21: good news to the poor, freedom, sight, the year of the Lord’s favor. Today this Scripture is fulfilled. They spoke well of him. Isn’t this Joseph’s son? He cuts them off: physician heal yourself; no prophet accepted in his hometown. Elijah sent to a widow in Zarephath, not Israel’s widows. Elisha cleansed none of Israel’s lepers, only Naaman the Syrian. The synagogue became furious, drove him to the brow of the hill to throw him off. He walked through the crowd.
First reaction: amazement. Then fury at a Gentile getting healed. Who is this Naaman, and why did first-century Jews try to kill Jesus for naming him?

excerpts: 2 Kings 5: Naaman, commander of Aram near Damascus, Gentile enemy, raider who takes captives. Great man, valiant, but leprosy. A young girl from Israel serves his wife: if only my master would see the prophet in Samaria. She is trying to help him after what his army did. The king of Aram sends a letter and a fortune in silver, gold, and clothes. Israel’s king tears his robes: am I God? Elisha: have the man come, he will know there is a prophet in Israel.

Naaman stops at Elisha’s door. A messenger: wash seven times in the Jordan. He leaves angry. He wanted the prophet to come out, call on the Lord, wave a hand. Abana and Pharpar are better. Rage over extra work—like dishes beside the sink, slow walkers, loud chewers, no turn signal. Servants: my father, if he had told you a great thing would you not have done it? He dips seven times. Flesh like a young boy.

The king of Aram sends a letter and a fortune in silver, gold, and clothes. Israel’s king tears his robes: am I God? Elisha: have the man come, he will know there is a prophet in Israel.
Naaman stops at Elisha’s door. A messenger: wash seven times in the Jordan. He leaves angry. He wanted the prophet to come out, call on the Lord, wave a hand. Abana and Pharpar are better. Rage over extra work—like dishes beside the sink, slow walkers, loud chewers, no turn signal. Servants: my father, if he had told you a great thing would you not have done it? He dips seven times. Flesh like a young boy.

documents.excerpt: Two people jump out. First, the wife’s servant: captured, family maybe dead, village destroyed, dignity gone. You might blame the raiders, Naaman’s family, even God. Unshakable: her God, not his gods, can heal even someone her sinner heart might not want healed. She does not stay quiet or celebrate misery. It bursts out to her mistress.

Nazareth later recognizes the carpenter’s son and his family but takes offense when he returns teaching with wisdom and power. Chris asks listeners to consider their own ordinary sphere of influence.

No room anticipates Jesus’ rejection. Narrow cloth strips and a stone manger make the living infant resemble a burial scene—arrival foreshadowing the death and resurrection he came to accomplish.
The Lamb of God arrives. Joseph is told to name him Jesus because he saves from sin; the Son of Man’s authority to forgive confirms that God has come in flesh.

Calling Jesus the light of the world, he asks God to open eyes, hearts, and minds so hearers believe, then entrusts the response to God’s will.

The law exposes sin but cannot save. Jesus lived perfectly, paid sin’s penalty, and sends the Spirit to remake people. Chris asks whether confusion about rebirth is keeping anyone from giving life to Christ.
documents.title: God’s wisdom and the meaning of new birth — Born Again?

documents.excerpt: Josh pauses before James because prayer cannot be understood without considering who receives it. God is the one living God, Maker of heaven and earth, eternal, immutable, independent, wise, holy, free, absolute, loving, gracious, merciful, truthful, righteous, providential, all-seeing, and Judge. God is not distant: like a father, he works in his people according to his unchanging will. God reveals himself as Father, Son, and Spirit—coequal and coeternal. excerpts: Josh pauses before James because prayer cannot be understood without considering who receives it. God is the one living God, Maker of heaven and earth, eternal, immutable, independent, wise, holy, free, absolute, loving, gracious, merciful, truthful, righteous, providential, all-seeing, and Judge. God is not distant: like a father, he works in his people according to his unchanging will. God reveals himself as Father, Son, and Spirit—coequal and coeternal. Josh insists that one cannot claim to know God while rejecting the Son.

Josh develops Christ’s eternal identity and incarnation. Jesus was not created; the Son already existed before his virgin conception. John 1 presents the Word as with God, as God, the agent of creation, and then as flesh dwelling among humanity. Josh cascades through biblical names and titles for Jesus to stress that no single title exhausts his glory.
The doctrinal detour is deliberate: at 07:03 Josh anticipates the question, “What does this have to do with James?” and answers, “Everything. You can’t apply James unless you know who God is.”

He moves from incarnation to atonement. The sinless Christ was made sin for sinners, bore sin on the cross, paid sin’s wage, declared the work finished, and secured redemption and forgiveness through his blood. The weekly Lord’s Supper physically reminds the church how far God went to save sinners.

He presents the cross as God’s wisdom outmaneuvering evil. Satan’s apparent victory became the means of his defeat; the serpent struck Christ’s heel and had his own head crushed. The rulers crucified the Lord of glory because they did not understand God’s wisdom; the cross was a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles.

Josh turns gospel proclamation into immediate response. He quotes Romans 10 and asks whether the church believes Jesus is Messiah and Son of God and will cry out for salvation. He quotes Jesus’ warning about public acknowledgment, asks professing believers to stand, and then asks first-time confessors to remain standing. A congregant responds; Josh celebrates, offers baptism that day, and urges immediate public testimony in the water.

He says receiving God’s wisdom requires a renewed mind because the gospel works through paradox: life through death, victory through defeat, and the Lion triumphing as a Lamb. Rahab becomes his illustration: a condemned Canaanite prostitute is rescued from Jericho, joined to God’s people, and becomes a picture of redemption. This gospel celebration transitions back to prayer: if the church truly believes God is this great, its prayer life should show it.

The doctrinal detour is deliberate: at 07:03 Josh anticipates the question, “What does this have to do with James?” and answers, “Everything. You can’t apply James unless you know who God is.”
He moves from incarnation to atonement. The sinless Christ was made sin for sinners, bore sin on the cross, paid sin’s wage, declared the work finished, and secured redemption and forgiveness through his blood. The weekly Lord’s Supper physically reminds the church how far God went to save sinners.
He presents the cross as God’s wisdom outmaneuvering evil. Satan’s apparent victory became the means of his defeat; the serpent struck Christ’s heel and had his own head crushed. The rulers crucified the Lord of glory because they did not understand God’s wisdom; the cross was a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles.
Josh turns gospel proclamation into immediate response. He quotes Romans 10 and asks whether the church believes Jesus is Messiah and Son of God and will cry out for salvation. He quotes Jesus’ warning about public acknowledgment, asks professing believers to stand, and then asks first-time confessors to remain standing. A congregant responds; Josh celebrates, offers baptism that day, and urges immediate public testimony in the water.
He says receiving God’s wisdom requires a renewed mind because the gospel works through paradox: life through death, victory through defeat, and the Lion triumphing as a Lamb. Rahab becomes his illustration: a condemned Canaanite prostitute is rescued from Jericho, joined to God’s people, and becomes a picture of redemption. This gospel celebration transitions back to prayer: if the church truly believes God is this great, its prayer life should show it.
documents.title: Prayer begins with the greatness of the triune God and the gospel of Jesus — Christian Care

documents.excerpt: Trouble: “Is anyone among you in trouble? Let them pray.” Josh notes that some translations use “afflicted,” but prefers “in trouble” because it captures the broad range of suffering believers are guaranteed to face. Prayer is the first responder to a believer’s fire. The believer may ask for removal, but should also ask for wisdom to understand the trouble and use it for God’s glory. God may remove it or provide grace to endure it. Jesus in Gethsemane illustrates a request not granted in the requested form: the cup remained, but the Father supplied strength for the cross. Simon of Cyrene and Hebrews 4 reinforce grace arriving in the time of need. Josh challenges resentment toward God when believers neglect the grace already supplied for endurance.

Let them pray.” Josh notes that some translations use “afflicted,” but prefers “in trouble” because it captures the broad range of suffering believers are guaranteed to face. Simon of Cyrene and Hebrews 4 reinforce grace arriving in the time of need. Josh challenges resentment toward God when believers neglect the grace already supplied for endurance.

Happiness: “Is anyone happy? Let them sing songs of praise.” Happiness and trouble can coexist. Anyone can sing after trouble ends; maturity sings while grief is still heavy. Paul and Silas praying and singing in prison show that other people hear a Christian’s “night song” and “prison prayers.” Josh asks who has heard the congregation’s. Believers must not credit themselves for happiness and blame God for trouble. Relationship with God remains intimate in both trouble and peace.
Prayer and praise as church health: when either is neglected, complaining and grumbling fill the space. Praise itself is prayer; the church had already sung three prayers that morning.

Public posture and witness: Josh contrasts careful prayer posture with reluctance to lift hands in surrendered praise. In an airport after his stepfather’s celebration of life, Josh prayed over a meal with his family. A stranger later told his children to thank God for a father willing to lead them in faith. The story illustrates the “quiet witness of public faithfulness.” Fear of others’ opinions must not turn worship into convenience rather than devotion.
Transition: Paul’s command to devoted, watchful, thankful prayer introduces James’s instructions for the sick.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · November 24, 2025 · James : A Faith That Works
documents.excerpt: Josh reads the instruction for the sick to call the church’s elders, receive prayer and anointing with oil in the Lord’s name, and trust the Lord to raise them up.
excerpts: Josh reads the instruction for the sick to call the church’s elders, receive prayer and anointing with oil in the Lord’s name, and trust the Lord to raise them up.

He slows down to define “sick.” The Greek term can denote weakness in several senses, but Josh judges physical illness to be primary here, without excluding spiritual weakness. His jokes about being “sick” of Chiefs championships and lazy men illustrate the range of ordinary word usage.

He examines anointing with oil. Mark 6 supplies the only other New Testament example of the same practice; Luke 10 depicts oil poured medicinally on the wounded man. His synthesis is prayer and medicine: Christian care brings both spiritual and natural resources and seeks to meet both spiritual and physical needs. This is not a foolproof technique. Josh has witnessed what he considers miraculous healing through prayer without oil, heard of healing through non-elders, prayed for relatives who nevertheless died of cancer, and prayed with elders for another cancer patient whose cancer disappeared inexplicably.

He stresses whom the sick person should call. James says the local church’s elders, not a celebrity faith healer. Elders carry responsibility for souls; a sick believer may be physically unable to pray, spiritually frustrated, isolated, or in need of help and confession. Josh rejects commercial or theatrical substitutes—blessing blankets, white coats, blowing, spitting, or special water—and names Crossroads’ elders as the people members should contact. Members may call Josh, who will arrange the group.
Transition: verse 16 exposes the confession component that popular discussions of healing often avoid.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · November 24, 2025 · James : A Faith That Works
documents.excerpt: Josh reads James 5:15b–16: forgiveness, mutual confession, mutual prayer, healing, and the powerful prayer of a righteous person belong together.
excerpts: Josh reads James 5:15b–16: forgiveness, mutual confession, mutual prayer, healing, and the powerful prayer of a righteous person belong together.
He emphasizes the condition in 1 John 1:9: if believers confess, God forgives and purifies.

Josh believes James is describing at least one situation in which sickness is connected to sin. He recounts one hospitalized man who reported an immediate physical release and healing during Josh’s phone prayer. The man apparently confessed to God but not to Josh or the elders, returned to the same lifestyle without accountability, and later became much worse. Josh connects the outcome to Jesus’ warning about an expelled unclean spirit returning with others and assigns Matthew 12 as homework.
Paul’s warning in 1 Corinthians 11 confirms that weakness, sickness, and even death can be divine discipline, intended to prevent final condemnation with the world.
Elders may therefore need to visit someone too ill, shut in, or isolated to come to church and confess.

The conclusion is explicit: God’s healing ministry cannot be disconnected from humble confession. Confession and prayer open the door to healing grace; sin’s grip loosens, heaviness lifts, and the Spirit has room to restore hearts and, at times, bodies.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · November 24, 2025 · James : A Faith That Works
documents.excerpt: Josh returns to James 5:15: “the prayer offered in faith” and “the Lord will raise them up.”
excerpts: Josh returns to James 5:15: “the prayer offered in faith” and “the Lord will raise them up.”

The agent of healing is clarified. The anointing does not heal; God does. Oil represents an ordinary medicinal resource, while prayer calls for God’s decisive touch. God can heal with or without oil or any particular minister, in whatever manner and timing he wills. Josh rejects healers who center their own résumé or claim the title that belongs to God. In his judgment, such ministries often produce more confusion than healing.

He confronts the claim that faith means having no doubt. In the imagined hospital room, the sick person is told that healing depends on eliminating doubt; if healing does not occur, suspicion, blame, and gossip follow. The father in Mark 9 openly combines belief with unbelief, exposing the cruelty of making perfect psychological certainty the condition.

Josh defines a prayer of faith as a desire for God’s will, not the absence of doubt. First John 5 grounds confidence in asking according to God’s will. Faith confidently expects God’s will to be accomplished while still making concrete requests.

His staff’s ninety-minute prayer meeting illustrates this posture: they asked for servant-hearted workers, protection for growing families and children, and unity in the body, while admitting uncertainty about the coming year.
At sickbeds Josh often does not know whether God means to heal or call his child home. His simple prayer is, “Lord, if it is your will, heal your child.”

He rejects the assertion that healing is always God’s will. Faith instead asks for joy and a way to glorify God in any outcome, ending with love and trust: “Whatever happens, Lord, I love you and I trust you.”

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · November 24, 2025 · James : A Faith That Works
documents.excerpt: James 5:16b–18 declares righteous prayer powerful and effective, then presents Elijah as a human being like everyone else whose prayers stopped and restarted the rain.
excerpts: James 5:16b–18 declares righteous prayer powerful and effective, then presents Elijah as a human being like everyone else whose prayers stopped and restarted the rain.

Josh retells Elijah’s story. Ahab and Jezebel led Israel into Baal worship; Elijah prayed for drought. On Mount Carmel he mocked Baal’s prophets, prayed, and God answered with fire, proving the Lord to be the living God. Elijah then prayed seven times for rain, and God sent it. Yet this prophet was not superhuman or perfect: after Carmel he became afraid, discouraged, and fled. His confidence rested in God’s faithfulness, not his own steadiness.

“Prayed earnestly” concerns the attitude rather than the sheer quantity or length of words. Jesus rejects pagan babbling. Josh describes Elijah’s “prayers having prayers”: a continual state of prayerful fellowship, request, and awareness of God.
Refrain: “If you’re not asking, you’re not really praying.”

Josh calls prayer the world’s greatest power—greater than political, economic, military, social, cultural, or religious power—and laments that the church holds this weapon while acting like an underdog.

Applications widen from personal healing to public intercession: pray for the nation and its leaders, including opponents; pray for and encourage younger generations rather than merely criticizing them; let prayers attest to the same greatness of God that Christian theology proclaims.
Paul’s instruction to Timothy confirms petitions, prayers, intercession, and thanksgiving for everyone and for rulers, toward peaceful and godly life and God’s saving purpose.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · November 24, 2025 · James : A Faith That Works
documents.excerpt: Josh reads the final two verses: bringing back one who wanders from truth saves from death and covers many sins.
excerpts: Josh reads the final two verses: bringing back one who wanders from truth saves from death and covers many sins.
For a series about doing the Word, James ends with perhaps the greatest action one believer can take for another: restoration, or “the opportunity to be Jesus to the already redeemed.”

Wandering can be a slow backslide or a sudden face-plant, but the mission is the same. Seek another’s restoration with the same urgency one would want shown toward oneself. Josh applies this to addiction, disruption, unforgiveness, and division. Refusing to speak truth in love leaves others exposed to further harm.

Ecclesiastes warns that one sinner destroys much good. Concerns should reach the elders before someone leaves or disaster occurs. Josh welcomes concerns but says the church’s job is to prevent a train wreck, not watch it happen and later announce that it was predictable. Restoration requires hard conversations; sometimes believers need to be “converted” or witnessed to by their own church.
Jesus’ care for Peter supplies the model: he prayed for Peter, spoke hard truth, and commissioned the restored disciple to strengthen his brothers.

The church sometimes must “seek and save the found,” always in love. Peter later teaches that deep love covers many sins. Love does not sweep sin under a family rug; love cannot exist without truth. Honest confession permits God’s purification and complete forgiveness.

Josh intensifies the appeal from wandering believers to unbelievers. If rescuing a believer matters, rescuing one whose future apart from Christ is hell is even more urgent. Because the devil aggressively prowls for prey and sin pays death, believers must pursue a deliberate gospel battle plan; God’s gift remains eternal life in Christ.

Final diagnostic questions: When did the hearer last take a social or cultural risk to present the gift? When did the hearer last confess, receive forgiveness, ask God to reveal someone to serve, pray over that ministry, and then show up to work?
Transition: the church must “grow up and start looking alive,” which leads into an embodied response rather than a merely verbal conclusion.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · November 24, 2025 · James : A Faith That Works
documents.excerpt: Josh uses a football stadium to reject a spectator model of church: 50,000 people watching eleven performers is not the church.
excerpts: Josh uses a football stadium to reject a spectator model of church: 50,000 people watching eleven performers is not the church.

James invites believers onto the field to walk by the Spirit. Josh gives a threefold response: At home: pray for the lost and the church’s mission, enter the Word, and actively kill sin. Out there: invite people to church and share one’s testimony, practicing first in a life group if needed. In the church: serve children and youth, encourage believers, meet needs through Crossroads Cares, become a need coordinator, give financially, or serve in café, tech, worship, and gospel ministry.
The Great Commission is carried out not by God’s “elite” but by God’s elect. Jesus said the workers—not spectators—are few; kingdom work requires belonging to him, not being exceptional.
Josh invites the church to offer God life, hands, time, gifts, home, heart, and wealth because the harvest is ready.

During the response song, members are to be the church: sign up through the app; seek the elders for prayer if ill or struggling; participate through the Lord’s Supper, singing, possible baptism, giving, and service.
Closing maxim: people will not see the church differently until believers see it differently. “The church does not exist to serve you. It exists so you can serve others.”

Closing prayer (44:32–46:38): Josh repents first for his own shallow prayer life before the great, living God. He asks God to change hearts, free people from shame, grant courage to confess, and grant gentleness to answer confession with grace. He invites the Spirit’s work through song, prayer, giving, service, baptism, and oil, asking for spiritual and physical healing according to God’s will.

Communion meditation (46:40–47:50): Communion is presented not merely as ritual but as a pattern for life: in trouble, pray, because God meets people amid struggle, doubt, and pain. Bread and cup proclaim Christ’s body and blood given for forgiveness and healing. Unbelievers should refrain and consider Christ’s call; believers should name what they must bring to God, then continue in daily prayer, trust, and community rather than leaving the response at the table.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · November 17, 2025 · James : A Faith That Works
documents.excerpt: Josh reconnects the sermon to the preceding treatment of James 4:13–17: Christians must stop planning as though God does not exist and instead live in humble dependence on him. He frames James’s recurring series-wide rebuke as a call for Christians to grow up, stop pointing fingers and making excuses, and receive life as God’s means of growth. The proud planner says where he will go and what he will do; James exposes that independence as evil because no one reaches the destination apart from God’s will.
excerpts: Josh reconnects the sermon to the preceding treatment of James 4:13–17: Christians must stop planning as though God does not exist and instead live in humble dependence on him. He frames James’s recurring series-wide rebuke as a call for Christians to grow up, stop pointing fingers and making excuses, and receive life as God’s means of growth. The proud planner says where he will go and what he will do; James exposes that independence as evil because no one reaches the destination apart from God’s will.

Josh says the same pride, greed, arrogance, and independence are especially tempting to the rich. Money reveals whether professed love for Christ is genuine. The independent heart asks why it needs God when it can provide for itself. Materialism from the surrounding culture is seeping into the church, so a faithful pastor must confront it rather than avoid a difficult subject.

He announces the opening address of the day’s text: “Now listen, you rich people.” These people are not merely prosperous; they obtained and retained wealth selfishly by harming others. A joke—“If money talks, all it ever says to me is goodbye”—contrasts ordinary financial frustration with the affluent oppressors James addresses.

Josh previews the final chapter’s two themes: trouble now and prayer in the following week. Together they show that mature believers pray in trouble and endure by asking God for help; immature people simply muscle through in self-reliance.

He carefully distinguishes wealth from sin. Abraham was wealthy and walked with God; the danger is that wealth makes humble dependence difficult. Josh cites the Bible’s extensive attention to money and possessions to argue that wealth can obstruct spiritual growth and entrance into God’s kingdom. Scripture is not fixated on account balances but on the way possessions shape the heart. Joseph of Arimathea is his clearest narrative example of a wealthy person serving God: he prepared Jesus’ body for burial. Proverbs 10:22 and Deuteronomy 8:18 establish that God may give wealth and gives the ability to produce it; wealth becomes a problem when the recipient forgets the giver.
Transition: Josh will read six verses and use them to expose areas where the congregation may be out of balance.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · November 17, 2025 · James : A Faith That Works
documents.excerpt: Josh reads James 5:1–6 in full. Wealth rots, clothing is moth-eaten, and gold and silver corrode. The corrosion testifies against the rich because they hoarded in the last days. Unpaid wages and the harvesters’ cries reach the Lord Almighty. The rich lived in luxury and self-indulgence, fattened themselves for slaughter, and condemned and murdered the innocent.
excerpts: Josh reads James 5:1–6 in full. Wealth rots, clothing is moth-eaten, and gold and silver corrode. The corrosion testifies against the rich because they hoarded in the last days. Unpaid wages and the harvesters’ cries reach the Lord Almighty. The rich lived in luxury and self-indulgence, fattened themselves for slaughter, and condemned and murdered the innocent.
He identifies two controlling issues for the first half of the sermon: How they acquired wealth. How they utilized wealth.

Before listeners dismiss this as another message about money, Josh stresses the urgency. Paul places greed beside sexual immorality, idolatry, slander, drunkenness, and swindling and tells the church not even to eat with a professed believer who persists in such sin. Greed therefore demands repentance just as adultery does; it is not a respectable lesser sin.

Josh leads a practical self-examination: Are you content with what you have, even if you now have less than before? Does a credit-card balance reveal habitual purchases you cannot afford—having “blessed yourself into debt”? Is your joy centered on what you receive or increasingly on what you can give? When work competes with worship, family, and church, which priority wins?
Proverbs 11:28 warns that those who trust riches will fall. Josh’s purpose is pastoral: he does not want his brothers and sisters to fall.

Jesus explains why divided allegiance fails: no one can serve both God and money. Josh then quotes Matthew 6:19–21: earthly treasures decay and can be stolen, but heavenly treasures endure; the location of one’s treasure exposes the location of one’s heart.

James 5:1–6 and the heart diagnostic of greed

Unpaid wages and the harvesters’ cries reach the Lord Almighty. The rich lived in luxury and self-indulgence, fattened themselves for slaughter, and condemned and murdered the innocent.
He identifies two controlling issues for the first half of the sermon: How they acquired wealth. How they utilized wealth.
Before listeners dismiss this as another message about money, Josh stresses the urgency. Paul places greed beside sexual immorality, idolatry, slander, drunkenness, and swindling and tells the church not even to eat with a professed believer who persists in such sin. Greed therefore demands repentance just as adultery does; it is not a respectable lesser sin.
Josh leads a practical self-examination: Are you content with what you have, even if you now have less than before? Does a credit-card balance reveal habitual purchases you cannot afford—having “blessed yourself into debt”? Is your joy centered on what you receive or increasingly on what you can give? documents.excerpt: Josh addresses an interpretive objection: because James’s warning is so severe, some claim it cannot be directed toward people in the church. Josh argues that James knew his letter would circulate among churches and also knew that many people claim to be Christians without possessing humble dependence on Christ. excerpts: Josh addresses an interpretive objection: because James’s warning is so severe, some claim it cannot be directed toward people in the church. Josh argues that James knew his letter would circulate among churches and also knew that many people claim to be Christians without possessing humble dependence on Christ. Some sermons gather crowds; others thin them. Even if James is confronting wealthy pretenders within the church, every listener must heed the warning lest the same trap capture them.
Josh returns to James 5:3–5 to show the chain of sin: They hoarded wealth. They withheld workers’ wages. They used the proceeds to live in luxury and self-indulgence.

Amos supplies the prophetic parallel. The affluent trampled the needy, commercialized the Sabbath, used dishonest scales, and cheated people out of hard-earned money. Josh translates “selling on the Sabbath” into a contemporary example: using church chiefly to promote one’s business. Amos’s judgment—festivals turned to mourning and songs to weeping—shows why James speaks so fiercely: God will shut down the party. Josh’s summary: praising the almighty dollar dishonors Almighty God.

The rebuke creates concrete workplace obligations for Christians and Christian businesses. Do not oppress workers. Pay them on time. Deal honestly and with integrity because employees depend on their wages. Leviticus 19:13 forbids fraud, robbery, and withholding a worker’s wages overnight. Jeremiah 22:13 pronounces woe on the person who builds through injustice and unpaid labor.
A humorous “Model S chariot with custom seat warmers” pictures the absurdity of defrauding workers to finance luxury.

Josh presses the church’s public witness: how can Christians reach people after robbing them? Echoing 1 Corinthians 5, he says the church must remove unrepentant evil because greedy professing Christians damage the reputation of generous believers. His intentionally severe pastoral warning is that anyone who makes money number one and refuses to repent should worship that god elsewhere; the gospel is too important and the time too urgent for the church to shelter the wicked rich.
Application: put God first regardless of income and trust him to supply what is needed.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · November 17, 2025 · James : A Faith That Works
documents.excerpt: Josh turns from unjust acquisition to misuse, repeating James 5:3: “You have hoarded wealth in the last days.” He calls hoarding one of the most overlooked sins of the day. God entrusts material goods to believers so those goods will be used for God’s glory.
excerpts: Josh turns from unjust acquisition to misuse, repeating James 5:3: “You have hoarded wealth in the last days.” He calls hoarding one of the most overlooked sins of the day. God entrusts material goods to believers so those goods will be used for God’s glory.

He distinguishes responsible saving from sinful hoarding. First Timothy 5:8 requires provision for relatives and one’s household. In the parable of the talents, Jesus rebukes the servant who buried the money and says even bank interest would have been preferable. Planning and saving for the future are not sins; motive determines the difference. Holding resources for legitimate family provision is saving. Accumulating merely to possess, boast, gain clout, secure an image, or feel significant is hoarding.

The plastic-wrapped couch becomes Josh’s main illustration. A couch exists to provide a place of rest, not to be preserved so completely that no one can use it. Rather than protecting it from children and grandchildren, sit with them and tell them what Jesus has done. The illustration turns stewardship from preservation toward meaningful, gospel-shaped purpose.

He then applies the same principle to an overfilled walk-in closet. The clothing itself is not automatically the problem; the owner’s attitude toward it is. The imagined house fire tests whether the possessions have become a source of identity requiring grief counseling. James’s rich guarded food, money, and clothing for security and status while walking past unclothed people.
Josh notes that Jerusalem fell to Rome about fifteen years after James wrote: accumulated treasure proved temporary.

He rejects a simplistic command that everyone must sell everything. A believer may do so if called, but must still care for family. Laying up treasure in heaven means good stewardship and viewing possessions through an eternal lens. Jesus’ command to the rich young ruler exposed that man’s ruling sin; Josh says it was not a universal prescription for identical behavior.

Josh asks the room to imagine the congregation’s combined net worth. The likely surprise leads to his central stewardship claim: the church possesses many things but owns nothing; God owns everything, and believers manage the “divine family trust.” Therefore, use what you have for God’s glory and trust his provision.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · November 17, 2025 · James : A Faith That Works
documents.excerpt: Josh identifies the final hazard in James 5:5: luxury. He acknowledges that luxury differs greatly between first-century Jerusalem and the modern world.
excerpts: Josh identifies the final hazard in James 5:5: luxury. He acknowledges that luxury differs greatly between first-century Jerusalem and the modern world.

The Antilia residence in Mumbai supplies the extreme illustration. Josh describes its 27 stories, roughly 400,000 square feet, $2 billion construction cost, 168-car garage, theater, snow room, pools, spa, health-care center, floating gardens, and temple. The joke about the owner having these things “because he can” exposes capacity detached from necessity.

Josh does not condemn enjoying God’s gifts or owning a comfortable home. The moral question is whether an alleged “need” is extravagant while someone else lacks something basic. Jesus’ warning in Luke 12:15—life does not consist in abundant possessions—sets the standard.
Josh contrasts suffering and luxury: if suffering produces character, unchecked luxury can ruin it.

James 5:6 shows how far the lifestyle can go. The rich used courts to silence and destroy the poor people they had defrauded. Such conduct has no place in the church; persistent, unrepentant exploiters must be removed and left to the Lord’s judgment.

Application: Enjoy what God has given, but never at another person’s expense. The scale of unmet need leaves no justification for waste. Every dollar, possession, and gift must serve God’s purposes. James says corroded wealth will stand as evidence at judgment; Josh adds that not only wasted words but wasted resources will be counted.
Transition: James moves from the destruction of greed to the power of patience.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · November 17, 2025 · James : A Faith That Works
documents.excerpt: Josh reads James 5:7–8: believers must patiently stand firm until the Lord’s coming, as a farmer waits for the valuable crop and seasonal rains.
excerpts: Josh reads James 5:7–8: believers must patiently stand firm until the Lord’s coming, as a farmer waits for the valuable crop and seasonal rains.

He names Christ’s return as the Christian’s blessed hope across two millennia. Until all things are made new, believers patiently endure heartache, loss, trial, tribulation, and trouble. This opposes the demand for instant gratification both outside and inside the church.

Two jokes about children thinking milk comes from the fridge by DoorDash and farmers should buy vegetables at Walmart expose cultural distance from agricultural patience. Crops do not appear overnight. Farmers cannot control rain, sun, early winter, or the precise timing of harvest. They must remain patient and prepared.

Josh explains why believers can become impatient by reading Revelation 21:1–5. John sees the new heaven, new earth, holy city, and God dwelling with his people. God wipes away every tear; death, mourning, crying, and pain end; the enthroned One makes everything new.

Josh responds personally to that promise. It fills his thoughts at the Lord’s Supper and when watching a sunset. All suffering moves toward the marriage supper of the Lamb: a real feast and joyful, everlasting union of Jesus the bridegroom with his bride, the church. Cana offers only a preview of the celebration to come.
Therefore, believers should hold tight. Josh does not know when Christ will return, but trusts the divine guarantee and is willing to give everything for it.

Returning to the farmer image, Josh says God is cultivating the Spirit’s fruit in his people for a coming harvest. Growth requires rainy, dry, cold, and hot days—hardship and trials. Rather than becoming impatient with God or one another, Christians must trust God with their lives, watch the fruit grow, and spur one another toward fruit that honors him.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · November 17, 2025 · James : A Faith That Works
documents.excerpt: A farmer does not stand around staring at the sky; he keeps working toward the harvest. Josh connects this to Acts 1: the disciples were not allowed to remain staring upward after Jesus’ ascension. The returning Christ is the reason to work, not an excuse for passivity. His compact charge is: keep working while you wait; witness and worship while you wait.
excerpts: A farmer does not stand around staring at the sky; he keeps working toward the harvest. Josh connects this to Acts 1: the disciples were not allowed to remain staring upward after Jesus’ ascension. The returning Christ is the reason to work, not an excuse for passivity. His compact charge is: keep working while you wait; witness and worship while you wait.

Farmers also model neighborly cooperation. When one person’s tractor fails, the community helps rather than passing by. Josh recalls visiting his farmer uncle during harvest and seeing the entire community rally around the work.

The church must practice the same patience with one another. Impatience with God becomes impatience with people. Fighting one another can prevent completion of God’s assigned work. Josh quotes James 5:9: do not grumble against one another, or you will be judged; the Judge stands at the door.
Josh says every believer is “a handful,” but Satan tempts each one to regard somebody else as the real problem. Muttering about others devours Christian effectiveness.

C. S. Lewis’s The Screwtape Letters becomes the extended illustration. Screwtape tells Wormwood not to despair when the “patient” becomes a Christian because the visible local church can become a demonic ally. The new Christian cannot yet see the church across time and eternity as a terrible army with banners; he sees an unfinished building and ordinary neighbors he previously avoided. Off-key singing, squeaky boots, double chins, and odd clothing make faith seem ridiculous when the convert fixates on surface defects. Disappointment with imperfect church people can turn professed humility into condescension.
Josh applies Lewis directly: looking for fellow believers’ weaknesses and grumbling about them ruins patient endurance and plays into the devil’s hand.
He closes the movement by returning to James 5:9: everyone is unfinished, the true Judge is at the door, and until he comes believers must watch their mouths.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · November 17, 2025 · James : A Faith That Works
documents.excerpt: Josh reads James 5:10–11. The prophets who spoke in the Lord’s name model patience in suffering. Those who persevere are called blessed. Job’s perseverance reveals that the Lord is full of compassion and mercy.
excerpts: Josh reads James 5:10–11. The prophets who spoke in the Lord’s name model patience in suffering. Those who persevere are called blessed. Job’s perseverance reveals that the Lord is full of compassion and mercy.

The prophets matter because they suffered while obeying God. Faithful preaching brought persecution, undermining the assumption that suffering necessarily reveals sin. Paul tells Timothy that everyone desiring a godly life in Christ will be persecuted. Jesus’ obedience led to the cross; suffering can therefore be a result of faithfulness rather than disobedience.

Josh gives Jeremiah as the detailed example. Jeremiah was arrested as a traitor and lowered into a cistern to die. God preserved and fed him through Jerusalem’s siege. Josh briefly adds Ezekiel and Daniel as sufferers whom the Lord delivered.

He qualifies the promise: not everyone who suffers will be delivered in this life, but those who suffer for Christ will be rewarded. Revelation 22:12 grounds the claim: Jesus is coming soon with his reward and will repay each person according to what he has done.

Josh challenges the congregation to become self-feeding students of Scripture rather than consumers who only arrive to be fed. Romans 15:4 explains that what was written in the past teaches and encourages believers so they may have hope. Like the farmer, keep working; like the prophets, keep preaching.

Job supplies the final pattern. Satan’s intended temptation did not defeat God’s purpose; God provides a way through. Josh pictures Job bruised, sitting in ashes, scraping his sores, and surrounded by unanswered questions. In the end Job saw the Lord—not the wrathful tyrant imagined by his friends or a distant deity unable to sympathize, but the compassionate and merciful Lord.

Application: Do not measure God by pain, emotion, or frustration; measure him by his heart, work, and faithfulness. God is not merely compassionate but full of compassion. Delay and discipline do not mean his heart has grown cold. Josh says Job’s ashes became altars and his tears became testimony; mercy had been working throughout the wait. When prayers seem unheard, do not judge God by life’s shadows or blame him for evil. Wait longer, and God’s mercy will become visible.

documents.excerpt: Josh identifies James 5:12 as the last verse and reads it: do not swear by heaven, earth, or anything else; let a simple yes or no suffice, or face condemnation.
excerpts: Josh identifies James 5:12 as the last verse and reads it: do not swear by heaven, earth, or anything else; let a simple yes or no suffice, or face condemnation.

Though the command may appear disconnected from wealth and patient suffering, Josh supplies the link: Trouble tempts people to say what they do not mean and make commitments they do not sincerely intend to keep.

He clarifies that Scripture does not ban every oath. The problem is deceptive, foolish, or half-hearted swearing. Hebrews records that God himself swore an oath to Abraham. People in James’s setting tried to avoid direct accountability to God by swearing instead by heaven, earth, Jerusalem, or their own heads.

Jesus’ teaching in Matthew 5:34–37 closes that loophole. Heaven is God’s throne, earth his footstool, Jerusalem the great King’s city, and even one’s own hair lies outside personal sovereignty. A truthful person needs only a simple yes or no; manipulative excess comes from the evil one.

Josh develops the contrast between integrity and performance. The genuine do not perform; actors are always trying to persuade. Truth can wait to be found, while falsehood restlessly spins delicate but deadly verbal webs. Integrity needs no stage, but deception must keep acting lest the curtain fall. When Christ rules the heart, simplicity becomes eloquence and one’s word becomes testimony; a divided heart multiplies smoke-like words that cannot bear weight.

He repeats the warning that the Judge stands at the door, then identifies the Judge as Jesus. This is the same Jesus who bore judgment on the cross and rose so mercy would have the final word. The Judge’s nail-scarred hands hold righteousness together with compassion and mercy.

Final invitation: “Come and see” the one who knows people fully and loves them still. Christ’s coming is not terror for those who trust him but the fulfillment they long for. Josh urges the church to remain patient, keep trusting, take heart, and hold on: Christ will reward his people, wipe away tears, right wrongs, and make all things new.

documents.excerpt: In the closing prayer, Josh pictures the woman of John 4. Shame led her to draw water at a time when she could avoid others. Multiple failed marriages and her present unmarried relationship left her expecting rejection. At the well she met not an ordinary man but the God-man. documents.excerpt: Josh opens by revising the series plan in a way that illustrates the day’s text: the church intended ten weeks in James, but week nine has only reached chapter 4. Rather than rush important material merely to launch another series, he scraps the next planned series for now — it will come sometime in 2026 — and welcomes the church to week nine of an eleven-week study.
excerpts: Josh opens by revising the series plan in a way that illustrates the day’s text: the church intended ten weeks in James, but week nine has only reached chapter 4. Rather than rush important material merely to launch another series, he scraps the next planned series for now — it will come sometime in 2026 — and welcomes the church to week nine of an eleven-week study.

He restates James’s recurring contrast: Worldly wisdom is built on human ideas about who God is and how God behaves. Divine wisdom receives God’s self-revelation in his Word and in Jesus Christ. Trying to define God better than God defines himself is audacious arrogance; receiving even what people cannot yet understand is humility.

The transition into the sermon’s subject is logical: people who presume to define God will soon presume to direct God. Those who trust God’s sovereignty, by contrast, cease insisting on an independent will and surrender with a joy greater than their circumstances.

Last week concerned being at war with God; this week concerns God’s will. A person can have peace with God yet resist his will, receive mercy yet reject purpose, possess eternal life yet waste this life, or be redeemed yet refuse faithful risks.

Josh illustrates the damage believers can do outside God’s will: Jonah’s disobedience endangered the sailors (Jonah 1:1–16). Lot’s move toward Sodom exposed his family to wickedness and harm (Genesis 13:10–13). David’s sin with Uriah’s wife brought misery upon his household and kingdom (2 Samuel 11:1–12:14). Peter confessed Jesus as Messiah and later denied knowing him three times (Matthew 16:13–16; 26:57–75).

Because God went to great lengths to save his children, Josh argues, he also has wise purposes for them. God’s ways are above human ways (Isaiah 55:8–9); believers should want to know, obey, and surrender to his will.

Josh announces James 4:13–17 as the primary text and reads the whole unit (James 4:13–17): self-confident merchants plan when and where they will trade and profit, although they do not know tomorrow; human life is a vanishing mist; plans should be conditioned upon the Lord’s will; arrogant boasting is evil; and refusing known good is sin.
He previews the organizing frame: two negative responses to God’s will followed by one positive response.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · November 10, 2025 · James : A Faith That Works
documents.excerpt: To ignore God’s will is to live as if God does not exist, does not care, or has no interest in human affairs. James’s “Now listen” is an urgent demand to pay attention.
excerpts: To ignore God’s will is to live as if God does not exist, does not care, or has no interest in human affairs. James’s “Now listen” is an urgent demand to pay attention.

Reading the passage alongside James’s opening rebuke in chapter 5, Josh understands the audience as prosperous businesspeople inside the church (James 5:1–6). They make strategic plans and measure success by goals and closed deals without praying about God’s purposes or how prosperity might bless God and neighbor.

Josh turns the ancient merchants toward the congregation: today’s planners, dreamers, administrative enthusiasts, and business strategists can commit the same sin. Planning itself is not wrong; the rebuke concerns planning that gives no thought to God.

Their repeated “I will” resembles the proud self-direction attributed to Satan in Isaiah 14:13–14. The merchants choose the time, place, duration, method, and desired profit. Their fault is not what they considered but the decisive reality they omitted.

Jesus’s warning against greed and parable of the rich fool exposes that omission (Luke 12:15–22): The rich man’s fields prosper, so he decides to enlarge his barns, preserve his surplus, and secure years of ease. God calls him a fool and demands his life that very night. Hoarding for oneself is the opposite of being rich toward God, and Jesus immediately warns his disciples not to worry about food or clothing.

Josh presses the parable’s urgency. Greed is more dangerous than a robber because it can take the soul rather than merely the wallet. The world disguises greed as success through screens, feeds, advertisements, and the heart’s demand for more, better, newer, mine, and now.

Possessions—car, savings, house, plans, business, retirement account—cannot satisfy. Josh recalls the miraculous catch and the fishermen’s call: they did not build a barn for the fish because they were called to fish for people (Luke 5:4–11, with Josh’s “other side” wording resembling John 21:6).
Christ, though equal with God, became a servant (Philippians 2:6–7). If the Master served, believers should not crown themselves.

Applications follow in rapid sequence: Answer greed with sufficiency in Christ. Answer fear of loss by remembering that life is not constituted by possessions. Do not spend life building larger barns; invest it in God’s kingdom through generosity, forgiveness, proclamation of Christ, meeting needs, and unconditional love. Josh hopes Christ will commend Crossroads for faithful work, echoing the faithful-servant commendation in Matthew 25:21, 23.

First negative response: ignoring God’s will and living under the illusion of control
To ignore God’s will is to live as if God does not exist, does not care, or has no interest in human affairs. James’s “Now listen” is an urgent demand to pay attention.
Reading the passage alongside James’s opening rebuke in chapter 5, Josh understands the audience as prosperous businesspeople inside the church (James 5:1–6). They make strategic plans and measure success by goals and closed deals without praying about God’s purposes or how prosperity might bless God and neighbor.
Josh turns the ancient merchants toward the congregation: today’s planners, dreamers, administrative enthusiasts, and business strategists can commit the same sin. Planning itself is not wrong; the rebuke concerns planning that gives no thought to God.
Their repeated “I will” resembles the proud self-direction attributed to Satan in Isaiah 14:13–14. The merchants choose the time, place, duration, method, and desired profit. Their fault is not what they considered but the decisive reality they omitted.
Jesus’s warning against greed and parable of the rich fool exposes that omission (Luke 12:15–22): The rich man’s fields prosper, so he decides to enlarge his barns, preserve his surplus, and secure years of ease. God calls him a fool and demands his life that very night. Hoarding for oneself is the opposite of being rich toward God, and Jesus immediately warns his disciples not to worry about food or clothing.
Josh presses the parable’s urgency. Greed is more dangerous than a robber because it can take the soul rather than merely the wallet. The world disguises greed as success through screens, feeds, advertisements, and the heart’s demand for more, better, newer, mine, and now.
Possessions—car, savings, house, plans, business, retirement account—cannot satisfy. Josh recalls the miraculous catch and the fishermen’s call: they did not build a barn for the fish because they were called to fish for people (Luke 5:4–11, with Josh’s “other side” wording resembling John 21:6).
Christ, though equal with God, became a servant (Philippians 2:6–7). If the Master served, believers should not crown themselves.
Applications follow in rapid sequence: Answer greed with sufficiency in Christ. Answer fear of loss by remembering that life is not constituted by possessions. Do not spend life building larger barns; invest it in God’s kingdom through generosity, forgiveness, proclamation of Christ, meeting needs, and unconditional love. Josh hopes Christ will commend Crossroads for faithful work, echoing the faithful-servant commendation in Matthew 25:21, 23.

Proverbs 16:9 supplies the corrective: human hearts plan a course, but the Lord establishes the steps.
What could drive an unbeliever mad becomes comfort for a Christian. The sovereign, omniscient, omnipotent, and loving God controls events and weaves what believers cannot know into his purpose.
Josh quotes Romans 8:28 and emphasizes its stated recipients: the promise belongs to those who love God and are called according to his purpose.

Illustration: after Josh and Kristen had once broken up, he drove nonstop from Los Angeles to Indiana, then ran back to her. At about 3:00 a.m. he encountered Missouri fog so dense that he could not see turns, signs, or even lane markings and had to slow drastically.

The fog pictures human uncertainty, not divine uncertainty. God has no blind spots and does not struggle to see what lies ahead. Confidence about the future therefore comes only through confidence in him.

documents.excerpt: James’s second reason is the brevity of life. Josh repeats James 4:14: human life is a mist that appears briefly and vanishes.
excerpts: James’s second reason is the brevity of life. Josh repeats James 4:14: human life is a mist that appears briefly and vanishes.
Human memory can look backward and make accumulated years feel long, but human beings cannot look forward. Against eternity, life is vapor—steam rising from hot coffee: “Get it while it’s hot.”
Sudden death teaches this brevity with unusual force. Old age can feel like the expected order; a younger death strips away the assumption that much time remains.

Josh invites the congregation to hear Isaiah’s warning to Hezekiah personally: put your house in order because you are going to die (Isaiah 38:1). Death respects neither character, age, optimism, nor experience.

Personal and congregational illustrations make the warning concrete: Josh’s strong, fit stepfather still died from cancer. His sister died at thirty-nine; death did not wait for her fortieth birthday. A woman in the church who had significant health struggles unexpectedly awoke to find that her husband and caregiver had died.

Josh turns to Job for ancient pictures of life’s brevity: Days move faster than a weaver’s shuttle (Job 7:6). A cloud vanishes, and those who descend to the grave do not return (Job 7:9). People were born only yesterday, know nothing, and pass like a shadow (Job 8:9).

Approaching his fortieth birthday, Josh treats birthdays as occasions for reflection rather than merely parties: Is he helping or hurting people? Shepherding well? Using his moments and gifts or wasting them?

God calls for that inventory daily, not yearly: Psalm 90:12 asks God to teach his people to number their days so they may gain wisdom. Psalm 39:4 asks to know life’s end, the number of one’s days, and how fleeting life is.
Josh has calculated that this is day 14,607 of his life—including leap days—but cannot know whether he will see day 14,608 or 28,000.

He confronts a common distortion: people know intellectually that they will die but still assume death is too distant to affect present behavior. Even late in life people tend to calculate in favor of more time and cling to life as it ends.
A wiser question is not why someone else died early but what makes anyone think the same cannot happen to them. Health, weight loss, or avoidance of one disease cannot guarantee freedom from another.

Therefore life and gifts must not merely be used; they must be invested in what has eternal significance. Jesus’s call in Mark 8:34–37 frames the choice as a profit-and-loss statement: deny self, take up the cross, follow Christ, lose life for Christ and the gospel in order to save it, and do not gain the world at the cost of the soul.

When time has been spent, it cannot be purchased back. Josh returns to the coffee image through a humorous household story: Kristen repeatedly reheats coffee, leaves the cup in the microwave, and Josh finds it when warming lunch. He once found it irritating but now sees it as an opportunity to serve her.
Unlike coffee, life cannot be reheated. This is the one opportunity: invite God into the planning and ensure that the planning pleases him.

documents.excerpt: Disobedience is worse than mere neglect. Josh repeats James 4:17: knowing the good one ought to do and refusing to do it is sin.
excerpts: Disobedience is worse than mere neglect. Josh repeats James 4:17: knowing the good one ought to do and refusing to do it is sin.
This attitude says openly, “I know what you want me to do; I just don’t want to do it.” It boasts in control even though control is an illusion.

Josh quotes 2 Peter 2:21–22: it would have been better not to know the way of righteousness than to know it and turn away; the proverb about a dog returning to its vomit makes deliberate apostasy viscerally repulsive. The embedded proverb comes from Proverbs 26:11.

Some disobedience also grows from misunderstanding God’s will. Believers may treat it as an option, but Josh calls it an obligation: God is Lord and Savior; believers were purchased, adopted, and made servants, and therefore must obey.
Obedience is not the enemy of liberty. Ultimate freedom is found within God’s will.

Counseling illustration: cohabiting couples do not usually approach Josh to celebrate a superior form of dating; they arrive in misery and confusion. His diagnosis is that they rejected God’s design and then expected blessing within disobedience. Believers should never expect God to bless either disobedience or discontentment.

Discipline should reassure rather than merely frighten: the Lord disciplines those he loves (Hebrews 12:6). Josh compares it to disciplining his son Nolan—the process is not pleasant, but its motive communicates love.

He rejects the picture of Christian life as miserable rule-keeping. Holiness frees him from intoxication, theft, lies, sexual unfaithfulness, and covetousness; those sins did not make life good. Serving God, giving, and “slaying sin in the name of Jesus” are his joy.

He contrasts earthly pleasure with heavenly treasure (Matthew 6:19–20) and says the crown follows the cross: Satan advertises glory that ends in suffering, whereas God tells the truth about suffering that will be transformed into glory.

Josh attributes his next quotation to Paul’s “second letter to the Corinthians,” but the words are actually 1 Corinthians 9:27: Paul disciplines his body so that, after preaching, he will not be disqualified for the prize. Josh interprets the prize not as salvation but as rewards when the Lord examines believers’ works.

Disobedience has consequences now, at Christ’s return, or both. Whatever faithful believers miss on earth will be more than repaid in the Lord’s presence; therefore they should discipline themselves and await the crown.

He closes the negative responses with Joshua 24:15—choose whom to serve; “as for me and my household, we will serve the Lord”—then connects Joshua’s resolve to James 4:15: “If it is the Lord’s will, we will live and do this or that.”
