documents.excerpt: Against practical atheism and self-sovereignty, James’s positive response is humble dependence.
excerpts: Against practical atheism and self-sovereignty, James’s positive response is humble dependence.
This is not superstition or a one-time phrase attached to plans. It is surrender: persistent, lifelong, daily submission in every decision and season—“Lord, I want what you want.”

James’s brief sentence opens the immense doctrine of sovereignty. Josh moves beyond merely saying God created in Genesis 1: God is not only Creator and uncaused cause but present Sustainer. Creation exists not only because he once spoke but because he continues to uphold it.
Every sunrise, sunset, heartbeat, breath, ruler, household, and even sparrow lies within God’s knowledge and care; the sparrow language echoes Matthew 10:29–31.

Josh presents the mystery of providence: God guides human plans while people make real choices, and divine sovereignty does not destroy creaturely freedom but fulfills it. Rather than fuel factional argument, that mystery should put believers on their knees in worship.
Corruption, disorder, pain, struggle, and life’s storms never occur outside God’s knowledge or control. Even when his action and reasons are hidden, there are no exceptions to his rule.
Like heaven’s elders, the church should declare Revelation 4:11: God is worthy of glory, honor, and power because he created all things and by his will they exist.
“He is worthy of it all” becomes the congregation’s answer. Thoughts, possessions, and treasures all belong to God, even when the world looks chaotic.
Josh then quotes Ephesians 1:11: God works everything in conformity with the purpose of his will.

The Spirit within the redeemed longs to obey. The same hand that orders the universe holds each believer; the wisdom governing governments watches households and hears prayers. Josh returns to Romans 8:28: the sovereign God is working all things for his glory and his people’s good.
He wishes believers lived as though they could see the “cloud of witnesses” behind them (Hebrews 12:1) and the heavenly forces contending for them. Such sight, he suggests, would change their lives.

documents.excerpt: A believer’s stumble does not destroy the relationship. Josh grieves the pattern in which fallen believers cut ties with the church or are effectively cast out.
excerpts: A believer’s stumble does not destroy the relationship. Josh grieves the pattern in which fallen believers cut ties with the church or are effectively cast out.
Paul’s restorative command in Galatians 6:1–2 governs the church’s response: when a Christian is drowning, failing to restore gently and carry the burden also places the observer outside God’s will.
Falling, missing the mark, discipline, and suffering are not the end. Abraham, Jonah, David, and Peter display God’s persistence with faltering saints—what many call the perseverance of the saints.

Growth in God’s will begins by knowing it: Paul tells Timothy that God wants all people to be saved and to come to a knowledge of the truth (1 Timothy 2:4). Peter says God does not want anyone to perish but everyone to come to repentance (2 Peter 3:9).
Within God’s desire to save sinners, believers perceive his saving plan, commands, and guidance into holiness. They must not merely be aware of his will but be filled and overflowing with it.
God’s will is not something to pick up and put down at convenience, because that would only preserve self-will. Maturing believers increasingly understand that every part of life matters to God.

documents.excerpt: Josh reduces the immediate response to one command: take a step. Mature life-group leaders were not always knowledgeable Christians; they leaned in and worked.
excerpts: Josh reduces the immediate response to one command: take a step. Mature life-group leaders were not always knowledgeable Christians; they leaned in and worked.
He recalls when he could not sit through a sermon without getting water or snacking on communion, much less write an eleven-part James series. Growth came through effort and attention.

New believers will encounter harsh or “crusty” Christians, but should not let others look down on them (1 Timothy 4:12). Keep eyes on Jesus, avoid comparison, and learn from failures as well as successes.

Jesus’s invitation in Matthew 11:29 provides the posture: take his yoke, learn from the gentle and humble Master, and find rest. Believers should walk closely with Jesus and practice obedience under the gentle Shepherd.

Josh insists twice that obedience must come from the heart. Jonah knew God’s command and eventually obeyed after the fish, but his heart remained resistant; he served to avoid another painful correction rather than because he loved God (Jonah 1:1–4:3).

Friends of Jesus instead delight to continue his work: David says, “I desire to do your will, my God; your law is within my heart” (Psalm 40:8). Jesus says his food is to do the will of the One who sent him and finish his work (John 4:34).
God’s will becomes praise, freedom, and nourishment when obeyed from the heart.

When believers fall short, they should rise, confess, receive forgiveness and purification (1 John 1:9), and resume faithful risk-taking within grace. The decisive matter is not a flawless success rate but a genuine heart that loves God, desires his will, and aims at his glory.

excerpts: Josh moves into communion and invites those who trust Christ to participate. Those still unsure of their standing with God may let the elements pass: bread and juice cannot save; only the true God can.
Anyone ready to entrust life to Christ can enter the prepared baptism waters and take communion there for the first time.
He asks each person to examine privately how they approach God’s will: Do they plan without considering it? Ignore God, his gifts, or his expectations? Know what he commands and still refuse?

This cannot be answered by a group, spouse, or preacher. Each individual must stand before God. The conversation is unavoidable; the choice is whether to have it willingly now or be forced to face it later.
Crossroads’s pastors and elders offer prayer, teaching, encouragement, and companionship, but each hearer must use this quiet moment to confess and repent.
Communion remembers the gospel: Jesus took sinners’ sin to the cross, satisfied divine wrath, rose again, and offers new life to believers—a material summary of 1 Corinthians 15:3–4.

In the closing prayer Josh asks God to: Make his voice heard and direct those seeking purpose and meaning. Help the congregation recognize and surrender to the work God has given. Free people trapped in a “tornado of shame” over yesterday and fill their minds with grace and mercy. Apply salvation not merely as a past rescue but as daily deliverance. Direct their steps and transform the church, hearts, homes, and marriages so their lives reflect God’s glory, goodness, and honor.
He closes the prayer at 50:47 with “Amen.”

Communion response: face God’s will now, confess, remember the gospel, and surrender
Josh moves into communion and invites those who trust Christ to participate. Those still unsure of their standing with God may let the elements pass: bread and juice cannot save; only the true God can.
Anyone ready to entrust life to Christ can enter the prepared baptism waters and take communion there for the first time.
He asks each person to examine privately how they approach God’s will: Do they plan without considering it? Ignore God, his gifts, or his expectations? Know what he commands and still refuse?
This cannot be answered by a group, spouse, or preacher. Each individual must stand before God. The conversation is unavoidable; the choice is whether to have it willingly now or be forced to face it later.
Crossroads’s pastors and elders offer prayer, teaching, encouragement, and companionship, but each hearer must use this quiet moment to confess and repent.
Communion remembers the gospel: Jesus took sinners’ sin to the cross, satisfied divine wrath, rose again, and offers new life to believers—a material summary of 1 Corinthians 15:3–4.
In the closing prayer Josh asks God to: Make his voice heard and direct those seeking purpose and meaning. Help the congregation recognize and surrender to the work God has given. Free people trapped in a “tornado of shame” over yesterday and fill their minds with grace and mercy. Apply salvation not merely as a past rescue but as daily deliverance. Direct their steps and transform the church, hearts, homes, and marriages so their lives reflect God’s glory, goodness, and honor.
He closes the prayer at 50:47 with “Amen.”

documents.title: The War Within

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · November 3, 2025 · James : A Faith That Works
documents.excerpt: Josh opens personally: the war inside him can drive him to war with other people and can put him opposite God as an enemy rather than beside God as a friend.
excerpts: Josh opens personally: the war inside him can drive him to war with other people and can put him opposite God as an enemy rather than beside God as a friend.

He extends the war image through several conditions: Sometimes the “bullets” are overhead and survival feels uncertain. Sometimes the immediate danger has eased, but the person is still stranded in hostile territory and cannot go home. Sometimes a believer feels less like a soldier than a prisoner of spiritual war, chained by Satan and unable to escape.

He names concrete forms of captivity in the congregation: Drug or alcohol addiction, where chemical craving dictates thought, feeling, speech, and behavior. Abuse or trauma, whose scars seem to return a person to the same place despite attempts to break free. Anxiety and depression, alternating between fear of tomorrow and suffocation beneath yesterday’s mistakes.

Josh locates himself inside the problem rather than above it: Jesus helped him escape nearly two decades of pornography addiction and a nicotine addiction. After those chains loosened, he says Satan changed the angle of attack toward doubt, worry, and episodes of depression that he can fight only with the Holy Spirit’s help. He describes the mental battle as sudden heaviness—sometimes a flash flood, sometimes water that remains.

He criticizes shallow church teaching that turns Paul’s unresolved “thorn in the flesh” into a blanket assumption that every mental, emotional, or physical stronghold is God’s will. Paul did not receive removal of his thorn, but Josh insists that this does not justify embracing every form of bondage as one’s assigned story. The devastation is knowing addiction and suffocating depression are not God’s desire while seeing no path out and simply sitting in chains.

Transition to the text: Whatever form the fight takes—physical, emotional, relational, or mental—the believer must recognize its spiritual dimension. Victory requires knowing both the enemy and the environment; his illustration is a soldier arriving in the Arctic wearing green “frog-skin” camouflage.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · November 3, 2025 · James : A Faith That Works
documents.excerpt: Josh announces the primary structure of the message from James 4: the church is at war with others, self, and God, and James explains how those wars stop.
excerpts: Josh announces the primary structure of the message from James 4: the church is at war with others, self, and God, and James explains how those wars stop.

Reading James 4:1–2, he stresses that quarrels among Christians arise from pleasures or desires battling within them. He explains the underlying Greek term hēdonē as sensual, natural, fleshly gratification and connects it to hedonism. His contemporary paraphrase of hedonism is “you do you”; beneath it lies selfishness.
He contrasts selfish gratification with Psalm 133’s picture of God’s people living in unity: the church’s witness shines when God’s house “sings in harmony.”

The New Testament churches demonstrate that this conflict is not theoretical: Corinth pursued pleasure and even took fellow believers to court. Galatia bit and devoured one another. Ephesus needed to be called back to a life worthy of its calling. Euodia and Syntyche in Philippi had to agree in the Lord, with Christ’s self-emptying servant posture presented as the corrective.
The Spirit of the selfless Christ cannot be blamed for selfishness or envy; those impulses come from somewhere else.

James is pulling back the curtain: Church “death fights” are not finally caused by someone taking a preferred seat or serving stale communion. The decisive problem is not what is happening around or even to a person, but what has gone wrong inside that person.

Josh quotes Baruch Spinoza’s criticism that professing Christians can display rancorous hatred more readily than love, joy, peace, temperance, and charity. His diagnostic question: why is Christian hatred sometimes more obvious than Christian love? Christians possess a new nature yet can revert to the old nature when fighting among themselves, becoming indistinguishable from the world once they are inside the church walls.

documents.excerpt: Josh presents two trajectories for believers: Grateful believers become skilled at noticing God’s goodness in family, home, health, children, career, church, leaders, friends, and spouse. Like putting on special glasses, they suddenly see God breaking chains and saving souls everywhere. Repeated recognition produces gratitude, then durable joy. Entitled believers become skilled at noticing what they regard as God’s misses—the blessing, opportunity, relationship, or promotion he “should” have given them.
excerpts: Josh presents two trajectories for believers: Grateful believers become skilled at noticing God’s goodness in family, home, health, children, career, church, leaders, friends, and spouse. Like putting on special glasses, they suddenly see God breaking chains and saving souls everywhere. Repeated recognition produces gratitude, then durable joy. Entitled believers become skilled at noticing what they regard as God’s misses—the blessing, opportunity, relationship, or promotion he “should” have given them.
The grateful believer knows he entered the world with nothing and will leave the same way, and therefore does not treat health, wealth, an effortless marriage, friends, or career as a debt God owes.
Entitlement reverses that posture: Instead of counting blessings, the person counts their absence. Another person’s promotion becomes an accusation against God rather than an occasion for joy.

Josh returns to James’s severe wording, “You desire and do not have, so you kill,” and repeats the movement’s thesis: coveting leads to conflict. People think they deserve an admission, family history, relationship, or opportunity; when they do not receive it, they throw a fit and expose slavery to sin. They do not truly want peace with God; they want God’s possessions. War with self, God, and others follows, producing joylessness, irritability, conflict, and blame.

He treats “kill” as deliberate rhetorical escalation rather than evidence that murder was the congregation’s normal practice. James is destroying the listener’s pity party by naming how believers fight for position, speak evil, judge, classify people, and weaponize the tongue instead of speaking truth in love. The war with others persists because the person refuses to face the war within.

Worldly pleasure cannot end the cycle because coveting is continuous and envy never declares itself satisfied. Josh urges listeners to accept now that selfish desire will not satisfy, sparing themselves and others the pain caused by trying to make it do so. Peace with others is impossible while one is constantly fighting for oneself.

He closes the movement with biblical examples of selfish desire: Eve ate in order to gain wisdom like God. Abraham lied to preserve himself. Achan kept Jericho’s devoted goods and brought defeat on Israel. David killed to conceal adultery. Isaiah’s diagnosis gathers them all: like sheep, each has turned to his or her own way.
Transition: people fight for themselves because they do not trust God.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · November 3, 2025 · James : A Faith That Works
documents.excerpt: Reading James 4:2–3, Josh identifies two failures: Some do not have because they do not ask God: a nonexistent prayer life. Others ask but do not receive because they ask from wrong motives, intending to spend the answer on their pleasures: an ineffective prayer life.
excerpts: Reading James 4:2–3, Josh identifies two failures: Some do not have because they do not ask God: a nonexistent prayer life. Others ask but do not receive because they ask from wrong motives, intending to spend the answer on their pleasures: an ineffective prayer life.
His maxim is, “If we don’t pray right, we can’t live right.” Selfishness is serious enough in daily life, but worse when carried unchallenged into private prayer with God.

Psalm 2 supplies the positive model: God tells his installed King and Son to ask for the nations as his inheritance. Josh reasons that if Jesus asks to receive, servants should not imagine themselves above asking their Master.

He turns conviction into a catalogue of intercession: Pray for world peace rather than mocking the cliché. Pray for every leader, not only those on one’s political side, asking for integrity, justice, and compassion. Pray for the lonely, orphans, widows, children without a home for the holidays, and young people. Pray for return to God and revival in the church instead of spending that energy complaining about another generation.

He contrasts another promotion request with the harder prayer for a compassionate heart that genuinely values others above self. People avoid that prayer because compassion may demand money, time, energy, and personal effort. They do not receive such transformation because they do not truly want its cost.

Josh supplies further corrective prayers: humility; exposure of places given to the devil; courage to do right at personal cost; opportunities to share testimony and gospel; God’s view of other people; awareness of blessing; contentment; and the capacity to bless others.
Transition: instead of praying for God’s will on earth as in heaven, people pray for their own will, then become angry with God when it is denied and carry that anger into relationships.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · November 3, 2025 · James : A Faith That Works
documents.excerpt: Josh identifies “You shall not covet” as the final commandment and argues that violating it can drive violations of the others—murder, lying, theft, dishonoring parents, and adultery. David’s story is his example.
excerpts: Josh identifies “You shall not covet” as the final commandment and argues that violating it can drive violations of the others—murder, lying, theft, dishonoring parents, and adultery. David’s story is his example.
James 4:4 intensifies the diagnosis: friendship with the world is hostility toward God, and choosing the world makes a person God’s enemy.
Josh connects James to Jesus’ Sermon on the Mount: The issue is the heart, not only the externally completed act. In that heart-level sense, all are implicated as murderers and adulterers.

“Adulterous people” addresses spiritual rather than sexual infidelity: Jeremiah depicts faithless Israel receiving a certificate of divorce while Judah repeats her adultery. Ezekiel calls Judah an adulterous wife who prefers strangers to her husband. The nations’ gods became illicit partners for God’s covenant people.

Jesus’ rebuke of a wicked and adulterous generation continues the theme: That generation demanded a sign but would receive Jonah’s sign. Nineveh would condemn it because Nineveh repented at Jonah’s preaching while Israel rejected the One greater than Jonah. Religious display—including prayer on street corners—could coexist with hearts that preferred strange gods to the true God.
John 5 sharpens the warning: people can study Scripture diligently while refusing to come to the Christ to whom Scripture testifies.

Josh applies James’s rebuke to nominal Christians: They join a church without a personal saving relationship with God through Christ. They say they love God while “laying with the world” and keeping other partners. No one can serve two masters.
From 1 John, he warns against loving the world’s sinful cravings, lust, and boasting because the world and its desires pass away; the one who does God’s will lives forever.
Transition: the church is Christ’s bride and must remain faithful to the end.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · November 3, 2025 · James : A Faith That Works
documents.excerpt: Reading James 4:5–6, Josh says human beings display an envious spirit from birth, but God jealously desires the spirit he placed within his people and “gives more grace.” God opposes pride and gives favor to humility.
excerpts: Reading James 4:5–6, Josh says human beings display an envious spirit from birth, but God jealously desires the spirit he placed within his people and “gives more grace.” God opposes pride and gives favor to humility.

He sets the conflict alongside Galatians 5:17: sinful nature and Spirit desire contrary things, preventing believers from simply doing whatever they want. This is the war within every follower of Christ. Like covenant jealousy between spouses, the Spirit guards the believer’s relationship with God and grieves over sin against God’s love.
Romans 8:6 supplies the battle plan for the mind: flesh-governed thought leads to death, while Spirit-governed thought brings life and peace.
Josh names the opposing strategies: God calls believers to depend on grace. The devil urges them to depend on themselves.

Romans 5:20–21 explains grace’s superiority: The law makes trespass visible. Josh illustrates this through Moses descending from Sinai into the golden-calf rebellion. The commands against other gods and false witness expose Aaron and every hearer as lawbreakers. Yet where sin increases, grace increases all the more and reigns through righteousness to eternal life in Jesus Christ.
He carefully denies that grace licenses sin; grace is power to overcome it. No quantity of sin exhausts grace. Grace does not barely cover the ledger; it overflows and wins decisively.
The gospel climax is the woman caught in adultery: God sees the act but, in Christ, does not join the stone throwers; condemnation gives way to the command to leave sin.
Josh summarizes grace as God turning “rebels into relatives,” then repeats the contrast between dependence on grace and dependence on self.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · November 3, 2025 · James : A Faith That Works
documents.excerpt: Josh gathers every battle, anxiety, stronghold, entitlement, and sinful desire under James 4:7–10: Submit to God. Resist the devil, who will flee. Draw near to God, who will draw near. Wash hands and purify divided hearts. Grieve sin and humble oneself before the Lord, who lifts up the humble.
excerpts: Josh gathers every battle, anxiety, stronghold, entitlement, and sinful desire under James 4:7–10: Submit to God. Resist the devil, who will flee. Draw near to God, who will draw near. Wash hands and purify divided hearts. Grieve sin and humble oneself before the Lord, who lifts up the humble.
He tells listeners to leave the throne of their own lives immediately. The demand for control, success, and relevance must be dropped at God’s feet because those demands are producing misery.

“Submit” is explained as a military term: take one’s proper rank. A sergeant acting like a four-star general would destroy military order. The believer must “fall in,” because in this war surrender to God is the only route to victory.

He addresses fear of making Jesus Lord: New and mature believers alike fear what Jesus might take away. Josh asks whether the feared loss is actually the very thing causing war in the mind. People cling to vices because they feel human or alive, but Jesus removes them to give something better and reveal that they were made for more.

David illustrates the transition from concealment to peace: After adultery with Bathsheba and Uriah’s death, secrecy made David increasingly miserable and put him at war with God, himself, and others. Surrender leads to Psalm 51’s cry for mercy, cleansing, and forgiveness.
Application: resisting the devil begins with submitting to God and drawing near through an honest plea for mercy. Confession receives faithful forgiveness and purification.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · November 3, 2025 · James : A Faith That Works
documents.excerpt: Josh develops James’s “wash your hands” image: Believers must watch what they touch, what they hold tightly, their recurring tendencies, nearby temptations, and the damage their choices can cause. They must recognize the heart’s deceitfulness, the mind’s darkness, and the seriousness of sin.
excerpts: Josh develops James’s “wash your hands” image: Believers must watch what they touch, what they hold tightly, their recurring tendencies, nearby temptations, and the damage their choices can cause. They must recognize the heart’s deceitfulness, the mind’s darkness, and the seriousness of sin.

His household illustration exposes misplaced urgency: Parents repeatedly tell small children to wash germ-covered hands. James calls adults to handle sin with still greater urgency; parents asking children to wash must ask whether their own hands are clean.

Grieving, mourning, and wailing mean taking responsibility rather than outsourcing blame. Josh confesses that it took him a long time to stop pointing at other people. He acknowledges painful childhoods and histories without allowing past harm to exonerate present sin.

Refusal to expose and mourn sin is pride, and Josh asks whether a current struggle might continue because God opposes the proud. A believer unwilling to own sin should expect divine opposition. God’s children cannot sin comfortably.

Pride is compared to facial hair and confession to shaving or washing: The work is recurring, not completed once. Believers repeatedly bring sin into God’s light, and God repeatedly lifts them because grace remains sufficient.

Jesus’ teaching that self-exaltation ends in humiliation and humility in exaltation sets up the prodigal son: The son returns willing to be a servant, owns and confesses his sin, and falls before his father. Josh’s personal maxim is that he would rather be a servant in God’s house than a king in his own. The father answers repentance with robe, ring, sandals, a feast, and restored sonship: the dead is alive and the lost is found.

Transition: when people submit, draw near, and humble themselves, God draws near, cleanses, forgives, and ends the wars with God, self, and others. Isaiah’s “quietness and confidence forever” names the resulting peace.

documents.excerpt: James 4:11–12 shows what inward peace does to community: Believers stop slandering and judging one another. Speaking against a brother or sister sets the speaker over the law rather than under it. God alone is Lawgiver and Judge, able to save and destroy.
excerpts: James 4:11–12 shows what inward peace does to community: Believers stop slandering and judging one another. Speaking against a brother or sister sets the speaker over the law rather than under it. God alone is Lawgiver and Judge, able to save and destroy.

Those who have received mercy, mourned sin, humbled themselves, returned home, and learned that God gives more grace become experts in other people’s strengths rather than weaknesses. They celebrate the Holy Spirit’s work in others. They build up rather than tear down.
Josh asks listeners what they instinctively notice: Another person’s fall or faithful stand? Failure or even the smallest growth? Do they voice encouragement when they see strength?
The answers reveal not merely whether someone can define grace, but whether they recognize their own need for it.

Becoming attentive to grace in others does not require naivety or refusal to confront wrongdoing. Jesus’ speck-and-plank teaching requires self-examination first. The problem is not wise recognition of poor behavior but the harsh, unkind, continually fault-finding spirit.
Proper humility before God prevents arrogance toward others. Love does right; slander does wrong.

documents.excerpt: Josh hands the message to the congregation for reflection: Where is confession needed? What sin must be owned? Is there a slandered believer who needs an apology? Where has the listener sinned against self by indulging evil thought and desire rather than taking thoughts captive? Where is self-dependence replacing trust in God?
excerpts: Josh hands the message to the congregation for reflection: Where is confession needed? What sin must be owned? Is there a slandered believer who needs an apology? Where has the listener sinned against self by indulging evil thought and desire rather than taking thoughts captive? Where is self-dependence replacing trust in God?

He returns to the adultery and throne images: In what areas has the listener been spiritually unfaithful? Who occupies the throne, and how far down the succession plan is Jesus? Does the listener intend to come home, or continue among the pigs? Is there a real desire to become God’s servant?
These answers are to disclose the heart’s condition.

As the congregation considers Jesus’ cross, Josh emphasizes that the sacrifice purchased freedom. The church should therefore behave as free people: break strongholds, slip chains, leave prisons, and reclaim hearts, minds, homes, church, and city. He is not searching for freedom; he says he has found it in Christ and intends to rest in its quiet confidence.
Conclusion of the sermon's central argument: resting in Christ’s freedom is the only way to win the war within.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · November 3, 2025 · James : A Faith That Works
documents.excerpt: Josh recounts Jesus’ words over the bread and cup on the night of his arrest: The bread represents Christ’s body given for his people and is taken in remembrance. The cup announces the new covenant in his blood.
excerpts: Josh recounts Jesus’ words over the bread and cup on the night of his arrest: The bread represents Christ’s body given for his people and is taken in remembrance. The cup announces the new covenant in his blood.

He explains the once-for-all force of the cross: Repeated sacrifices for sin are no longer needed because Christ is the final sacrifice. Believers need not live under anxiety, burden, or an unfulfilled debt; Christ fulfilled the saving work in his death, vindicated by resurrection. “The debt is paid in full” and “It is done” become reminders that the battle for souls has been won.
He invites everyone who has put faith in Jesus to share the Lord’s Supper and simply urges, “Trust Jesus.”

In the closing prayer, Josh asks for courage to pray courageous prayers. He admits that during many years of following Jesus he retained things God never wanted for him. Recognizing the spiritual battle around mind, heart, soul, family, home, town, and church revealed that these things needed to be dropped at God’s feet.
The final act of surrender names envy, covetousness, desires, and pleasures, then releases them all: “Take this world. And just give me Jesus.”
He closes with allegiance and the Lord’s Prayer’s posture: God’s will in his life and in the church, as in heaven; “We’re yours”; Amen.

documents.excerpt: Chris opens by asking whether the church is ready for a tough question, then greets them first. He usually gets to sit out there and sing and listen with them; this morning he’ll be up front, but they are still worshiping together.
excerpts: Chris opens by asking whether the church is ready for a tough question, then greets them first. He usually gets to sit out there and sing and listen with them; this morning he’ll be up front, but they are still worshiping together.

The question: how many of us struggle with selfishness? He raises both hands. Sometimes he thinks he’s doing okay, doing the dishes or taking out the garbage for his wife, and then realizes he did it just so he wouldn’t have to deal with her frustration and the uncomfortable “How many times did I ask you?” conversation.

To the ladies, after a quick “that came out wrong,” he says every marriage is different, but maybe dinner is ready, the laundry is done, or the diaper is changed so you don’t have to hear him complain that he’s hungry, naked, or dying from the smell.

So why do we do the things we do? To avoid upsetting or disappointing someone? To feel good about ourselves? Do we sign up for Crossroads Cares, serve in a ministry, or give because we don’t want to feel guilty or disappoint leadership? The question to hold on to this morning: what is my mindset?

The question: how many of us struggle with selfishness? He raises both hands. Sometimes he thinks he’s doing okay, doing the dishes or taking out the garbage for his wife, and then realizes he did it just so he wouldn’t have to deal with her frustration and the uncomfortable “How many times did I ask you?” conversation.
To the ladies, after a quick “that came out wrong,” he says every marriage is different, but maybe dinner is ready, the laundry is done, or the diaper is changed so you don’t have to hear him complain that he’s hungry, naked, or dying from the smell.
So why do we do the things we do? To avoid upsetting or disappointing someone? To feel good about ourselves? Do we sign up for Crossroads Cares, serve in a ministry, or give because we don’t want to feel guilty or disappoint leadership? The question to hold on to this morning: what is my mindset?

Two things he can’t say better than Scripture: conduct yourselves worthy of the gospel, and stand firm in the one Spirit, striving together as one. Then back to “Therefore, if you have any encouragement from being united with Christ.” Do you see the connection? Standing firm and striving together, therefore, and now we’re into Philippians 2.

documents.excerpt: Do you see the progression? These are almost rhetorical ifs. Of course we are encouraged by being united with Christ; having Christ brings love, and being loved is comforting; Christ gives us the Holy Spirit, which every believer shares; and the Spirit brings tenderness and compassion we couldn’t have before Christ.
excerpts: Do you see the progression? These are almost rhetorical ifs. Of course we are encouraged by being united with Christ; having Christ brings love, and being loved is comforting; Christ gives us the Holy Spirit, which every believer shares; and the Spirit brings tenderness and compassion we couldn’t have before Christ.

Paul is essentially saying, “If you have these things… but because you’re in Christ, I know you do.” Chris treats it as an “if” word game: “Well, if… no, I have that. I got all of them. Okay, Paul, what now?” Paul tricks us into affirming the four ifs so he can hit us with the “then”: make my joy complete by being like-minded, having the same love, being one in spirit and of one mind.

In two verses Paul wraps up all his letters to the churches, because Paul writes some long sentences; Chris can’t even get punctuation right. Paul calls churches to be one in spirit, to deal with those who break unity, and to call them to repentance so unity can be restored. Every letter dealing with junk in a church aims to restore a believer or rid the church of sin and false teaching, so it can focus on sharing Christ, loving one another, and glorifying God.

excerpts: We must humbly value others above ourselves. Romans 12:10: be devoted to one another in love; honor one another above yourselves. 1 Peter 5:5: clothe yourselves with humility toward one another, because God opposes the proud but shows favor to the humble.

This is not easy; look at all the Scriptures on pride and humility. It has to be a day-to-day, moment-by-moment thing. Paul gives the final piece of the how-to in verse 4: not looking to your own interests but to the interests of others. 1 Corinthians 10:24 says it a touch differently: no one should seek their own good, but the good of others.

If we struggle to follow this, it comes down to what is good for the other person. Who gains from what I’m doing? Who loses from the decisions I’m making? Is this going to be great for me or for someone else?

The world says live your truth (Chris doesn’t even know what that means), get what’s yours, climb over people. Show them that following Jesus looks different, that the values, expectations, and love are different because it is God’s love. Like the old song says, though Chris won’t sing it because Josh sings and they’d all leave: they will know that we are Christians by our love.

excerpts: So God the Son, who created all things and knew his creation would reject him, chose to leave God’s side and lower himself to nothing, becoming a servant and taking on human likeness, flesh and bones and everything that comes with being us, minus sin.

Chris can’t fathom what heaven is like; the greatest thing he can imagine isn’t even close. Jesus left that and stuck all that glory in a flesh suit. He recalls the first Men in Black, where a huge, powerful alien bug hides inside an “Edgar suit,” while insisting he isn’t comparing Jesus to a cockroach, so please don’t send emails. It is a terrible example, but what human example could compare?

The God of the universe became a helpless baby who needed a mom and dad to meet his every need, diaper changes included. documents.excerpt: Done picking on married people, since he is one, Chris asks: why are you here? To love and serve one another, worship God together, raise up the next generation, and spur one another on? Or for what you can get: the kids’ programming, the music, the preaching, the breakfast and coffee? Those aren’t bad, but if they are the only reasons, your mindset needs to change.
excerpts: Done picking on married people, since he is one, Chris asks: why are you here? To love and serve one another, worship God together, raise up the next generation, and spur one another on? Or for what you can get: the kids’ programming, the music, the preaching, the breakfast and coffee? Those aren’t bad, but if they are the only reasons, your mindset needs to change.

If we all had the mindset of Jesus, kids and youth programs wouldn’t be short of volunteers, and they wouldn’t worry about adding students on Wednesday nights for lack of adults. He wonders why no men volunteer with Kids for Truth, though he just learned two signed up. These kids are the next generation who will carry the gospel forward; the children’s and youth directors should not know what to do with all the volunteers.

Crossroads Cares needs the care center staffed and more coordinators. It is the church’s outreach to Anthem, Phoenix, and the world, often to lost souls, giving a real opportunity to share the gospel, and it also helps our own spiritual family and lightens the heavy load many volunteers carry. Gifts land in different places, from the engaged team to the office, facilities, and worship and tech, but use your gifts.

It doesn’t stop with serving through the church. In every interaction, a conversation, an event, a meal, or coffee, we still need the mindset of Jesus, valuing the other person above ourselves and looking to their interests.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · October 20, 2025 · James : A Faith That Works
documents.excerpt: Josh defines wisdom as the ability to use knowledge and experience to make good decisions and judgments. Christian wisdom knows God’s truth and applies it to ordinary situations and choices. The unwise may possess the same information yet be unable—or unwilling—to act rightly. Therefore intelligence and wisdom are not interchangeable: “the fool didn’t miss an email” or lack a puzzle piece; truth simply fails to govern the fool’s attitudes, priorities, values, and actions.
excerpts: Josh defines wisdom as the ability to use knowledge and experience to make good decisions and judgments. Christian wisdom knows God’s truth and applies it to ordinary situations and choices. The unwise may possess the same information yet be unable—or unwilling—to act rightly. Therefore intelligence and wisdom are not interchangeable: “the fool didn’t miss an email” or lack a puzzle piece; truth simply fails to govern the fool’s attitudes, priorities, values, and actions.

He uses playful audience categories to separate knowledge from wise practice. A book-smart person might understand quantum physics but be unable to cook ramen. A street-smart person might build computers but fail to manage a budget. Looking back, people often wish they could put present knowledge and experience into their twenty-year-old selves; their scars came partly from thinking they saw the whole picture when they did not. Some learn from those collisions, while others continue making the same destructive decision despite repeated bruises.

Wisdom, like faith, is not immediately visible. Eye color can be sorted at a glance; genuinely wise people cannot. Wisdom must work itself out over time, so James compares the eventual “fruit baskets” of true and false wisdom.

Josh reconnects the passage to James 3’s warning about would-be teachers. Desire to lead God’s people can be noble, but anyone can stand up and say attractive things. A polished sermon can miss God’s heart and therefore miss faithful application.

Illustration: a distorted Good Samaritan sermon. Josh recalls a preacher promising “a different take on an old classic,” which made him wary of novelty supposedly missed by every believer since Pentecost. The preacher centered the innkeeper, even though Jesus’s parable calls God’s people to stop when religious elites pass by, tear down hostile boundaries, love the stranger, and bear the cost of helping the wounded. Josh’s corrective is, “We don’t charge to house the hurting. We foot the bill.” The preacher likely knew the story and possessed greater academic credentials, yet missed its point; this is precisely the knowledge without wisdom James confronts.
Transition: Josh says the two kinds of wisdom will be tested in two areas—where each originates and what each creates.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · October 20, 2025 · James : A Faith That Works
documents.excerpt: Josh begins with the source of false wisdom and rereads James 3:15. Heavenly wisdom comes from God; earthly wisdom is made by humanity apart from God. Man-made wisdom can look, sound, smell, and taste good, pass normal tests, and even work temporarily, but it eventually fails.
excerpts: Josh begins with the source of false wisdom and rereads James 3:15. Heavenly wisdom comes from God; earthly wisdom is made by humanity apart from God. Man-made wisdom can look, sound, smell, and taste good, pass normal tests, and even work temporarily, but it eventually fails.
Tower of Babel illustration: the project likely began with energy, unity, diversity, ambition, and visible progress—“Let’s build a name for ourselves”—but ended in failure and confusion.

David and Saul’s armor illustration: ordinary prudence said an outmatched David should use Saul’s armor, but God intended to use David’s particular gifts and presence with him was more than enough. Josh’s principle: common sense often looks foolish beside wisdom from God.

Crossroads Cares illustration: While the ministry was being launched, Josh feared that designated generosity to practical needs might weaken the church’s general fund. Earthly wisdom worried about the bank account even though God had placed the ministry on their hearts. Since Crossroads Cares began in 2021, giving has risen slowly and steadily, the church has opened a care center, avoided layoffs, paid its utilities, maintained its budget, and did not need its contingency that summer. The congregation’s proper response is gratitude and praise to God.

Josh connects James’s “earthly, unspiritual, and demonic” description to the believer’s three enemies: the world, the flesh, and the devil. As the Trinity gives wisdom from above, this “unholy trinity” offers wisdom from below. The world has more freely available knowledge than ever but little wisdom.
He quotes 1 Corinthians 1:20–21 to show that God exposes worldly wisdom as foolish and saves believers through what the world calls foolish preaching.

Human progress has not produced moral or spiritual peace. Despite extraordinary communication technology, humanity is not meaningfully closer to ending poverty, hunger, imbalance, ignorance, racism, hatred, crime, or immorality than in Paul’s day. Steve Jobs created transformative devices yet reportedly kept them from his own children because he understood the danger of replacing human interaction with technology; many parents nevertheless use the same technology as a babysitter. Josh repeats Ecclesiastes’ verdict that everything is “meaningless” to distinguish increased knowledge from enduring wisdom. Medical and technological advances can serve good, but progress without morality also multiplies evil: communication improves while listening declines; knowledge of the mind increases while mental-health problems rise; knowledge of human nature increases while crime, war, hate, and racism persist.

Human wisdom treats surface symptoms; God’s wisdom reaches the root. Even resistance to injustice can press so hard that reformers become what they sought to eradicate. God answers injustice through humility, but human wisdom considers humility foolish.
Application and transition: read the first two chapters of 1 Corinthians during the week. Man’s wisdom arises from reason and fades; God’s wisdom arrives by revelation and lasts forever.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · October 20, 2025 · James : A Faith That Works
documents.excerpt: Josh laments statistics indicating that fewer than half of Christians regularly read Scripture outside church. He celebrates increases among Gen Z (11% to 15%) and millennials (12% to 17%) but insists the numbers must continue climbing.
excerpts: Josh laments statistics indicating that fewer than half of Christians regularly read Scripture outside church. He celebrates increases among Gen Z (11% to 15%) and millennials (12% to 17%) but insists the numbers must continue climbing.

Practical application: replace worldly inputs with God’s Word. Josh describes deleting social media for thirty days and feeling as though he had “taken a shower from the world.” He replaced Instagram with the Glorify app, which offers a daily quotation, verse, and devotional. His family also uses weekly Scripture cards from teachingschool.com at the dinner table. A different person leads on four days using one of four approaches: silent meditation, discussion of motivation, attention to proper meaning, and memorization. The humorous threat that the last person to recite the verse loses dessert is not their actual rule. The goal is one text supplying more heavenly wisdom to the home throughout the week. Commands: get into the Word; bathe children, grandchildren, and spouse in it; teach family members to wash themselves in the Word and away from the world; lead the home into something meaningful instead of letting YouTube raise the children.

Josh states that turning from God has cost the world its wisdom, and increasing advancement only makes the underlying problem more visible. He quotes Proverbs 9:10: fear of the Lord begins wisdom. He contrasts it with Romans 3:10–18, where humanity neither understands nor seeks God, practices deceit and violence, does not know peace, and has no fear of God. Humanity’s disorder comes from taking its eyes off the Holy One; believers must fix their eyes on Jesus or risk clinging to demonic wisdom.

Genesis 3 establishes the old pattern of demonic wisdom. Satan deceived Eve, and since the fall this self-centered wisdom has opposed God’s wisdom. The serpent’s lie persuaded Eve to seek godlike autonomy. Josh gives the issue a stark either/or: those who do not cling to God’s wisdom will fall for Satan’s wisdom.

Transition to wisdom from above: Josh quotes James 1:17, where every good and perfect gift comes down from the unchanging Father. Wisdom in James 3 is one of those gifts, and the Father supplies more than his children deserve. Josh locates Christian identity above: heavenly citizenship, primary allegiance to God’s kingdom, and heavenly treasure outrank every human institution and possession.

Christ is the content and source of divine wisdom. Josh recalls Jesus’s teaching that one must be born again and that Spirit gives birth to spirit. He expands into the gospel: God demonstrated love in Christ; Jesus lived perfectly, bore the curse and condemnation at the cross, rose, holds the keys of death and Hades, saves all who call on him, gives eternal life, will return, make all things new, and receive the confession of every knee and tongue. The emotional point is not abstract: Josh says he wakes smiling because human rejection cannot undo God’s demonstrated love and purchased freedom.

Josh quotes Colossians 2:2–3: the mystery is Christ, in whom all treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden. Hidden treasure must be sought. Jesus’s “ask, seek, knock” promise and Deuteronomy 4:29 agree that wholehearted seekers find God.

Concluding application for the source question: Get into the Word and seek the Lord; Scripture makes people wise for salvation. Those who lack wisdom should ask God. Do not settle for worldly, demonic counterfeits; seek Christ alone, receive wisdom from God, remain in Scripture, and walk by the Spirit.
Transition: Josh moves from where the two wisdoms originate to what they create.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · October 20, 2025 · James : A Faith That Works
documents.excerpt: Josh rereads James 3:14–16 and begins inspecting the “fruit basket” of false wisdom.
excerpts: Josh rereads James 3:14–16 and begins inspecting the “fruit basket” of false wisdom.
The first fruit is bitter envy, also rendered bitter jealousy or zeal. It naturally joins selfish ambition. James 3 began by warning believers against ambition for positions of teaching authority.

Personal testimony about calling: Josh says he has been called throughout his life to preach and lead, but he did not arrive in his role because he wanted the job. Because the role rests on calling rather than a honeymoon phase, difficulty will not make him quit. God changed his life and gave him purpose; he will go elsewhere if God calls, but until then he remains where God placed him.

Worldly wisdom instead says to climb the ladder, chase promotion, insist another person is not special, and imagine, “That should be me.” This pressure appears in workplaces, politics, relationships, and churches. Even Jesus’s disciples argued over who was greatest in the kingdom.

Josh reads Mark 9:33–35. The disciples’ embarrassed silence shows that they already knew their argument did not honor God. Jesus overturns worldly rank: whoever wants to be first must be last and servant of all. This marks the difference between disciples and Pharisees: both possessed religious information, but the elite missed the Messiah because their wisdom came from below and desired human praise. Human praise is the only reward such ambition receives; the servant shares in God’s glory.

Diagnostic application: ask, “Why do you do what you do?” Is the motive title, visibility, ego, influence, or relevance? Josh invokes Jeremiah and Paul: boasting belongs only in the Lord. He tests envy through paired questions: gratitude for one’s mission or resentment of another’s place; gratitude for one’s gift or desire for hers; grief and help when another falls or relief that it was someone else; kingdom use of one’s resources or preoccupation with a different lot.

documents.excerpt: The next false fruit is selfish ambition. Josh explains the Greek term as language used for a politician working a crowd for votes. Josh notes that James heard Jesus before believing and uses that fact to urge Christians to continue preaching the gospel to family members even through rejection.

The ESV renders James 3:13 as “the meekness of wisdom.” Meekness is not weakness but power under control; wisdom is knowledge used properly. Jesus says the meek inherit the earth. A truly wise person does not work for human praise but seeks God’s glory, and this orientation can be heard in how the person describes experiences and accomplishments.
True wisdom is pure. Because God is holy, wisdom from him is pure. False wisdom leads to sin; God’s wisdom leads to purity. Josh connects this to Jesus’s promise that the pure in heart will see God.

True wisdom is peace-loving. False wisdom yields competition, rivalry, and backbiting; God’s wisdom yields peace, unity, and calm in a storm. Josh rejects a common church counterfeit: ignoring sin or sweeping it under the rug is not biblical peace. Jesus blesses peacemakers, not passive “peacekeepers.” Wisdom-made peace does not hide or ignore sin; believers confess to one another, creating opportunities to show mercy. Showing mercy is central to the church’s identity.

documents.excerpt: True wisdom is considerate. Josh says this word alone needs to be recovered by the church. He cites Matthew Arnold’s phrase “sweet reasonableness”: extending to others the kind consideration one wishes to receive. He links this posture with poverty of spirit and the kingdom of heaven.
excerpts: True wisdom is considerate. Josh says this word alone needs to be recovered by the church. He cites Matthew Arnold’s phrase “sweet reasonableness”: extending to others the kind consideration one wishes to receive. He links this posture with poverty of spirit and the kingdom of heaven.

True wisdom is submissive. It is charitable rather than stubborn, like a soldier receiving an order instead of organizing a mutiny. It listens, works toward unity, knows when rigidity is inappropriate, lays down the sword, and embraces a brother.

True wisdom is full of mercy. Josh connects it to Jesus’s blessing on the merciful. Mercy supplies evidence of saving faith by forgiving wrongdoers and reaching down to help them when they suffer. He returns to the Good Samaritan: the wise believer is not an innkeeper eager to charge but a compassionate neighbor concerned for anyone who needs support. The result is deep love among believers.

True wisdom is full of good fruit. The Spirit’s fruit pours from the believer. These works are not disguised selfish ambition but the overflow of a divinely transformed heart—a godly ambition that hungers and thirsts for righteousness.
True wisdom is impartial. Because God shows no favoritism, believers treat one another equally. Instead of hunting for faults, they build fellow believers up and spur them on in the good fight.

True wisdom is sincere. A false appearance can be maintained only temporarily. Josh explains “hypocrite” as a mask-wearer or actor; eventually the wearer must come up for air. God’s children do not need masks. Wisdom from above makes them open, genuine, transparent, truthful, and able to speak the truth in love.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · October 20, 2025 · James : A Faith That Works
documents.excerpt: Josh warns that a church, life group, or Christian circle characterized by pretending, backbiting, undermining, and criticism is saturated with false wisdom; the hearer should retreat.
excerpts: Josh warns that a church, life group, or Christian circle characterized by pretending, backbiting, undermining, and criticism is saturated with false wisdom; the hearer should retreat.

He condemns religious politics and personal campaigns. God’s hatred must be preached alongside God’s love. God’s children do not scheme or build names for themselves; they kneel with towel and basin, wash feet, and treat others as more valuable—not merely in speech but in action.
Josh states the contrast in compact form: earthly wisdom creates schemers; heavenly wisdom creates servants; false wisdom leads to cursing; true wisdom leads to blessing.

He quotes James 3:18 about peacemakers sowing in peace and reaping righteousness. This remains consistent with James’s letter: professed Christianity must be demonstrated by works. Genuine faith bears godly wisdom, and godly wisdom lets the Lord use a believer’s life to bring righteousness and peace to others. The warning is equally serious: a believer’s life can become an instrument through which Satan spreads sin, war, disorder, division, and every evil practice.

Central diagnostic: “What are you sowing—peace or discord?” The Lord’s house should be full of peacemakers. Josh recalls Proverbs’ condemnation of wicked schemes and conflict-stirring because the church’s familial bond matters to God. He suggests unity may be the only godly measure of a healthy church that ultimately matters.

Transition to invitation: exchange false wisdom for true wisdom and return to the Word, because needed wisdom is found in the person and work of Jesus Christ. Jesus is wisdom, and obeying him is everything.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · October 20, 2025 · James : A Faith That Works
documents.excerpt: Josh quotes Proverbs 3:13 in the KJV—“Happy is the man that findeth wisdom”—and interprets the invitation christologically: happy is the person who finds Jesus.
excerpts: Josh quotes Proverbs 3:13 in the KJV—“Happy is the man that findeth wisdom”—and interprets the invitation christologically: happy is the person who finds Jesus.
He joins it to Jesus’s promise of full, abundant life.

Invitation to ashamed and wounded hearers: A person’s past sin will not shock the congregation; the church is a dysfunctional family of misfits whose polished present often hides disastrous former lives. Josh includes himself in that testimony and tells newcomers not to compare themselves with long-time Christians. Stop looking at Christians and stare at Christ, who writes a distinct story in each believer; envy of another person’s story is another form of the false wisdom just exposed. Everyone came to Jesus as a mess. Bring whatever burden or sin remains, lay it at Jesus’s feet, and do not take it back. Read about Christ, find his promises, memorize them, and remember both what he has done and what he promises to do. Josh cannot predict the details of the hearer’s future story, but he insists encounter with Christ will not leave the person unchanged.

Closing prayer (47:18–49:18): Josh thanks the Father for what happens when God’s children gather around his promises, submit to his Word, and desire to look like Jesus. He points to needs being met naturally through transformed lives and to people entering church eager to report progress in their fight against addiction. He asks God to make Crossroads a place where broken people resist a world that calls sin acceptable, listen to God, and put the sin down. The prayer renounces love for the world’s possessions: God may take it all; retaining Christ is gain. Josh thanks God for saving him, saving the congregation, and shaping the church; he asks for continued focus and closes in God’s name with “Amen.”

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · October 13, 2025 · James : A Faith That Works
documents.excerpt: Josh opens after the hailstorm with a personal declaration of committed love for the church—not infatuation, but a durable willingness to pray, remain available, and walk with Jesus together even when ministry is difficult. His stated ministry desire is simple: help the congregation know who God is, how God sees them, what God has done for them, and how grace should shape what they do for others. Because pastoral teaching sometimes requires confronting sin, he publicly apologizes for any hurt he has caused, even when harm was not his intention.
excerpts: Josh opens after the hailstorm with a personal declaration of committed love for the church—not infatuation, but a durable willingness to pray, remain available, and walk with Jesus together even when ministry is difficult. His stated ministry desire is simple: help the congregation know who God is, how God sees them, what God has done for them, and how grace should shape what they do for others. Because pastoral teaching sometimes requires confronting sin, he publicly apologizes for any hurt he has caused, even when harm was not his intention.

He recounts the church wound that shaped his youth. After his parents’ divorce, the church in which he had grown up did not visibly support him and his sisters. These were not casual acquaintances but people with whom he had worshiped, prayed, eaten, stayed, and celebrated his baptism. He let their failure produce bitterness, rebellion against God and the church, and more than a decade of sinful choices. His concise diagnosis is that he let their sin create sin in him.

Josh then complicates his own account rather than merely blaming the former church. Those people may have thought he did not want contact; unspoken expectations kill relationships. People cannot always perceive an unexpressed need, so someone who needs care sometimes must raise a hand and ask. He asks the congregation to make that commitment, promising that he will be there when they do. Looking back, he believes that if he had asked for prayer he would have received love. Instead, he assumed the worst and treated his burden as uniquely heavy.

Becoming a pastor exposed the uneven expectations people place on church leaders and forced him to own his part. He contacted leaders from his childhood church, not first to receive their apology but to give his: he had imposed unspoken expectations, judged them by a stricter standard than himself, and carried a decade-long grudge. He trusted the Holy Spirit to convict them. They, in turn, admitted that they could and should have done more and apologized for not being present. Reconciliation occurred three years earlier. During his family’s present bereavement, that same church is mowing his mother’s lawn, providing food and facilities, and hosting the coming celebration of life.

Josh presents this repaired relationship as a picture of the church and of the unity for which Jesus prayed (John 17:20–23, 06:05). Unity is not the absence of every rupture; it is the shared determination to pursue restoration when unity is lost. Whether one is hurt or doing the hurting, both parties bear responsibility to pursue reconciliation. Pointing a finger while refusing that work disgraces the cross. He pleads with the church to learn from his error: do not harbor decades of resentment; instead, “make every effort to keep the unity of the Spirit through the bond of peace” (Ephesians 4:3, 06:47).

The transition from reconciliation to the sermon’s primary subject sharpens through two texts. James says that everyone stumbles in many ways (James 3:2, 07:01); therefore, believers should not answer another person’s stumbling by attacking character, kicking the person while down, destroying relationships, or halting the church’s progress. Josh and the elders recommit themselves to building a healthy church. He does not promise that no one will be hurt, but he does promise that restoration can be pursued biblically. He summarizes the process in Matthew 18:15–17 (07:40): go directly to the person; if necessary, take witnesses who seek unity rather than a factional victory; then involve church leadership; separate only after every effort has been exhausted.
Transition: At 08:15, Josh identifies the tongue as “the number one cause of all church hurt” and turns from the personal reconciliation frame to James 3.

documents.excerpt: Josh places the day’s text inside the series’ progression through James. James 1:2–4 is summarized as teaching that the mature Christian is patient in trials (08:20). excerpts: Josh says the average person speaks about 16,000 words per day—the equivalent of a 64-page book—and turns the statistic into James’s implied question: What kind of story are your words writing?

A humorous contrast between internal and external processors makes the application personal. Some people need help stopping; others need encouragement to speak. He invokes Shrek’s complaint about Donkey, then has the congregation identify which style describes them. Couples often pair one internal with one external processor. Josh jokes that two external processors may need the church’s Bind marriage ministry.

He uses his marriage as the main illustration. Josh externally processes and appreciates that his wife listens well. When she speaks less, he can assume something is wrong; he must remember that she is processing without needing his volume of words. He briefly invites couples married four years or forty to the upcoming marriage-enrichment course.

documents.excerpt: Josh repeats James 3:1 (14:05): not many should presume to teach because teachers are judged more strictly.
excerpts: Josh repeats James 3:1 (14:05): not many should presume to teach because teachers are judged more strictly.

He reconstructs the church problem behind the warning. Believers were gathering in homes but using speech for gossip, lies, and slander rather than prayer and encouragement. Verse 1 implies that many wanted spiritual influence and the pulpit’s visibility.

James is not rejecting the gift or office of teaching. Paul calls church oversight a noble task (1 Timothy 3:1, 14:59). The warning is that gifting is insufficient by itself; leadership must be joined to humility, responsibility, and accountability. The would-be teachers wanted to stand and declare rather than deny themselves.

Josh applies the standard to himself and church governance. If his work is to teach biblical truth, his life must demonstrate a desire to obey what he teaches. Congregations often demand leader accountability while leaders themselves evade it. Although he does not make governance a salvation issue, he considers genuine eldership highly significant. He rejects both leaderless churches and token boards made of friendly insiders. Crossroads’ elders are described as godly men who humble him and hold him responsible so that he does not obstruct God’s work; he reciprocates that accountability.

He repeats the point of James 3:1 at 17:02: stricter judgment concerns obedience and integrity, not a separate route of salvation. Given a choice between an extraordinary communicator who does not obey and a poor communicator who first applies the Word to himself, Josh chooses the latter. 2 Timothy 4:2 (17:37) defines the teacher’s task: preach the Word, remain ready in and out of season, and correct, rebuke, and encourage with patience and careful instruction. A teacher who is unprepared or unwilling to examine himself should not hold the microphone.
Transition: Teachers are not the only people who sin. At 17:52, Josh widens James’s demand from leaders to every Christian.

documents.excerpt: Josh repeats James 3:2 (17:58): everyone stumbles, and control of speech demonstrates capacity to keep the whole body in check. James includes himself; universal failure does not make failure acceptable. Everyone has weaknesses and blind spots and therefore needs other believers. Josh paraphrases the verse’s force: if a person can control “that big hole in your face,” the rest of the body can also come under control.
excerpts: Josh repeats James 3:2 (17:58): everyone stumbles, and control of speech demonstrates capacity to keep the whole body in check. James includes himself; universal failure does not make failure acceptable. Everyone has weaknesses and blind spots and therefore needs other believers. Josh paraphrases the verse’s force: if a person can control “that big hole in your face,” the rest of the body can also come under control.

He argues that the mouth may be the believer’s foundational self-control problem. Addiction, pornography, anxiety, comparison, social-media envy, and substance abuse are real problems, but many remain undefeated because the person has never learned to govern speech. The church is “a hospital for sinners, not a holiday for saints”; wounded people are welcome if they desire healing, while self-satisfied people will resist correction.

Proverbs supplies concrete speech disciplines. Proverbs 15:1–2 (20:07): a gentle answer turns away wrath, whereas harshness stirs anger; wisdom handles knowledge rightly while folly gushes from the mouth. When accusations fly, do not retaliate—learn what is possible, speak life, and move on. Proverbs 12:22 (20:25): God detests lying lips and delights in trustworthy people. The standard is what delights God, not what wins human approval. Josh invokes Zephaniah 1:7 (20:39) to counsel silence before God rather than lying. Proverbs 10:19 (21:08): multiplying words does not end sin; prudence restrains the tongue. These practices make the tongue a training ground for resisting temptation. Learning to stop a lie can train a person to stop cheating, pornography, or destructive drinking.

The dog-leash illustration tests who is controlling whom. A strong man walking a Chihuahua depicts the desired mastery: the small animal is fully restrained. Josh’s wife being pulled by a Great Dane depicts many people’s relationship to speech: when the tongue bolts, the person goes wherever it leads. His diagnostic question is, “You got that tongue on a leash, or does it have you on a leash?”

Josh returns to James’s bit and rudder (James 3:3–4, 22:53). Both small instruments can guide something massive when properly controlled and can permit disaster when not. As bit and rudder resist beast, wind, and waves, Christians resist the old nature, flesh, and sinful desire. An impulse does not automatically deserve expression. Write it down, pray over it, and ask whether speaking would be beneficial or destructive.

Control also requires the right master. A bit is useless without a trained rider, and a rudder is useless without a captain. Many have assigned Jesus the role of deckhand while remaining in the captain’s chair. Josh calls them to step down and let the Master of creation lead. Some try to restrain speech without receiving a new heart; others have a new heart but refuse to ask the Lord for help.

Scripture ties life-giving speech to heart-level dependence. Proverbs 18:21 (24:45) says the tongue carries the power of life and death. David’s prayer in Psalm 141:3–4 (24:55) asks God to guard his mouth, watch the door of his lips, and keep his heart from evil. Jesus’ warning in Matthew 12:34–37 (25:17) says the mouth speaks from the heart’s overflow and that every empty word will face judgment; words reveal either acquittal or condemnation.
Transition: The tongue guides, so believers must guide people in the right direction. At 25:53, Josh turns to its power to destroy.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · October 13, 2025 · James : A Faith That Works
documents.excerpt: Josh repeats James 3:5 (25:55): the small, boastful tongue resembles a spark that can ignite a great forest.
excerpts: Josh repeats James 3:5 (25:55): the small, boastful tongue resembles a spark that can ignite a great forest.

The Great Chicago Fire becomes the opening scale illustration. Josh tells the traditional story of Mrs. O’Leary’s cow kicking over a lantern on October 8, 1871, followed by 100,000 people displaced, 17,500 buildings destroyed, 300 deaths, and $40 million in damage. His sermonic point is not the historical cause itself but the disproportion between a small ignition and enormous devastation: one match can burn a house, and one mouth can start relational fires.

He translates wildfire “burn scars” into relational damage. Some hearers have left scorched places in a marriage, workplace, or church through their words. Proverbs 26:20–21 (27:02) says a fire dies without wood and a quarrel without gossip; a quarrelsome person kindles strife as fuel feeds flame. Churches can be scarred by members and leaders who cannot govern speech. Yet removing persistent fire starters can allow a green shoot of unity and love to emerge; God can redeem a blackened field.

Hurtful words do not merely burn institutions; they wound people. Jesus himself was called a glutton, drunkard, and friend of tax collectors and sinners (Matthew 11:19, 27:57). Opponents attributed his miracles to Satan (Matthew 12:24, 28:10), and mockery continued at the cross. Josh’s point is that hostile tongues injured even the sinless Son of Man.

He broadens destructive rhetoric from relationships to societies. Hitler’s communication gathered a furious army under the language of patriotic duty; Josh uses this as an example of gifted rhetoric serving profound evil. He argues that dehumanizing language supports abortion by calling a baby a “clump of cells.” He similarly connects the endurance of American slavery to rhetoric that devalued and dehumanized people. The transition back to ordinary hearers is deliberate: they may not direct wars or systems, but everyone should examine whether their words have broken a heart, damaged a reputation, or turned someone away from the gospel.

“Your tongue is your testimony” becomes the corrective. Colossians 4:6 (30:26) calls every conversation to be full of grace and seasoned with salt so the believer knows how to answer each person. Josh defines gracious speech as spiritual, good, wholesome, appropriate, kind, sensitive, truthful, uplifting, gentle, purposeful, loving, and thoughtful. “Seasoned with salt” means preparing and praying rather than unloading unfiltered “verbal vomit.”
Transition: At 31:03, Josh returns to James’s animal and poison images to deepen the destructive-power warning.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · October 13, 2025 · James : A Faith That Works
documents.excerpt: Josh repeats James 3:7–8 (31:03): people tame animals, birds, reptiles, and sea creatures, but no human being can tame the restless, poison-filled tongue.
excerpts: Josh repeats James 3:7–8 (31:03): people tame animals, birds, reptiles, and sea creatures, but no human being can tame the restless, poison-filled tongue.

A family visit to Out of Africa supplies the illustration. Zoo barriers can make wild animals look domesticated. Josh talked to a tiger through the fence until it stood against the barrier and revealed its true size and danger. Without the fence, Josh says, he would have been a snack. The tongue similarly pounces and kills when its nature is left unchecked.

Not every dangerous tongue appears large or overpowering. Some look small and harmless but carry enough relational toxin to bring down something much larger. In fifteen years of pastoral ministry, Josh has watched toxic speech harm individuals, families, life groups, and entire churches. His sharp application is that people who avoid a snake on a hiking trail may still converse with one in the church lobby. Believers should avoid people whose loose lips spread poison.

He pauses to inventory tongue-enabled sins. Against God: profanity, irreverence, and blasphemy. Against people: deceit, gossip, backbiting, division, verbal abuse, manipulation, and seduction. Additional patterns include boasting, bragging, comparison, complaining, and whining. Speech is the interface among thought, intention, and action, which is why so much sin travels through it.

Human inability is not God’s inability. Josh carries forward James 3:6 at 34:48: no one must remain a tongue set aflame by hell. God can instead ignite speech with a “heavenly blaze,” enabling believers to tell sinners about the Savior, carry light into darkness, and serve the Great Commission (Matthew 28:18–20, 34:59). Hate in the heart lets the tongue drag the person wherever it wants; love in the heart gives speech a divine purpose to speak life.
Transition: At 35:27, Josh announces James’s final reminder: the tongue also has power to bless.

documents.excerpt: Josh names the contradiction in James 3:9–10 (35:36) “cross-contamination.” Christians praise the Lord and Father and then curse people made in God’s likeness. James is speaking not merely to nominal Christians but to participants who attend worship, seek Scripture, and say they want to obey.
excerpts: Josh names the contradiction in James 3:9–10 (35:36) “cross-contamination.” Christians praise the Lord and Father and then curse people made in God’s likeness. James is speaking not merely to nominal Christians but to participants who attend worship, seek Scripture, and say they want to obey.

Josh stages the contradiction in a Sunday-morning sequence. Worshipers sing that God is worthy, shout amen and hallelujah, take the Lord’s Supper, and then argue in the lobby or curse family members on the drive home. His memorable line is that they have just eaten the Lord’s Supper and now want to “eat a believer.”

Cursing an image-bearer is an offense against the God whose image that person bears. A person cannot excuse domestic rage by saying at least it was not directed at God. Spouses, parents, and children who verbally shred one another attack someone marked by the Creator.

The hypocrisy is intensified by the believer’s claim to possess the Spirit who raised Jesus from the dead (Romans 8:11, 37:33). Someone comes seeking Christ’s fresh water but receives the Christian’s salt water instead. James’s spring image makes such output evidence of a source problem.

Josh locates the source in the heart, not in the tongue as an isolated organ. Matthew 15:18 (38:01) says what comes from the mouth comes from the heart and defiles the person. Persistent criticism, gossip, and character assassination cannot finally be blamed on the target; the occasion exposed wickedness already present in the speaker. “That’s not really me” fails as an excuse: the words had to be within the person before they could come out.

The proper prayer is therefore deeper than “help me control my tongue.” Believers must run to God with destructive speech and ask him to soften the heart. Josh relieves the intensity with a joke: a woman wants to put her tongue on the altar, and the pastor replies that the altar is not that big. He then returns to the leash image: for many people, life feels like a constant fight because their tongue drags them. Give God the heart, and he will help with the tongue.
Transition: At 39:51, Josh offers practical “ammunition”—sincere, life-giving phrases to replace habitual destruction.
