documents.excerpt: Josh warns that these phrases are not mechanical substitutions. They produce relational change only when meant sincerely and spoken from a transformed heart.
excerpts: Josh warns that these phrases are not mechanical substitutions. They produce relational change only when meant sincerely and spoken from a transformed heart.

“I appreciate you” (40:19). People’s lives change when they know what they mean to someone. Related practices include “please,” “thank you,” and, especially in marriage, “I don’t know what I’d do without you.” Children should recognize that their parents’ anniversary is also a blessing to them and say so.
“I’m sorry” (40:51). Christians still need to apologize for their actions. Delaying an apology is like skipping a medical checkup: it may save time now but costs more later.
“I love you” (41:11). This belongs not only in homes and marriages but among the family of believers. If Christians do not sincerely love one another, something in the church requires repair.

“I’m praying for you” (41:26). The phrase is good only if the speaker actually prays rather than using a Christian blanket statement and forgetting the person. Private intercession places people in the Father’s care and makes public cursing less likely.

“I see God working in your life” (41:57). Saying this requires enough relational closeness to notice grace at work. Josh offers two related blessings: “Watching you grow in Christ has been a blessing to me” and “I see Christ in you.” Sincere recognition helps form unshakable bonds within the family of faith.
Josh recaps James 3:5, 9–10 at 42:20: the tongue is small and often troublesome, but among God’s people it should be a blessing.
Transition: Because the tongue insists on being busy, Josh urges the church to put it to work for the Lord. The leash image then leads directly into the gospel invitation.

documents.excerpt: Josh addresses anyone still being dragged by the tongue. The invitation is to confess sin, repent, and put faith in Jesus Christ. The gospel is not a to-do list but good news about what Christ has done. Grace received through faith gives new life and identity, and God begins a work that ends in eternal life.
excerpts: Josh addresses anyone still being dragged by the tongue. The invitation is to confess sin, repent, and put faith in Jesus Christ. The gospel is not a to-do list but good news about what Christ has done. Grace received through faith gives new life and identity, and God begins a work that ends in eternal life.

The call is framed as decisive discipleship. Stop and drop the old direction, deny oneself, take up the cross, and follow Christ (Matthew 16:24; Mark 8:34; Luke 9:23, 43:10). Put away the past, release grudges, and walk with Christ. Josh repeats Zephaniah’s summons to silence before the Lord because his day is near (Zephaniah 1:7, 43:17).
The ready baptism waters turn transformed speech into public testimony. He invites hearers to use the tongue for its created purpose: testifying to God’s goodness.

Josh’s prayer asks God to use Scripture to produce not merely Christian-sounding speech but Christlike lives. He asks God to shape, mold, and use the congregation. The morning rainbow reminded him of God’s covenant never again to deal with earthly wickedness by a flood (Genesis 9:8–17, 44:09). He contrasts that old flood with the “flood of grace and mercy” made available to repentant sinners through the Savior’s blood. At the Communion table, he asks the church to remember promises already given and promises awaiting fulfillment. The prayer closes in longing for Christ’s return and presence, followed by “Amen” at 45:16.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · October 6, 2025 · James : A Faith That Works
documents.excerpt: Josh opens by calling faith indispensable to Christian life. The sinner is saved by grace through faith, not works, so glory belongs to God rather than the believer (Ephesians 2:8–9). He reads the Westminster Confession of Faith on effectual calling and justification: God pardons and accepts sinners because Christ’s obedience and satisfaction are imputed to them; faith receives and rests in Christ’s righteousness but is itself God’s gift. He distills the confession: faith is the means by which believers receive and rest beneath Christ’s righteousness.
excerpts: Josh opens by calling faith indispensable to Christian life. The sinner is saved by grace through faith, not works, so glory belongs to God rather than the believer (Ephesians 2:8–9). He reads the Westminster Confession of Faith on effectual calling and justification: God pardons and accepts sinners because Christ’s obedience and satisfaction are imputed to them; faith receives and rests in Christ’s righteousness but is itself God’s gift. He distills the confession: faith is the means by which believers receive and rest beneath Christ’s righteousness.

He establishes several biblical functions of faith in sequence. A person is justified through faith in Christ, not law observance (Galatians 2:16). The believer walks by faith rather than by visible circumstances (2 Corinthians 5:7); God’s Word, not merely sensory experience, governs decisions, priorities, and worldview. Faith is necessary to please God (Hebrews 11:6). The rescued believer longs to please the Father as a child longs for a father’s return. He surveys Hebrews 11 in the chapter’s order: Noah, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, Moses and his parents, Israel at the Red Sea, Jericho, Rahab, and persecuted saints all acted on promises they had not yet received. documents.excerpt: Josh stages the apparent conflict. James says a person is justified by what they do and not by faith alone (James 2:24). Paul says a person is justified by faith apart from works of the law (Romans 3:28). Skeptics treat those statements as a contradiction and force a false choice between “team Paul” and “team James.”
excerpts: Josh stages the apparent conflict. James says a person is justified by what they do and not by faith alone (James 2:24). Paul says a person is justified by faith apart from works of the law (Romans 3:28). Skeptics treat those statements as a contradiction and force a false choice between “team Paul” and “team James.”

Perspective resolves the apparent conflict. James writes pastorally to lead professing believers into a living faith that blesses God and others; he is concerned with the effectiveness of the believer and the church. Paul writes as a missionary emphasizing entry into right standing with God. The early church treated James and Romans as complementary, and the Jerusalem council reached agreement (Acts 15). James addresses works of love; Paul rejects works of the law as a means of becoming right with God.

Josh explains two uses of “justify.” His word illustration contrasts an original sense of “nice” with its common modern use: words can carry more than one accepted sense. “Justify” can mean make right or prove right. The push-up illustration makes the distinction concrete: asking a man to “justify” his claim that he can do one hundred push-ups does not make the claim true; it asks him to demonstrate that it is true.

Applied to Paul and James: Paul’s “justified by faith” means sinners can only be made right with God through Jesus Christ’s person and finished work. James’s works of love prove that someone has been made right with God. A profession alone cannot provide that proof; consistent life change and an outpouring of love do.

Josh presses the diagnostic implication. If only the claimant can detect the supposed faith, and the life does not show it, the faith is dead or worse. Christians should not need to advertise the label; people should see the reality. He invokes Jesus’s warning to the lukewarm church about being spit out, then quotes the synthesis: “We’re saved by faith alone, but not by a faith that remains alone.” Works do not make a sinner right; in saving faith, works are not optional but inevitable—never perfect, yet consistent.

documents.excerpt: Dead faith replaces works with words. A person may pray fluently, speak Christian language, and recite verses while never letting talk shape the walk. Jesus warns that saying “Lord, Lord” is not equivalent to doing the Father’s will (Matthew 7:21).
excerpts: Dead faith replaces works with words. A person may pray fluently, speak Christian language, and recite verses while never letting talk shape the walk. Jesus warns that saying “Lord, Lord” is not equivalent to doing the Father’s will (Matthew 7:21).

Josh returns to James’s needy-brother example (James 2:14–16). Empty wishes that a hungry or poorly clothed person be warm and fed accomplish nothing. A visitor should not leave a believer’s presence unaffected: when material needs are absent, offer the gospel and prayer; when needs are present, offer the gospel, prayer, and practical help. Paul likewise commands believers to do good to everyone, especially the family of believers (Galatians 6:10).

Crossroads Care Center becomes the immediate congregational application. Josh presents its opening as the church’s faith forcing it outward rather than allowing it to sit still. Members are the church’s eyes and ears: notice needs in family, neighborhood, workplace, or community; recommend the center and pass needs to people ready to serve. Because the local body is committed to this work, those who call Crossroads home have no excuse for ignoring another person’s physical need. Such help expresses love and changes how outsiders see the church—love extends to believers, strangers, and enemies.

Paul’s phrase “faith expressing itself through love” (Galatians 5:6) becomes Josh’s compact test. Religious accomplishments do not count if faith does not express itself in love. Josh includes himself: his sermons mean nothing without love; Elijah’s music is only noise and clanging if unaccompanied by love (1 Corinthians 13:1–3).

The Good Samaritan exposes respectable dead faith. A priest and Levite possessed formal religious standing and doctrine but passed the wounded man rather than ministering to him (Luke 10:30–32). Josh criticizes a modern church culture that trains as though defending the gospel were its sole purpose while neglecting active love. Defense matters, but Christianity has already survived for centuries and has moved believers to establish hospitals, schools, charities, welfare programs, and governments. Too many Christians measure effectiveness by pages turned rather than feet washed; unlimited sermon clips can make anyone appear theologically informed.

James’s question remains: Can a faith never seen in love save? Josh answers no. Any faith producing neither life change nor an outpouring of love is dead. He quotes John Calvin’s formulation that faith alone justifies, but justifying faith can never remain alone, then repeats James 2:17. Dead faith reduces salvation to a tidy intellectual exercise without personal trust in Jesus. Application: do not be deceived; examine whether faith is saving or counterfeit, because saving faith works.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · October 6, 2025 · James : A Faith That Works
documents.excerpt: James imagines an objector and answers from James 2:18–19: deeds display faith, while even demons believe there is one God and shudder.
excerpts: James imagines an objector and answers from James 2:18–19: deeds display faith, while even demons believe there is one God and shudder.

Josh says this second counterfeit comes frighteningly close to saving faith. Demons are real, and he treats demonic activity as a reality even around church life, listing guilt, fear, depression, anxiety, discrimination, addiction, confusion, hatred, worry, and unexplained changes or reactions as ways people may describe its activity. Demons are neither atheists nor agnostics; they are theists.

Their doctrine is extensive. They recognize Christ’s deity: Josh cites the fullness of deity dwelling bodily in Christ (Colossians 2:9) and the evil spirits calling Jesus the Son of God (Mark 3:11). They know a place of punishment exists and beg Jesus not to send them into the abyss (Luke 8:31). They respect divine authority and power, fear judgment, and submit because they have no alternative.

The warning: humans can approach saving faith just as closely and remain lost. A person may affirm God’s greatness, respect his power, fear punishment, and become moral and religious, yet possess only shuddering terror. James invokes the Shema, Israel’s daily confession that the Lord is one (Deuteronomy 6:4), then observes that demons affirm the same monotheism (James 2:19).

Josh distinguishes valid components from saving evidence. Solid doctrine and intellectual understanding are good. Strong emotion in worship is also good; Josh admits worship moves him deeply. But neither intellect nor emotion proves authentic saving faith. A person may have correct beliefs and feelings and still be lost. Authentic faith is not merely believing in God; it is believing God—taking him at his Word regardless of cost because he is faithful.
Transition to living faith: saving faith can be seen, witnessed, shared, and celebrated because it produces a changed life and God’s love toward others.

documents.excerpt: James and Paul again converge: faith cannot be displayed without deeds, and believers are God’s workmanship, created in Christ for prepared good works (Ephesians 2:10).
excerpts: James and Paul again converge: faith cannot be displayed without deeds, and believers are God’s workmanship, created in Christ for prepared good works (Ephesians 2:10).

Josh’s staff-painting illustration explains visibility. His poor winter landscape belongs in the laundry room where only the dogs see it. God’s workmanship is a masterpiece, not something hidden in a laundry room or garage; he puts it in the foyer for everyone to see.

That visible grace shapes Christian testimony. Christians may describe their former condition with humiliating language—“wretched, pitiful, poor, blind and naked” (Revelation 3:17)—because they recognize what grace changed. Josh rejects sentimental claims that every person is already God’s child: all people bear God’s image, but adoption as God’s children comes through faith in Christ. Appeals that stop at intellect produce dead faith; appeals that stop at emotion can produce something no better than demonic faith. The decisive issue is not what someone feels or thinks but whom they trust.

James now demands evidence that faith without deeds is useless (James 2:20). Josh recalls an earlier point in the James : A Faith That Works series: God gives birth through the word of truth (James 1:18); the received word saves (James 1:21); faith comes by hearing the message about Christ (Romans 10:17). James’s positive evidence will be Abraham and Rahab—social and moral opposites united by saving faith.

documents.excerpt: Josh reads James’s first example: Abraham was shown righteous when he offered Isaac (James 2:21).
excerpts: Josh reads James’s first example: Abraham was shown righteous when he offered Isaac (James 2:21).

He distinguishes two moments in Abraham’s chronology. Genesis 15: Abraham trusts God; God credits righteousness to his empty spiritual account. This is Abraham’s justification by faith. Genesis 22: the already-justified Abraham offers the promised son. This does not purchase salvation; it demonstrates faith and receives blessing.

Josh defines justification carefully. God declares the believing sinner righteous on the basis of Christ’s finished work on the cross. It is a completed divine act, not a process and not something the sinner performs. The ensuing changed life and obedience reveal that God has done it.
He frames the change as movement from disobedience in Eden to surrender in Gethsemane; “your will be done” becomes the believer’s battle cry.

Abraham’s ascent of the mountain supplies the evidence. He was willing to surrender the child of promise. His obedience proved the salvation he had already received. God’s gift in Genesis 15 enabled Abraham’s surrender in Genesis 22.

Conclusion: Faith and works are partners, not rivals. By faith Abraham was declared righteous before God; by works that righteousness was displayed before people. Abraham was not saved by faith plus a work, but by a faith that works.

documents.excerpt: Josh reads James’s second example, Rahab sheltering the spies and sending them out another way (James 2:25). Abraham demonstrates true obedience; Rahab demonstrates true sacrifice. The Jewish patriarch and the Gentile prostitute stand at opposite social locations, yet both possess saving faith.
excerpts: Josh reads James’s second example, Rahab sheltering the spies and sending them out another way (James 2:25). Abraham demonstrates true obedience; Rahab demonstrates true sacrifice. The Jewish patriarch and the Gentile prostitute stand at opposite social locations, yet both possess saving faith.

He retells Joshua 2. Rahab hears that Israel’s God is the true God, hides the spies, risks her life, seeks protection for her family, and shares the news with them. Authentic faith reaches mind, heart, and hands together; it sacrifices for others, dies to self, and lives for God. Her transformed identity illustrates the new creation in Christ (2 Corinthians 5:17).

Josh contrasts Rahab’s limited revelation with the congregation’s abundance. She had only a garbled report about the Red Sea drying up, yet acted. Present believers possess the full revelation of God, evidence after Calvary, and the Spirit’s guidance and conviction. Her response to a small amount of testimony becomes Josh’s “mustard seed” picture of faith.

Her lie creates a moral-pressure application. Rahab defies her government, hides the spies, and lies to protect them. Josh acknowledges the command against false testimony, then asks what someone should do when the available choices are lying or helping a murderer. His answer: when trapped between sinful options, choose the act that brings God greater glory and seek God in the moment. He analogizes to Corrie ten Boom in Germany, who lied to German officers while hiding Jews: truth-telling in that setting would have assisted murder. Rahab does not convene a study group or wait for a long counseling session; she walks by faith, acts courageously, and does what she believes honors God.
James’s closing image (James 2:26) seals the argument: as a body without the spirit is dead, faith without works is dead.

documents.excerpt: Josh summarizes living faith. Christians practice truth; they do not organize faith as an external system—faith reorganizes them. Abraham risks everything because God is able; Rahab takes courageous risks because God is with her.
excerpts: Josh summarizes living faith. Christians practice truth; they do not organize faith as an external system—faith reorganizes them. Abraham risks everything because God is able; Rahab takes courageous risks because God is with her.

He asks every believer to examine the heart, repeating Paul’s command to test whether one is in the faith (2 Corinthians 13:5). This is the most important test a person can take. The listener must evaluate self rather than spouse, neighbor, or anyone else.

The questions proceed in Josh’s order: Conviction of sin: Was there a time of humble, honest admission to God that you are a sinner? Has sin against a holy and just God ever disturbed and crushed you, even if others would call the offenses minor? Understanding the gospel: Do you understand that the Maker became man, bled and died for sins, and rose so sinners could have life—and that you cannot save yourself? Repentance: Have you sincerely turned from sin? Repentance is not apology followed by an unchanged sinful lifestyle; it includes frustration with and hatred of sin rather than secret preference for it. Trust and relationship: Have you trusted Christ for salvation? Do you enjoy him through the Word and fellowship, place anxieties and burdens at his feet, experience his help, and find joy in walking with him? Response to conviction: Do you welcome the Spirit’s correction, put down fleshly desires, and walk God’s way? Observable change: Can you identify changed attitudes, weakened addictions, altered mindsets, or renewed treatment of a spouse as places Jesus is working? Consistency and dependence: Does faith work consistently through sanctification, or repeatedly stall? “Do you have a faith that works?”: the self-examination
Josh summarizes living faith. Christians practice truth; they do not organize faith as an external system—faith reorganizes them. Abraham risks everything because God is able; Rahab takes courageous risks because God is with her.
He asks every believer to examine the heart, repeating Paul’s command to test whether one is in the faith (2 Corinthians 13:5). This is the most important test a person can take. The listener must evaluate self rather than spouse, neighbor, or anyone else.
The questions proceed in Josh’s order: Conviction of sin: Was there a time of humble, honest admission to God that you are a sinner? Has sin against a holy and just God ever disturbed and crushed you, even if others would call the offenses minor? Understanding the gospel: Do you understand that the Maker became man, bled and died for sins, and rose so sinners could have life—and that you cannot save yourself? Repentance: Have you sincerely turned from sin? Repentance is not apology followed by an unchanged sinful lifestyle; it includes frustration with and hatred of sin rather than secret preference for it. Trust and relationship: Have you trusted Christ for salvation? Do you enjoy him through the Word and fellowship, place anxieties and burdens at his feet, experience his help, and find joy in walking with him? Response to conviction: Do you welcome the Spirit’s correction, put down fleshly desires, and walk God’s way? Observable change: Can you identify changed attitudes, weakened addictions, altered mindsets, or renewed treatment of a spouse as places Jesus is working? Consistency and dependence: Does faith work consistently through sanctification, or repeatedly stall? Are you dependent on a church service, pastor, or other believers to feed you, or on God to fill, renew, and accompany you? Witness: Do you tell others about Jesus, or are you ashamed to speak the gospel plainly? Corporate worship: Do you delight to worship with God’s people, or can you barely bring yourself to attend? Christ’s return: When Jesus appears, will you rejoice that he has come, or look back anxiously at what you are leaving?

excerpts: Josh prays after acknowledging that the test gives the congregation much to consider.

He asks God to expose faith that is not working itself out through love. Some are still wrestling with the first question and need conviction. Others feel the burden of sin but have not fully trusted the One who lifts it. He asks Jesus to give them the promised rest offered to those who come to him (Matthew 11:28–29).

Recognizing that self-examination can itself be deceived, he turns the language of Psalm 139:23–24 into prayer: Search and know the heart more deeply than the worshiper can. Reveal any way that is not pleasing to God. Lead the congregation in the everlasting way.

As believers approach the communion table and sit under God’s promises, he asks for assurance and peace. Their security rests in God’s hands and in his promise never to leave or forsake them (Hebrews 13:5). He closes, “Thank you, Lord. We love you. It’s in your name we pray. Amen.”

documents.excerpt: Josh begins by restoring the weight of Scripture and clarifying his posture toward the church. He is not speaking down from a place of having “cracked the code”; he is a man who sits under the Word, loves Jesus, and wants the church to reflect Christ’s goodness, grace, mercy, and faithfulness. His pastoral responsibility is to bring God’s Word before believers so they will wrestle with it and ultimately submit to it. He asks the congregation to honor the fact that he has wrestled first: preparation is not an attempt to make the sermon pleasing, but an attempt to align his own life before pressing the text upon them.
excerpts: Josh begins by restoring the weight of Scripture and clarifying his posture toward the church. He is not speaking down from a place of having “cracked the code”; he is a man who sits under the Word, loves Jesus, and wants the church to reflect Christ’s goodness, grace, mercy, and faithfulness. His pastoral responsibility is to bring God’s Word before believers so they will wrestle with it and ultimately submit to it. He asks the congregation to honor the fact that he has wrestled first: preparation is not an attempt to make the sermon pleasing, but an attempt to align his own life before pressing the text upon them.

He draws the sermon’s opening dividing line: immature Christians talk about what they believe; mature Christians strive to live what they believe. The room includes mature believers, immature believers, and unbelievers, so each person will receive the Word according to his or her position before God. Last week’s warning continues: a person can look and sound Christian, display the expected Sunday behaviors, and still possess only a tradition-shaped “Sunday show,” not life-altering faith. James will press mature believers but may feel crushing to immature believers or unbelievers. Josh promises to walk arm in arm with them as they wrestle and submit; the series will not get easier.

The YMCA workout with his fourteen-year-old nephew illustrates calibrated spiritual pressure. Josh did not give the boy a workout built for Josh’s strength or drop a 225-pound bar on him; he gave him enough weight to make him strain, improve, and grow. Likewise, James is not satisfied with hearing or discussing God’s Word. Those activities cannot substitute for doing it (James 1:22).

A statement of faith is useful for defining agreement, but agreement alone cannot produce Christian character. Josh recounts serving beside someone who agreed with him on essentials: Scripture’s authority, the Trinity, Christ’s person and work, the gospel, and historic creeds. They also agreed on secondary and tertiary matters: baptism, the Lord’s Supper, church governance, women in ministry, gifts, covenant theology, worship styles, communion frequency, eschatology, politics, alcohol in moderation, schooling, and indifference to the young-earth/old-earth argument. Josh uses humor—including the flat-earth joke—and then reveals the point: the man was his theological “twin” but had an enormous ego and treated people badly.

The transition into James 2 is relational and diagnostic. Beliefs do not by themselves reveal one’s view of God; treatment of other people does. Human relationships cannot be detached from relationship with God. Josh quotes 1 John 4:20: claiming love for God while hating or demeaning a visible brother or sister makes the claim a lie. He asks the church to hold that verse in mind as the sermon moves into favoritism.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · September 29, 2025 · James : A Faith That Works
documents.excerpt: Josh states the primary passage and defines the problem before reading it. James 2:1–13 is one continuous treatment of favoritism and discrimination. Discrimination is not limited to race; it is unjust treatment of someone because that person differs from you. Prejudice is the inward attitude that may be hidden; discrimination is that attitude made visible in action. James is retraining believers away from worldly preferences and into God’s preferences for how people are treated.
excerpts: Josh states the primary passage and defines the problem before reading it. James 2:1–13 is one continuous treatment of favoritism and discrimination. Discrimination is not limited to race; it is unjust treatment of someone because that person differs from you. Prejudice is the inward attitude that may be hidden; discrimination is that attitude made visible in action. James is retraining believers away from worldly preferences and into God’s preferences for how people are treated.
He reads James 2:1–4: believers in the glorious Lord Jesus Christ must not favor the finely dressed, gold-ringed visitor over the poor person in filthy clothes.

Josh lingers over James’s title, “our glorious Lord Jesus Christ.” He understands it as pointing to Christ’s exalted heavenly status: Christ sits at God’s right hand and will return to judge and save. The title is strategically opposed to the church’s error. They are giving excessive glory to people, so James directs glory to the One who deserves it.

Their beliefs are not informing their behavior. They infer inward worth from outward appearance and permit worldly markers to determine spiritual value. Favoritism mistreats someone who fails to meet personal standards even while meeting God’s standards. Josh exposes the pride: the discriminator effectively claims the place of God by devaluing someone who pleases God but does not please him.

The desire for recognition and relevance is dangerous. Josh points to Jesus’s table parable in Luke 14 and its conclusion that self-exaltation ends in humiliation while humility ends in exaltation. He refuses to let the local congregation blame only the wider institutional church. Clique-seeking and attempts to climb a church ladder for visibility are present “in this very church.”

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · September 29, 2025 · James : A Faith That Works
documents.excerpt: Josh confronts people who rarely leave their favorite group to help newcomers connect. The “discipleship” defense can become an excuse for maintaining only deep relationships with existing friends. The Great Commission speaks of nations being taught what Jesus commanded; one need not be a person’s best friend before teaching the Lord’s words. The church needs new relationships to fulfill its mission, not only tighter circles among existing buddies.
excerpts: Josh confronts people who rarely leave their favorite group to help newcomers connect. The “discipleship” defense can become an excuse for maintaining only deep relationships with existing friends. The Great Commission speaks of nations being taught what Jesus commanded; one need not be a person’s best friend before teaching the Lord’s words. The church needs new relationships to fulfill its mission, not only tighter circles among existing buddies.

He acknowledges the natural pull toward similarity and ease. People gravitate to those who look, talk, think, work, serve, or recreate like they do: wealthy people toward the wealthy, military members toward military members, musicians toward musicians, and fitness enthusiasts toward fitness enthusiasts. Harder people demand more and may feel draining, which makes the easy affinity group attractive. His bald-men joke briefly lightens the rebuke, after which he asks forgiveness and returns to the point.

The cost is visible at the church door: seekers enter and see everyone’s back. Josh asks when listeners last sought out a newcomer, took that person to lunch, invited the person into a life group, heard the person’s story, and offered a blessing. That shared work belongs to the congregation, not merely to the pastor.

Jesus models freedom from status judgments. Josh quotes Jesus’s opponents in Matthew 22:16: even they admitted that Jesus taught truth without being swayed by who people were. The widow’s two small coins outweighed the rich people’s large gifts in kingdom valuation; sacrificial poverty reverses ordinary arithmetic.

Jesus sees usefulness and potential rather than only a person’s present shame. Peter could move from denial to being a “rock.” Mary Magdalene could become a witness at the empty tomb. Levi the tax collector could become Matthew, leading people toward gospel treasure. Josh asks when listeners last saw a brother’s or sister’s potential rather than only shortcomings. Even confessed sexual sin and embarrassment can become effective testimony in Jesus’s hands rather than grounds for exclusion.

Christ himself destroys appearance-based valuation. Jesus had nowhere to lay his head, came from despised Nazareth, was known as a carpenter’s son, lived in poverty, and possessed no outward appearance that naturally attracted people—yet he is heaven’s champion. Josh applies John 7:24: stop judging by mere appearances and judge correctly. Because people cannot see the heart directly, they should observe fruit and name both harmful fruit and evidence of change—patience, kindness, generosity, and gentleness—in a way that honors God’s work.
The controlling practice is to view everyone through Christ’s eyes and remember that God may use anyone he desires for his glory. That claim transitions into James 2:5.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · September 29, 2025 · James : A Faith That Works
documents.excerpt: Josh reads James 2:5–7 and gives the theological charge: Partiality dishonors God and displays ignorance of how God works and saves. God sovereignly saves people who cannot earn and do not deserve salvation, entirely on the basis of Christ’s cross rather than personal impressiveness. Romans 8:33–34 grounds his confidence: God justifies his chosen people, and the crucified, risen, enthroned Christ intercedes for them. Josh’s hope rests not in occasionally hitting the target but in Christ as his righteousness.
excerpts: Josh reads James 2:5–7 and gives the theological charge: Partiality dishonors God and displays ignorance of how God works and saves. God sovereignly saves people who cannot earn and do not deserve salvation, entirely on the basis of Christ’s cross rather than personal impressiveness. Romans 8:33–34 grounds his confidence: God justifies his chosen people, and the crucified, risen, enthroned Christ intercedes for them. Josh’s hope rests not in occasionally hitting the target but in Christ as his righteousness.

He distinguishes two senses of poverty. In Matthew 5:3, being poor in spirit is humility: awareness of sin, deserved death, dependence, and the necessity of grace. In Revelation 3:17–18, Laodicean self-sufficiency is a wicked poverty: a person claims wealth and needlessness while actually being wretched, poor, blind, and naked; Christ alone supplies true riches. A person may be materially poor now and rich in eternity, materially rich now and poor in eternity, poor in both, or rich in both. The decisive issues are one’s response to Christ and stewardship of material wealth. God promises the kingdom to those who love him, not those who love his things. Josh lets the room’s discomfort stand and names ordinary signs of wealth, such as a new car or expensive purse.

He prevents an equal-and-opposite misreading. James is not replacing favoritism toward the rich with favoritism toward the poor, nor commanding hatred of the rich. Jesus pressed the rich young ruler but still offered him a real opportunity to put wealth in its proper place; the man walked away sad. The command is no partiality, not redirected partiality: love people as Jesus wants rather than as the world expects.

God’s impartiality extends through nationality and social status. Romans 2:11 states that God does not show favoritism; therefore believers must not. Acts 10 shows God sending Peter to share fellowship with the Gentile Cornelius despite the predominantly Jewish church’s suspicion. Acts 15 then resolves whether Gentiles must become Jews to become Christians; the Spirit-led answer is no. Josh summarizes Paul’s equal verdict on Jew and Gentile in condemnation and salvation, then quotes Romans 2:12 about judgment both apart from and under the law. Grace makes the wealthy unable to depend on wealth and makes the poor heirs of every spiritual blessing in Christ; it is the great equalizer.

James’s accusation against rich oppressors sharpens the contradiction. The same wealthy people who exploit believers, drag them into court, and blaspheme Christ’s name receive privileged treatment in the gathering. Josh loosely cites the love of money as the root of evil and argues that Christ, himself poor and victimized by wealthy corrupt leaders, taught his people to care for the poor rather than profit from them. Matthew 25:40 identifies service to “the least of these” with service to Christ. Ephesians 2 declares the dividing wall destroyed. Rebuilding divisions of wealth, age, ethnicity, education, or nationality is sin against the God who tore those walls down.
Josh pauses—“Breathe”—and summarizes the negative case: partiality sins against God and neighbor. Verse 8 will now state the positive way.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · September 29, 2025 · James : A Faith That Works
documents.excerpt: Josh reads James 2:8: keeping the royal law, “Love your neighbor as yourself,” is doing right. James reaches back to Leviticus 19:18, where love of neighbor is opposed to revenge and grudges.
excerpts: Josh reads James 2:8: keeping the royal law, “Love your neighbor as yourself,” is doing right. James reaches back to Leviticus 19:18, where love of neighbor is opposed to revenge and grudges.

The Good Samaritan reframes neighbor love. Josh’s “pop quiz” asks what question prompted the parable: “Who is my neighbor?” Jesus’s answer makes the neighbor anyone whose need one can meet, regardless of origin, location, or prior activity. The right question is not “Who is my neighbor?” but “Who needs me to be a good neighbor?”

The State Farm illustration challenges church mission. Josh jokes that a large insurance company’s “good neighbor” slogan can sound more biblical than vague church slogans about discovering one’s best self, “reach in/reach out,” or mere acceptance. He contrasts those with a church commitment to change how people see the church by serving the needs of Anthem, Phoenix, and the world, and invites the congregation to join that work.

He gives three ordered reasons “love your neighbor” is the royal law. The King gave it. The Father gave it in the law, the Son taught it to his disciples, and the Spirit fills and convicts God’s children to share divine love. First Thessalonians 4:9 says believers have been taught by God to love one another. It is the law of laws. Romans 13:10 says love does no harm to a neighbor and therefore fulfills the law; universal obedience to the royal law would remove the need for the other restraints. It keeps the royal court open to seekers. Jesus is the way to eternal life, and Christian love is meant to direct people to him rather than close the door.

Luke 6 raises love beyond ordinary reciprocity. Doing good only to those who reciprocate, lending only when repayment is expected, and loving only those who love you do not distinguish disciples from sinners. Jesus commands love for enemies, generosity without expected return, and mercy patterned after the Father’s kindness to the ungrateful and wicked.

Josh crystallizes the application: A person only truly believes what he or she is willing to do. Obedience means loving neighbor, stranger, and enemy as oneself. Anyone in need deserves from the believer what the believer never deserved from God.

documents.excerpt: Josh reads James 2:9 and warns that the sermon is becoming heavy again. Favoritism is not merely an unfortunate fairness problem or a small weakness excused by saying, “At least I have not killed anyone.” James calls the “isms” sin: classism, culturalism, racism, favoritism, sexism, and ageism. Those sins remain inside churches because churches do not consistently treat them as sin.
excerpts: Josh reads James 2:9 and warns that the sermon is becoming heavy again. Favoritism is not merely an unfortunate fairness problem or a small weakness excused by saying, “At least I have not killed anyone.” James calls the “isms” sin: classism, culturalism, racism, favoritism, sexism, and ageism. Those sins remain inside churches because churches do not consistently treat them as sin.

Josh uses his own experience of ageism as a lead pastor. Others look down on him because of his age. He interrupts the argument for an urgent pastoral appeal: no one should be allowed to throttle another person’s usefulness in God’s kingdom. God gives gifts to whom he wants, when he wants, and uses them for his glory. Young people must not let someone assume God’s authority by declaring what they cannot do. The wording deliberately echoes 1 Timothy 4:12: do not let anyone look down on you because of your youth.

He returns to James and reads James 2:10–11. Breaking one point makes a person a breaker of the whole law because the same God forbids adultery and murder. Josh extends James’s logic in sequence: murderer—lawbreaker; adulterer—lawbreaker; discriminator—lawbreaker; racist—lawbreaker; ignoring the person on the street who needs help—lawbreaker. The intended result is humility, not a ranking system that leaves respectable church people above others.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · September 29, 2025 · James : A Faith That Works
documents.excerpt: Josh reads James 2:12–13: believers must speak and act as those who will be judged by the law that gives freedom; judgment without mercy comes to the unmerciful, while mercy triumphs over judgment.
excerpts: Josh reads James 2:12–13: believers must speak and act as those who will be judged by the law that gives freedom; judgment without mercy comes to the unmerciful, while mercy triumphs over judgment.

Christ’s return includes judgment. The Apostles’ Creed affirms that Christ will judge the living and the dead even where Christians disagree over timing and sequence. Josh distinguishes condemnation for sin from evaluation and reward: Christians are accepted through Christ, yet what they do, say, and display toward others still matters. He repeats Matthew 25’s compassion test, quotes 1 John 3:24 about command-keeping as evidence of abiding union, and quotes 2 Corinthians 5:10 about everyone appearing before Christ’s judgment seat.

Grace does not abolish obedient concern. Believers are not condemned by the law and possess freedom through Christ, but the law remains the standard by which conduct is judged. James’s command is practical: “Act like it.”

Josh turns the doctrine into a Spirit-enabled inventory. What has the believer accomplished with the Holy Spirit’s help? Whom has the believer blessed? When mercy and judgment were both possible, is the person increasingly choosing mercy? Where hate was once the default, is love increasingly being chosen?

James 2:13 echoes and reverses the Beatitude in Matthew 5:7. Jesus states the positive: the merciful will be shown mercy. James states the negative: the person who withholds mercy will face judgment without mercy.

The core issue is understanding what Christ has done, not accumulating moral achievements. A person who claims Christ’s forgiveness and peace through his life, death, burial, and resurrection but refuses to treat others as God treated him must examine whether God’s love is present at all. A merciful disposition is evidence of Christ within. Union with the One who fulfilled the law gives confidence in judgment. Josh repeats the controlling line: “Mercy triumphs over judgment.”

excerpts: Josh closes the exposition with a guided picture of the two men from James 2:2. He asks listeners to imagine the poor visitor in filthy, cheap, borrowed, unclean, smelly clothes—an appearance that is revolting and uncomfortable. If that man enters the Lord’s house and a believer protects a saved seat, sends him elsewhere, refuses courtesy, or will not treat him as an equal, James sends that believer back to “Gospel 101.”

The reason is not sentimental hospitality but spiritual identity. The believer looks like that poor man before God. Human righteousness is like filthy, discarded rags (Isaiah 64:6); every sinner is the shabby visitor hoping someone will extend a hand. Until a person sees himself in that light, he will neither notice the poor nor treat them as equals.

The gospel moves beyond identifying sinners with the poor man: God became the poor man before human eyes. Christ became poor for others, made himself nothing, took a servant’s nature, was born in a manger, and was raised in Nazareth. Josh quotes Isaiah 53:5: Christ was pierced for transgressions, crushed for iniquities, bore the punishment that brings peace, and heals by his wounds. He then quotes Philippians 2:8: Christ humbled himself in obedience to death on a cross. Jesus was mocked, ridiculed, and cast out even among those who claimed to love God most.

Josh presses the contradiction: how can one claim to receive the poor and rejected Christ while rejecting the poor person present in the church? Jesus slept in dirt so his people could sit on a throne; he was judged so they could receive mercy. Knowing that mercy produces service from inward desire, not merely external compulsion. The Spirit-led impulse to show up for difficult people is evidence that Christ’s love exists within.

Treatment of others is therefore a test of genuine faith—not only treatment of friends and similar people, but of people who require more. Listeners must remember how much they required of God: they were the high-maintenance party, yet he still showed up. Josh ends the movement with the question: Who can you show up for like that?

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · September 29, 2025 · James : A Faith That Works
documents.excerpt: Josh transitions from the poor Christ to the Lord’s Supper. Believers are to remember Jesus’s body given and blood poured out and to dwell in the mercy and grace made available in him. To those uncertain what they believe, Josh says he is glad they are present. Without Jesus he sees them as spiritually poor people needing a hand, and he wants to show them Christ rather than speak down to them.
excerpts: Josh transitions from the poor Christ to the Lord’s Supper. Believers are to remember Jesus’s body given and blood poured out and to dwell in the mercy and grace made available in him. To those uncertain what they believe, Josh says he is glad they are present. Without Jesus he sees them as spiritually poor people needing a hand, and he wants to show them Christ rather than speak down to them.

He carefully denies saving power to the physical elements. The cracker and grape juice cannot help during the week or forgive sin. Their importance lies in the body and blood they represent; believers should rest in the joy of salvation. Anyone newly drawn to Christ is invited to speak with Josh, the pastors, or the elders. Skeptics are welcome to wrestle with truth while the church walks with them.

He reads 1 Corinthians 11:26–28. Eating the bread and drinking the cup proclaim the Lord’s death until he returns. Receiving them unworthily sins against the Lord’s body and blood, so each participant must examine himself or herself first. Those confident in salvation through Christ’s person and cross may participate; those who are not should let the elements pass and continue wrestling.

Josh gives his personal testimony and final appeal. Jesus changed his life permanently rather than temporarily. Everyone needs a Savior; the risen Christ alone conquered death. He paraphrases John 14:6: the God-man says the only way to heaven is through him, then asks, “Do you believe him?”

excerpts: Josh begins with personal repentance for elevating human beings into a glorious place belonging only to God.
He tells the Lord, “You’re my favorite,” turning the sermon title into worship rather than human preference.
He asks God to dismantle circles in the church so that when the poor person enters, the congregation will see that person as God does and extend the mercy God has extended to them.
He prays for a church marked not by polished Christian behavior but by hearts divinely altered by the Holy Spirit.
He thanks Christ for undeserved death on the cross and asks the church not merely to change its internal culture but to change the city, including offering hope through the care center.
The sermon ends with gratitude and “Amen” at 53:53.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · September 22, 2025 · James : A Faith That Works
documents.excerpt: Josh identifies this as week three in James and locates the message in the final section of chapter 1. Weeks one and two dealt with trials and temptations and with Satan’s attempts to twist God’s Word. James now pivots from external deception by Satan to internal deception by oneself and asks how believers respond to God’s sanctifying work through his Word. Josh warns that it is more serious when Satan does not need to deceive someone because that person will deceive himself.
excerpts: Josh identifies this as week three in James and locates the message in the final section of chapter 1. Weeks one and two dealt with trials and temptations and with Satan’s attempts to twist God’s Word. James now pivots from external deception by Satan to internal deception by oneself and asks how believers respond to God’s sanctifying work through his Word. Josh warns that it is more serious when Satan does not need to deceive someone because that person will deceive himself.

He restores the immediate context by rereading James 1:18. God gives new birth through “the word of truth.” Those who hear and believe the message of Jesus trust the sufficiency of his sacrifice and saving power; Josh invokes Jesus’ “It is finished” to describe the completed victory and release from the law’s condemning weight under Christ’s blood.

He develops James’s seed image. The Word has been planted or engrafted in the believer, and the Holy Spirit lives and works within. Scripture is therefore not merely a self-help book but food, air, water, life, nourishment, and an “umbilical connection” to God. The Word grows within believers, changes them, and produces increasing freedom, peace, and confidence.

New birth does not end every problem; it begins God’s redemptive work in a person and ultimately in creation. The confusion often lies not in how salvation begins but in what its continuing work—sanctification, God’s pursuit of holiness in the believer—looks like.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · September 22, 2025 · James : A Faith That Works
documents.excerpt: Josh names the most frightening form of self-deception: people may think they are saved when they are not. He recounts reading Matthew 7:22–23 to two Mormon missionaries at his dinner table and challenging their confidence in a message he regards as adding a false prophet to Scripture. He immediately broadens the warning beyond Mormonism: people currently sitting in church may also wrongly assume they are saved. His pastoral prayer is that the Holy Spirit would expose that deception so they can run to Jesus.
excerpts: Josh names the most frightening form of self-deception: people may think they are saved when they are not. He recounts reading Matthew 7:22–23 to two Mormon missionaries at his dinner table and challenging their confidence in a message he regards as adding a false prophet to Scripture. He immediately broadens the warning beyond Mormonism: people currently sitting in church may also wrongly assume they are saved. His pastoral prayer is that the Holy Spirit would expose that deception so they can run to Jesus.

Self-deception also afflicts genuine believers. Some saved people live an unserious, performative Christian life, mistaking self-created spirituality or gifts for the work of God. A mature Christian can admit, “I’m a sinner saved by grace,” and walk with Jesus while being honestly exposed as a sinner; there is no promotion beyond grace. The self-deceived Christian cannot afford honesty because maintaining a spiritual appearance has become the priority.

Biblical portraits contrast false sufficiency with honest dependence. Jesus’ warning to Laodicea exposes people who claim wealth and needlessness while remaining wretched, poor, blind, and naked without him. Paul’s struggle in Romans 7 models mature honesty: he names his wretchedness and then praises God for rescue through Jesus Christ.

Josh states the controlling solution: the only protection from self-deception is a right relationship with God through his Word. Jesus’ prayer in John 17 identifies God’s Word as the truth by which his people are sanctified. Properly received, the Word drives out dishonesty, performance, and deception.

He previews the sermon’s three responsibilities: receive the Word, obey the Word, and share the Word. These enable honest fellowship with God, unity with other believers, and faithful witness in a dark world.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · September 22, 2025 · James : A Faith That Works
documents.excerpt: Josh reads James 1:19–21, which calls believers to be quick to listen, slow to speak, slow to anger, rid themselves of moral filth and prevalent evil, and humbly receive the planted Word that can save them.
excerpts: Josh reads James 1:19–21, which calls believers to be quick to listen, slow to speak, slow to anger, rid themselves of moral filth and prevalent evil, and humbly receive the planted Word that can save them.

He connects James’s planted Word to Jesus’ parable of the soils. The hard heart cannot understand or receive the seed and bears no fruit. The shallow heart responds emotionally but has no depth and bears no fruit. The crowded heart never truly repents, so sin chokes the Word and no fruit remains. The fruitful heart receives the Word, lets it take root, puts off old ways through repentance, and yields a harvest.

He defines fruit as evidence of a divinely altered life: Christian character, consistent conduct, and selfless gospel ministry for God’s glory. Fruit includes attempting to lead someone to Christ, repeatedly fighting addiction, and refusing evil temptation. It includes sharing resources with believers and the Spirit’s fruit of love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control. Colossians shows fruit in every good work and in growing in the knowledge of God. Hebrews identifies praise and public profession of Christ’s name as fruit offered to God.

Genuine salvation produces fruit in many forms, but churches also contain fake, performative, man-made fruit. Fake fruit becomes recognizable once someone has tasted the real work of God. The decisive difference is the source: Jesus says branches bear fruit only by remaining in the vine; apart from him they can do nothing.

Jesus’ rebuke of religious leaders shows that exposure to Scripture is not enough. Matthew 13 describes people who see without seeing and hear without understanding because their hearts have become calloused. Josh also paraphrases Jesus’ challenge that people search Scripture for life while refusing to come to him, the one in whom life is found.

If growth and fresh fruit are absent, the seed and vine are not defective; the problem is the soil or branch. Citing Hebrews 5:11 in the ESV, Josh says teaching may be hard to explain because hearers have become “dull of hearing,” not because the truth requires elite academic credentials. His transition is that James wants the Word received in a way that actually produces a harvest in the soul.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · September 22, 2025 · James : A Faith That Works
documents.excerpt: Be quick to listen (15:20–17:22). Josh repeats the series progression—trials, temptation, then God’s Word—and says flourishing believers become eager to hear Scripture or at least prioritize it when eagerness is absent. He compares this urgency to a first-time mother immediately responding to her newborn’s faintest cry, joking that the response may change with a second child. Application: when an issue arises, rush to Scripture first, develop a godly mindset, and only then move forward. Christians too often begin with “I think.” The decisive question is whether they have listened to God; Scripture should be the first line of defense, not a last-quarter “Hail Mary.”
excerpts: Be quick to listen (15:20–17:22). Josh repeats the series progression—trials, temptation, then God’s Word—and says flourishing believers become eager to hear Scripture or at least prioritize it when eagerness is absent. He compares this urgency to a first-time mother immediately responding to her newborn’s faintest cry, joking that the response may change with a second child. Application: when an issue arises, rush to Scripture first, develop a godly mindset, and only then move forward. Christians too often begin with “I think.” The decisive question is whether they have listened to God; Scripture should be the first line of defense, not a last-quarter “Hail Mary.”

Be slow to speak (17:25–20:36). Josh jokes that two ears and one mouth should convey the point, then quotes Proverbs 10:19 about multiplied words and the prudent person restraining the tongue. He explains that first-century church gatherings could include real-time debate with the speaker, even contentious exchanges. In the present congregation, order matters: he prepares and prays over the biblical “meal” all week, asks hearers to receive it, and invites later conversation in the lobby rather than live interruption. He defines the “Christian dummy” not by intelligence or education but as someone who speaks without seeking God’s counsel and lets feelings lead. Feelings unchecked by Scripture endanger both the person and the surrounding community. He corrects a common misuse of “slow to speak”: James is not forbidding clear, loving intervention when God’s Word plainly addresses a brother walking toward disaster. The call is for speech rooted in Scripture and directed toward another’s good.

Be slow to anger (20:39–25:14). In context, Josh says the command means not becoming angry with God or his Word when Scripture rebukes and corrects. Proverbs 12:1 labels hatred of correction as stupidity. God’s purpose is not merely to affirm desires but to call people to repentance; Josh connects this to a saying he appreciated. He applies this to cultural claims about sexual identity and same-sex desire, asserting that Scripture calls the lifestyle unnatural and calls every person to deny sinful desire. He broadens the point by admitting his own unwanted desires and emphasizing the Spirit’s strength for repetitive discipline and self-denial. Nathan’s stolen-lamb story illustrates misdirected anger: David demanded justice without realizing that justice was aimed at him. Peter’s sword in Gethsemane illustrates acting before listening: he tried to strike a man, cut off his ear, and forced Jesus to heal the injury before addressing the soldiers. The application is to slow down, hear the Word, stop reacting, seek wisdom, and then apply God’s counsel. Josh distinguishes sinful human anger from godly hatred of evil, quoting Psalm 97:10. Pursuit of justice need not be lethargic, but it must be governed by godly wisdom.

Human tantrums cannot produce God’s righteousness (25:04–27:49). A child’s checkout-line tantrum cannot force a wise parent’s hand, and anger cannot force God to retract what his Word reveals. He briefly announces a planned space for new parents and infants, expected to open in October, then returns to the parenting analogy: once a parent says no, surrendering to the tantrum teaches the child that escalation works. When God exposes sin, the response should be gratitude and removal, not anger. Anger at correction is pride claiming to know better than God; humility can honestly dislike the process while still submitting. Jesus in Gethsemane models the posture: “not my will” but the Father’s. Josh identifies surrender to God’s will as the location of peace and maturity.

Practical preparation of the heart (27:53–29:24). First, confess sins specifically rather than generally. Josh quotes 1 John 1:9 and tells hearers to work through the actual list while meditating on God’s love, grace, forgiveness, and faithfulness. Ask God to plow, tenderize, and soften the heart so the seed of truth can flourish; he calls this a dangerous but necessary prayer. Stay humble: stop fitting God into one’s personal story and instead discover how one fits into God’s story. Do not drag the skeleton of the old, dead life into the new life Christ has given; leave it behind.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · September 22, 2025 · James : A Faith That Works
documents.excerpt: Josh reads James 1:22–25 and moves from receiving to obeying. Hearing without doing is self-deception. The forgetful hearer resembles someone who sees his face in a mirror, leaves, and immediately forgets what he saw. The blessed person looks intently into the perfect law of freedom, continues in it, remembers it, and acts.
excerpts: Josh reads James 1:22–25 and moves from receiving to obeying. Hearing without doing is self-deception. The forgetful hearer resembles someone who sees his face in a mirror, leaves, and immediately forgets what he saw. The blessed person looks intently into the perfect law of freedom, continues in it, remembers it, and acts.

He contrasts salvation and subsequent blessing. Salvation comes through hearing the message of Christ. Once saved, blessing flows from doing rather than hearing alone. His memorable contrast is that many people write in their Bibles but never let the Bible “write on” them. Church attendance and sermon listening do not by themselves make anyone spiritual or Christian: spectators listen and watch; believers listen and do.

The mirror tells the truth (31:55–34:16). A mirror permits an honest look at oneself when other people may withhold uncomfortable truth. Josh tells of spending an hour with family before discovering in a mirror that he had a large whitehead; unconditional love was welcome, but a warning would also have helped. People do not blame a mirror for reporting an ugly truth. Likewise, divine revelation shows who a person really is rather than the flattering self-image that person prefers.

Mistake one: glancing instead of examining (34:19–36:01). A rushed devotional can become mere religious habit: Scripture is consumed quickly but not allowed to change the reader. Rather than always racing ahead to the next sermon text or “spiritual fix,” Josh urges the church to sit all week with what has already been preached and act on it. The diagnostic question is when the hearer last entered Scripture asking God to reveal how God sees him. Reject the “magical mirror” that shows only what one wants; ask God to expose evil spots, dangerous tendencies, blemishes, and laziness, then work with him to clean them.

Mistake two: seeing and then forgetting (36:04–37:45). Conviction demands response. Josh names social media as a present blemish in his own life: celebrity and megachurch conflict, hostile strangers, and unsolicited advice about shepherding have become spiritually corrosive. He says he deleted the apps that morning and is shutting social media and news off for thirty days, perhaps permanently, inviting others to join the experiment. Doing nothing after the Lord redirects him would reproduce James’s forgetful-hearer error. Isaiah, Peter, and Job responded to revelation with confessions of ruin, sinfulness, and self-disgust; Josh contrasts this with Christians who admire themselves in the mirror.
He rereads James 1:25 and makes the governing point explicit: the blessing comes in the doing, not merely the reading.

Isaiah, Peter, and Job responded to revelation with confessions of ruin, sinfulness, and self-disgust; Josh contrasts this with Christians who admire themselves in the mirror.
He rereads James 1:25 and makes the governing point explicit: the blessing comes in the doing, not merely the reading.

excerpts: God’s mirror reaches beneath behavior to motives, desires, heart, and soul; it is a deep and potentially frightening examination. This is not a one-time inspection. Believers must look again and again and be ready to fight recurring blemishes daily. Addressing men especially, Josh asks what might change in homes, churches, and the community if men inspected their souls through Scripture as carefully as their wives inspect a physical mirror. Instead of expertly identifying everyone else’s problems, turn the examination inward and invite the Lord into that space.

He urges hearers to dust off Scripture and begin by testing whether their faith is genuine. He mentions 1 Corinthians, Romans, and Ephesians as direct places to begin, while his phrase “see if you’re in the faith” echoes 2 Corinthians 13:5. Anything built on counterfeit faith will collapse.

James calls Scripture the “perfect law that gives freedom” because obedience is God’s means of liberation. Josh quotes John 8:31–32: true disciples hold to Jesus’ teaching, know the truth, and are set free—especially from sin. He returns to the Mormon missionaries and asks why a perfect Word would need Joseph Smith’s addition, insisting that one cannot carry the words of a liar alongside the words of the Savior. He says Scripture is without error and wholly true, and expresses grief over the young missionaries and the men who led them astray.

Confession without transformation stops short of experienced freedom. Josh invokes Paul’s “more than conquerors,” then reads 2 Corinthians 3:9 to contrast the glorious old-covenant ministry that brought condemnation with the more glorious new-covenant ministry that brings righteousness. The old covenant condemned and killed; the new covenant in Christ brings forgiveness and life.

Moses’ veil becomes the bridge between James’s mirror and Paul’s transformation imagery. Josh retells Exodus 34: Moses descended with a shining face, veiled the fading glory from Israel, and removed the veil when returning to God. At Jesus’ death the temple veil was torn, removing the barrier between humanity and God. Unlike fading reflected glory, the new-covenant believer beholds the Lord with an unveiled face and is transformed into his image with ever-increasing glory, as 2 Corinthians 3:18 states.

Scripture helps believers contemplate Christ and be transformed over time. The pace differs from person to person, but the church is coming along together. Combining Paul and James, Josh calls believers to look intently into the law of liberty with unveiled faces: stop the Christian cover-up, remove the mask, and admit that everyone is broken. He leads into David’s Psalm 139 prayer asking God to search, test, expose offensive ways, and lead in the everlasting way.

Self-examination is like resuming exercise after a long absence: it may hurt at first, but repetition brings strength. His final exhortation is to get in the Word, stay there, keep returning, and let it nourish, restore, and lead.

excerpts: Josh introduces the final responsibility—share the Word—and reads James 1:26–27. Religion without a restrained tongue is self-deception and worthless. Religion God accepts as pure and faultless cares for distressed orphans and widows and remains unpolluted by the world.

He defines James’s “religion” as outward practice rather than ceremonies, temples, special days, or traditions. Pure religion means practicing God’s Word by sharing it, serving people, and pursuing personal holiness.

The first outward test is the tongue. A person may perform every expected spiritual activity, but uncontrolled speech makes the claimed religion worthless. Transformation becomes audible when former patterns of cursing give way to the Spirit’s self-control and when believers stop tearing others down to elevate themselves. Josh postpones fuller treatment until James 3, joking that the future sermon will be fun in a terribly convicting way. The mouth is the first place where good soil becomes visible because speech reveals the heart. Not every thought needs to be spoken.

documents.excerpt: Proper self-examination redirects attention from personal need to the needs of others. Josh reads 1 John 3:16–18: Christ’s self-giving defines love, believers should lay down their lives for one another, and material resources must become concrete help rather than words alone.
excerpts: Proper self-examination redirects attention from personal need to the needs of others. Josh reads 1 John 3:16–18: Christ’s self-giving defines love, believers should lay down their lives for one another, and material resources must become concrete help rather than words alone.

He presents Crossroads Cares as the congregation’s practical expression of that command. He asks those who have given or received through the ministry to acknowledge God’s blessing. As the church grows, people may decide that Crossroads is their church, but Josh says identification without joining the work of meeting needs is incomplete. Service is not a side program but the congregation’s core identity: they would rather wash feet with a basin and towel than pursue brand visibility, television, or online prominence. He calls for servants, not consumers seeking flash.

A church without compassion—or one that merely outsources compassion—is not pure and undefiled before God. Local churches must do mission work in their own cities, even while also supporting global work financially. If a church vanished and its city would not notice, it should step aside and let active saints serve.

Josh returns to the final clause of James 1:27: ministry to the world must be joined to freedom from the world’s pollution. Christians are physically in the world without belonging to it spiritually, seeking to win people to Christ while maintaining healthy separation. A church cannot model radical generosity after becoming selfish like the world, heal others while sharing their sickness, guide the blind while blind itself, or build Christ’s name while consumed with its own. Jesus is the model: perfectly holy while present among sinners. Josh asks God to teach the church to do the same by the Spirit’s power.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · September 22, 2025 · James : A Faith That Works
documents.excerpt: Josh returns to the central danger: the most frightening deception is not Satan’s lie but the lie a person tells himself.
excerpts: Josh returns to the central danger: the most frightening deception is not Satan’s lie but the lie a person tells himself.

Religious consumption can coexist with unchanged living. A person can hear sermons, read Scripture, consume podcasts and Bible teachers, join studies, nod at truth, and say “Amen” at the proper moments without ever letting the truth shape life. That gap between hearing and doing is self-deception.
He asks whether hearers have allowed God’s Word to set their agenda or are still calling the shots.
Repeating James 1:25, he says the person who looks into the perfect law of liberty and does it is the one who is blessed.
The final question is not merely whether God’s Word has been heard but whether it will be obeyed.
His invitation supplies the sermon title’s contrast: do not leave deceived; leave devoted—devoted to God’s sanctifying process and letting his Word govern one’s words, works, and worship.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · September 22, 2025 · James : A Faith That Works
documents.excerpt: Josh thanks God for working through the Word and for giving the church an honest mirror.
excerpts: Josh thanks God for working through the Word and for giving the church an honest mirror.
The mess exposed by the mirror reminds him why Jesus came: no amount of moral work removes the need for a Savior.

He returns to the gospel: Jesus came down, bore sin on the cross, and was forsaken so sinners could be forgiven. He asks that anyone not resting confidently in Christ’s power to save would run to him inwardly, admit need, recognize sin, and come to the Savior.
For those already redeemed, he asks that they leave a subpar spectator life and become doers.
The prayer ends by asking God to reveal what is spiritually “nasty” and lead the church in the everlasting way, echoing Psalm 139:23–24.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · September 15, 2025 · James : A Faith That Works
documents.excerpt: Josh opens emotionally and thanks the church for praying for his family, accepting his weariness, and preaching the hope of Jesus back to him. His prior church experience was marked by pain, disappointment, and institutions that knew the right words but did not love as God loves. God overturned that cynicism by giving him a vision of a church that knows truth and permits the gospel to transform people from the inside out. He describes Crossroads as a once-shipwrecked vessel being revived for God’s glory through a return to God and submission to his will.
excerpts: Josh opens emotionally and thanks the church for praying for his family, accepting his weariness, and preaching the hope of Jesus back to him. His prior church experience was marked by pain, disappointment, and institutions that knew the right words but did not love as God loves. God overturned that cynicism by giving him a vision of a church that knows truth and permits the gospel to transform people from the inside out. He describes Crossroads as a once-shipwrecked vessel being revived for God’s glory through a return to God and submission to his will.

Josh recounts writing the sermon beside his mother after the death of her husband. Together they counted both blessings and losses; both lists were long. In the last two years she had lost a daughter, a brother, and a husband, yet told Josh that nothing she lost could remove praise from her lips because God is good. Josh calls this a mother’s sermon to her son.

Psalm 34:18: the Lord remains close to the brokenhearted and saves those crushed in spirit. Grief strips away lesser concerns and prompts a reset around what truly matters. Josh confesses that he often lives in the past, evaluating what could have been done better, or in the future, planning what must be done next, while neglecting what God is doing now. He cannot control the church’s history or predict its future, but if Christ remains central, neither uncertainty is decisive.
Transition: he thanks the congregation for the way their gospel transformation blesses him, then announces the day’s topics—wealth, eternal rewards, temptation, and God’s unshakable goodness.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · September 15, 2025 · James : A Faith That Works
documents.excerpt: Josh identifies James 1:9–18 as the day’s continuing primary text and reads verses 9–11. Believers in humble circumstances should boast in their high position. Rich believers should boast in their humiliation because wealth and its beauty fade like a flower under scorching heat.
excerpts: Josh identifies James 1:9–18 as the day’s continuing primary text and reads verses 9–11. Believers in humble circumstances should boast in their high position. Rich believers should boast in their humiliation because wealth and its beauty fade like a flower under scorching heat.

He places the paragraph within the series’ three-week opening treatment of James 1. Trials are inevitable, and immaturity in the church is a real problem. A trial gives an immature believer an opportunity to grow; God ordinarily forms character through lived circumstances rather than merely through books, sermons, songs, poems, or counseling. Character formation requires the believer’s cooperation through surrender and submission. When believers wander, the loving Father disciplines his children and brings them back.

Josh distinguishes maturity from sinlessness. Jesus supplied the perfection sinners could not. God’s goal in believers is a complete, mature work—“perfection in the faith”—rather than autonomous sinless performance.

Parenting illustration: Children must eventually grow up and leave shelter, even though greater independence exposes them to danger. Christians who refuse faith, risk, and bold obedience remain spiritually sheltered and immature.
Transition: one practical arena for maturity is learning to view both self and wealth as God does.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · September 15, 2025 · James : A Faith That Works
documents.excerpt: Josh explains the original socioeconomic setting. James writes to Jewish Christians displaced from Jerusalem and rebuilding in Syria and northern Palestine. Their economic outcomes differ, but all share the condition of being outcasts.
excerpts: Josh explains the original socioeconomic setting. James writes to Jewish Christians displaced from Jerusalem and rebuilding in Syria and northern Palestine. Their economic outcomes differ, but all share the condition of being outcasts.

To the poor believer: look beyond present circumstances and boast in the high position received from God. Josh distinguishes healthy boasting from sinful pride through Jeremiah 9:23–24: wisdom, strength, and riches are not grounds for boasting; knowing the Lord—who delights in kindness, justice, and righteousness—is. Paul’s call to live quietly does not mean remaining silent about Christ. Josh warns that a faith that never offends anyone may have become too quiet. The real question is not whether one boasts, but what so defines a person that even strangers can see it. Christians must be publicly defined by their position in Christ rather than by what they possess or lack. Philippians 3:20–21: believers’ citizenship is in heaven, and Christ will transform their lowly bodies to be like his glorious body. James 2:5: those poor in the world’s eyes may be rich in faith and heirs of the promised kingdom.

To the rich believer: boast in the low position embraced in Christ rather than accepting the world’s elevation of wealth. The world regards wealthy Christians as irrational when they give sacrificially instead of maximizing comfort or early retirement. Josh answers that kingdom giving is itself an investment. Illustration: a very wealthy Christian drove a battered twenty-year-old Honda. His voluntary self-denial ministered to Josh because wealth did not dictate his identity. Clarification: the point is not that Christians may never replace a car or own something good; it is that possessions, ability, success, reputation, and worldly position must never become their boast.
Transition: because worldly wealth easily exposes immaturity, God gives believers a way to convert temporary resources into eternal investment.
