documents.context: Josh Wyatt · September 15, 2025 · James : A Faith That Works
documents.excerpt: Josh introduces why he and Kristen give at least ten percent of all they earn to the local church, then delivers his central confrontation: “Stop giving God your scraps and calling it generosity.” In a 90/10 frame, God is the generous giver of the ninety; returning ten does not make the recipient generous. Humans enter and leave the world with nothing; everything belongs to God.
excerpts: Josh introduces why he and Kristen give at least ten percent of all they earn to the local church, then delivers his central confrontation: “Stop giving God your scraps and calling it generosity.” In a 90/10 frame, God is the generous giver of the ninety; returning ten does not make the recipient generous. Humans enter and leave the world with nothing; everything belongs to God.

He contrasts complaints that giving “hurts” with Christ’s sacrifice. Jesus endured nails, public condemnation, the curse, forsakenness, and the rupture required to reconcile sinners to God. Josh therefore refuses to treat a tithe as sacrifice on the scale of the cross.

Congregational application: Given the visible resources of the church body, the church should not face chronic financial inability, the care-center shelves should not remain empty, and genuine needs among members should not go unmet. Help must retain wise structure and avoid enabling destructive patterns, but Jesus’ people follow him into sacrifice.

Josh gives seven ordered reasons that he and Kristen tithe: Without the tithe, the Lord’s house cannot function as the hope of the world. Tithing expresses trust that God will meet their needs. It renews the mind rather than allowing conformity to the world. It unifies them with the church’s mission and purpose. It gives their work eternal significance; Kristen’s bank career contributes to ministry just as Josh’s church work does. It breaks greed and self-reliance and moves wealth from temporary use to eternal purpose. It shows that God is first in their home.

Returning to James 1:11, Josh states the unavoidable outcome: either a person loses wealth or wealth loses the person—one goes broke or dies. Kingdom investment outlives both outcomes. Buildings decay, but lives reached by the gospel are sealed forever in Christ.
Transition: how believers view self and wealth matters; Josh turns next to eternal rewards.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · September 15, 2025 · James : A Faith That Works
documents.excerpt: Josh reads James 1:12: the one who perseveres under trial is blessed and, after standing the test, receives the crown of life promised to those who love God. This returns to the previous week’s teaching from James 1:2–3 that many kinds of trials should be counted as joy because tested faith produces perseverance. Verse 12 adds the future reward attached to perseverance: the crown of life.
excerpts: Josh reads James 1:12: the one who perseveres under trial is blessed and, after standing the test, receives the crown of life promised to those who love God. This returns to the previous week’s teaching from James 1:2–3 that many kinds of trials should be counted as joy because tested faith produces perseverance. Verse 12 adds the future reward attached to perseverance: the crown of life.

Josh identifies verse 12 as a beatitude and corrects two misunderstandings of blessing. Blessing does not flow from worldly alliances; it accompanies humble endurance. “Blessed” does not mean emotionally happy. A believer can be deeply sad and genuinely blessed at the same time. Emotions fluctuate; assurance rests in enduring by faith, keeping one’s eyes on Jesus, and receiving God’s favor.

“Trial” includes anything that threatens love for Christ or faithful obedience—disagreement, division, disease, divorce, and death. Last week emphasized present joy within trials; this movement emphasizes the future reward beyond them.

Crown imagery: James’s hearers would picture the victory wreath awarded to an athlete, not merely a jeweled royal crown. 1 Corinthians 9:25: athletes accept strict training for a perishable crown; Christians train for one that lasts forever. Josh’s athletic analogy stresses self-control, discipline, blood, sweat, tears, effort, and surrender to the process. Olympians sacrifice thousands of hours for roughly ninety seconds on a podium and then return to training. Revelation 2:10: Jesus tells suffering believers in Smyrna to remain faithful to death and promises life as the victor’s crown.

Josh answers the objection that Christians should never be motivated by reward. He rejects transactional obedience and “What have you done for me lately?” calculations. Nevertheless, God communicated promises so believers could remember them under pressure, reject material bait, prioritize spiritual reality, and rejoice during loss. Only a believer can properly value this reward; unbelievers do not boast in a victor’s crown of life. Application: stop starting pointless church fights over the legitimacy of reward language and serve someone instead—“go wash somebody’s feet.”
Transition: Josh moves from reward under trial to how believers should handle temptation.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · September 15, 2025 · James : A Faith That Works
documents.excerpt: Josh reads James 1:13–15 and gives the conclusion first: the person responsible for one’s sin is oneself. He reinforces the point with a congregational exercise, asking everyone to point at the person responsible for their sin.
excerpts: Josh reads James 1:13–15 and gives the conclusion first: the person responsible for one’s sin is oneself. He reinforces the point with a congregational exercise, asking everyone to point at the person responsible for their sin.

He distinguishes trials from temptations. God may send or allow trials that appeal to the Spirit’s work in believers and train them to listen, obey, and mature. Temptations appeal to sinful nature, seek rebellion against God, and may be deployed by Satan. Thanksgiving-plate illustration: Christians prefer trials and temptations not to “touch,” just as some people separate food, but James connects them closely. God is not temptation’s author, yet Satan can turn a sanctifying trial into a spiritually slippery occasion.

Josh shows how a trial can become a temptation to accuse God. Financial hardship can generate doubts about provision. Bereavement can generate doubts about love. Persecution combined with apparent wicked prosperity can generate doubts about justice. The proper response is to call out and run to God rather than complain against him.

He returns to Eden to explain freedom and choice. God placed the tree of life and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil in the garden, prohibited eating from the latter, and warned of death. God spoke first; the devil then twisted God’s word. Real freedom requires a meaningful choice. Without the possibility of disobedience, obedience would be automatic rather than freely rendered.

Application: Temptation itself is not the decisive problem; response is. Each right choice strengthens faith, while wishing temptation away does not produce maturity. God allows temptation not to destroy believers but as an occasion in which they may choose obedience and grow stronger with his help. These daily opportunities often begin before the first cup of coffee is finished.
Transition: having established where temptation does not originate, Josh asks where it does originate.

God is not temptation’s author, yet Satan can turn a sanctifying trial into a spiritually slippery occasion.
Josh shows how a trial can become a temptation to accuse God. Financial hardship can generate doubts about provision. Bereavement can generate doubts about love. Persecution combined with apparent wicked prosperity can generate doubts about justice. The proper response is to call out and run to God rather than complain against him.
He returns to Eden to explain freedom and choice. God placed the tree of life and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil in the garden, prohibited eating from the latter, and warned of death. God spoke first; the devil then twisted God’s word. Real freedom requires a meaningful choice. Without the possibility of disobedience, obedience would be automatic rather than freely rendered.
Application: Temptation itself is not the decisive problem; response is. Each right choice strengthens faith, while wishing temptation away does not produce maturity. God allows temptation not to destroy believers but as an occasion in which they may choose obedience and grow stronger with his help. These daily opportunities often begin before the first cup of coffee is finished.
Transition: having established where temptation does not originate, Josh asks where it does originate.
documents.title: James 1:13–15: God tests for maturity, but temptation exploits desire — Burdened but Blessed

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · September 15, 2025 · James : A Faith That Works
documents.excerpt: Josh repeats James 1:14: each person is dragged away and enticed by his or her own evil desire. Proverbs 19:3 supplies the wisdom parallel: a person’s own folly produces ruin, yet the heart rages against the Lord. The pattern is self-caused harm followed by blame directed at God.
excerpts: Josh repeats James 1:14: each person is dragged away and enticed by his or her own evil desire. Proverbs 19:3 supplies the wisdom parallel: a person’s own folly produces ruin, yet the heart rages against the Lord. The pattern is self-caused harm followed by blame directed at God.

Josh broadens “desire” beyond sexual appetite. Hunger, thirst, sexual desire, sleep, and marriage have legitimate God-given places. The problem begins when people satisfy desires apart from God’s will. Ordered contrasts: eating versus gluttony; sleep versus laziness; sex versus sexual immorality; marriage versus same-sex union. Hebrews 13:4: marriage must be honored and the marriage bed kept pure because God judges adultery and sexual immorality. Diagnostic question: with respect to desire, are you servant or master?

Personal testimony and parental warning: Josh says Jesus enabled him to master a pornography addiction and saved his marriage. A choice at age fifteen developed into an addiction that nearly destroyed his marriage at twenty-nine. He urges parents to discuss pornography and temptation directly with children who are not hearing the sermon.

Marketing and fishing illustrations explain “enticed.” Satan does not advertise consequences with integrity or provide a surgeon general’s warning. Like tobacco marketing, temptation packages danger attractively. Josh says the Greek image behind “enticed” is “bait the hook”: the fish sees a shiny offer, not the hook, photograph, and meal awaiting it. Temptation is never presented as a naked hook; it promises that sin will be easier, better, faster, or pleasurable while covering what lies underneath.
Biblical examples: Lot saw Sodom’s well-watered land without foreseeing the outcome. David saw Bathsheba without seeing the suffering and tragedy that would follow.

Preventive application: Remain in Scripture so that, like Jesus in the wilderness, believers can discern God’s will from their own and surrender to his. Remain in fellowship so mature believers can restore anyone who falls and help that person return to the right path.
Transition: James changes metaphors from fishing to childbirth.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · September 15, 2025 · James : A Faith That Works
documents.excerpt: Josh repeats James 1:15 and traces sin’s development: desire conceives, gives birth to sin, and mature sin gives birth to death.
excerpts: Josh repeats James 1:15 and traces sin’s development: desire conceives, gives birth to sin, and mature sin gives birth to death.

He carefully locates moral culpability. The mere existence or intensification of a desire is not itself the “birth” of sin. Sin occurs when the idea becomes a decision—when someone acts on desire mentally or bodily. Jesus’ teaching about lust distinguishes noticing beauty from intentionally entertaining lustful thoughts or fantasies.

Maturity therefore governs reactions rather than obeying feelings. Immature Christians act from reluctance, hurt, revenge, or impulse without reflection. Mature Christians pursue what is right regardless of fluctuating emotions. Josh’s sequence is desire → decision → consequence; disobedience yields death rather than life.

He explains death as separation as well as physical cessation. Adam and Eve did not die physically the instant they ate, yet death entered immediately in spiritual, relational, and emotional forms. Fellowship with God and one another broke: they hid, covered nakedness, blamed one another, experienced fear, and eventually saw sin mature into Cain’s murder of Abel. A sin’s full death-bearing outcome may take years to appear.
Josh repeats the warning: “Don’t take the bait.”

1 Corinthians 10:13 gives the alternative. Temptation is common rather than uniquely overpowering. God is faithful, limits what believers face, and provides a way out so they can endure. Practical response: pause, look for the exit, and ask a mature Christian for blunt counsel rather than rationalizing adultery, pornography, or another sin.
Transition: after the emphatic call to “find the way out,” Josh pauses, then turns to the final topic—God’s unshakable goodness.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · September 15, 2025 · James : A Faith That Works
documents.excerpt: Josh reads James 1:16–17: believers must not be deceived; every good and perfect gift comes from the Father of heavenly lights, who does not change like shifting shadows.
excerpts: Josh reads James 1:16–17: believers must not be deceived; every good and perfect gift comes from the Father of heavenly lights, who does not change like shifting shadows.

The topics belong together rather than standing as isolated sermons. Meditating on God’s goodness is a means of overcoming temptation. Satan imitates God and seeks to make God appear withholding, as with Eve and with hungry Jesus in the wilderness. When believers doubt God’s goodness or look away from eternal reward, temporary bait begins to look good. Israel’s history illustrates the danger: people brought from slavery into land ownership forgot the God who delivered them.

Josh orders four truths in James’s wording: God gives only good gifts. Everything truly good comes from God; some gifts develop like seeds whose growth remains hidden before they sprout. God’s method of giving is good. Unlike a gift delivered manipulatively or in an “icky” manner, both God’s gift and his manner of giving are good. God gives by downpour. “Coming down” carries the continuing sense that gifts keep coming. Believers may not perceive the flow, but Scripture declares it; Ephesians 1:3 says God has blessed believers with every spiritual blessing in Christ. God is unchanging. His holiness means he cannot become worse; his perfection means he cannot become better.

If a shadow or distance exists between a believer and God, Josh assigns responsibility to the believer, not to an alteration in God. God cannot change, but through the gospel he makes human change possible.
Josh reads James 1:18: God chose to give believers birth through the word of truth so they would be firstfruits of creation.

Three ordered keys for fighting temptation: Cultivate a healthy fear of God; awareness that judgment begins with God’s household helps keep the church on course. Never forget God’s goodness; temptation loses its shimmer beside God’s promises. Walk according to the new divine nature rather than the old desire-driven one.

James redeems the childbirth image. Desire gives birth to sin and death, but God gives new birth through the word of truth. The redeemed are the opening act of God’s restoration of creation and reestablishment of Eden on earth. Revelation 21:5: the enthroned Lord declares that he is making all things new.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · September 15, 2025 · James : A Faith That Works
documents.excerpt: Josh gathers the sermon into two paths: Temptation → sin → death. Trials → perseverance → life. At the center stands the unchanging God, whose trials mature rather than destroy and whose greatest gift is new life through Jesus.
excerpts: Josh gathers the sermon into two paths: Temptation → sin → death. Trials → perseverance → life. At the center stands the unchanging God, whose trials mature rather than destroy and whose greatest gift is new life through Jesus.

Everyone feels temptation’s inward lure: “just once,” “no one will know,” or “it’s fine.” Unresisted desire becomes decision and can carry a person away from God. Gospel hope is that believers do not have to bite or be dragged away; Jesus can deliver them every time as they run to him.

Jesus’ wilderness victory answers Adam’s garden failure. Satan whispered lies, twisted Scripture, and offered shortcuts, but Jesus stood on the word and won the battle sinners could not win. Where Adam failed, Jesus overcame; where human desire gives birth to sin, Jesus gives new life through the word of truth.
Jesus offers transformation, not forgiveness alone. He attacks sin’s root as well as its fruit. He gives power to resist, grace to stand, and mercy after a fall.

Josh returns to James 1:12. The crown of life awaits those who love God and endure, not because they never fail but because they keep returning to the life-giver. The victor’s crown is not for self-perfect people but for those who trust the perfect One.

Final appeal: The tired, weary, and wandering should join Josh in fixing their eyes on Jesus. Jesus wore the crown of thorns so believers could receive the crown of life; was treated as a criminal so they could become God’s children; broke sin’s power; defeated death; endured the cross; rose from the grave; gives new birth; makes all things new; and will return. Until then: do not take the bait. Turn and run to Jesus, the way, truth, and life; salvation is found in no other name.

42:55–44:10 — Closing communion prayer: Josh thanks the Father for the elements that recall Christ’s sacrifice, for Jesus’ righteous life and substitutionary death, and for salvation through his blood. He prays that amid tragedy, loss, suffering, sickness, and sadness, the church would silence the noise, quiet heart and mind, reflect on Jesus, and trust him as the answer to what ails them.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · September 8, 2025 · James : A Faith That Works
documents.excerpt: Josh opens by asking who enjoys controversy, debate, and friction. He welcomes “sparks” only when they sharpen believers for battle against evil—not when church members prepare to fight him or one another. Crossroads is to build a culture of unity on Jesus Christ. Josh recalls Jesus’ prayer that his followers would be one (John 17:20–23) and asks the congregation to recommit publicly to that work: “I will.” He does not want “mini me” disciples who merely look or sound like him. He wants people to know the revelation of Jesus, trusting that people centered on Jesus can work through lesser disagreements together.
excerpts: Josh opens by asking who enjoys controversy, debate, and friction. He welcomes “sparks” only when they sharpen believers for battle against evil—not when church members prepare to fight him or one another. Crossroads is to build a culture of unity on Jesus Christ. Josh recalls Jesus’ prayer that his followers would be one (John 17:20–23) and asks the congregation to recommit publicly to that work: “I will.” He does not want “mini me” disciples who merely look or sound like him. He wants people to know the revelation of Jesus, trusting that people centered on Jesus can work through lesser disagreements together.

He introduces James as perhaps the New Testament’s most controversial book. Martin Luther called it an “epistle of straw,” and some modern theologians treat it as a Jewish carryover that fails to express Christianity’s essence. Yet ordinary believers gravitate toward James and frequently quote it from memory.

Josh gives three reasons for James’s popularity. Efficiency and practicality: James gives concise guidance for living the Christian life, epitomized by “Do not merely listen … Do what it says” (James 1:22). James is not constructing a complete theological framework; he is spurring Christians to live their faith. Rapid movement: Like Jewish wisdom literature such as Proverbs, James often states a point, lets it stand, and moves on rather than exhausting it. Memorable metaphors: James uses pictures that lodge his teaching in the believer’s mind.

Transition: Today will differ from later messages because Josh must establish the framework for the entire series. He compares that preparation to packing for a trip: he hates the tedious planning and procrastinates with any available chore, but the journey goes better when he first considers its length, weather, clothing, and needs.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · September 8, 2025 · James : A Faith That Works
documents.excerpt: Josh urges listeners to prepare for any biblical book by answering four questions in order: Who is the author—not merely his name, but who he is? Who are the recipients as actual people? Why is the author writing to them? Only after that groundwork, what can readers far removed from the original audience learn?
excerpts: Josh urges listeners to prepare for any biblical book by answering four questions in order: Who is the author—not merely his name, but who he is? Who are the recipients as actual people? Why is the author writing to them? Only after that groundwork, what can readers far removed from the original audience learn?

He begins with James 1:1a: “James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ.” Because James was a common name, Josh evaluates the New Testament candidates. James son of Zebedee, John’s brother, was called from fishing by Jesus (Matthew 4:21–22) but was killed by Herod around AD 44 (Acts 12:1–2), before Josh’s proposed AD 49 date for the letter. James son of Alphaeus is too obscure to connect confidently with the letter. Josh notes that Levi/Matthew is also called a son of Alphaeus (Mark 2:14; 3:18) and playfully raises, without asserting, the possibility that they were brothers. James associated with Judas is even less likely because Scripture tells so little about him (Luke 6:16).

Josh accepts the traditional identification: the author is James, Jesus’ half-brother, Jude’s brother, and the leader of the Jerusalem church (Matthew 13:55; Galatians 1:19). He recommends comparing the Jerusalem Council in Acts 15 with James and Galatians 2, because their language and concerns show striking similarities. “Half-brother” matters because Joseph was James’s father, while Jesus was conceived by the Holy Spirit; James and Jesus shared Mary but not a human father (Matthew 1:18–25).

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · September 8, 2025 · James : A Faith That Works
documents.excerpt: Josh says James’s testimony is the greatest reason redeemed people love his letter. He imagines the difficulty of growing up with a brother who never lied, sinned, retaliated, or joined sibling schemes. The humor gives way to John 7:5: even Jesus’ brothers did not believe in him.
excerpts: Josh says James’s testimony is the greatest reason redeemed people love his letter. He imagines the difficulty of growing up with a brother who never lied, sinned, retaliated, or joined sibling schemes. The humor gives way to John 7:5: even Jesus’ brothers did not believe in him.

Application to Christian households: Being raised near faith does not regenerate anyone. “People don’t raise Christians. God calls Christians.” Josh asks his children what they truly believe and whether they want self-rule or to follow Jesus. If James could live with Jesus and reject him for decades, children can live with Christians and still deny the faith. Parents should create a safe place for children to wrestle honestly, cover them in prayer, plead for God to save them, and trust God’s timing. They cannot manufacture an “upper room experience.” Josh connects this conviction to Crossroads’ practice of believer’s baptism: a confession of faith is required, which makes him oppose infant baptism and cautious about baptizing children prematurely.

The resurrection changes James. In the upper room, Mary and Jesus’ brothers join the disciples in constant prayer (Acts 1:14). The family that once rejected Jesus is present at the birth of the Jerusalem church. Paul reports that the risen Jesus appeared to more than five hundred believers and then specifically to James (1 Corinthians 15:6–7). Josh answers his own question—what changed James?—with the resurrection. “He is risen” remains Christianity’s greatest historical claim. The risen Christ turned James around in AD 33, turned Josh around in 1995, and still transforms lives. Josh asks listeners when that encounter changed them.

Salvation leads James into local-church service. Paul calls James, Cephas, and John “pillars” and recounts their fellowship and mission agreement with Paul and Barnabas (Galatians 2:9). Josh pictures an apostolic staff meeting in which leaders discern who can best reach Jews and Gentiles. Their shared Great Commission and movement toward “the ends of the earth” model gospel partnership (Acts 1:8). Against social media’s appetite for failure and armchair criticism, Josh wants Crossroads to display leaders and members who cooperate, love, sacrifice, and preserve unity. He illustrates this with a recent firm disagreement with a church member. They recognized Satan’s attempt to divide them, prayed for each other, and restored unity. The church needs to tell more stories of believers overcoming evil rather than highlighting only abuse, adultery, theft, division, and defeat.

James finishes faithfully. Tradition says the Pharisees threw him from the temple and clubbed him to death in AD 62; some accounts say he prayed for his killers, following Jesus’ “Father, forgive them” (Luke 23:34). Scripture presents him as a strong leader who brings peace and direction in the Jerusalem Council (Acts 15:13–21), a defender of the gospel, a man of prayer, and a leader Paul could esteem as a pillar. Tradition describes his knees as hardened like a camel’s from prayer. His Jewish formation under Moses’ law remains visible in his letter.

Hope for unbelieving loved ones: Although James did not believe during Jesus’ teaching ministry, he had listened closely; Josh notes at least fifteen echoes of the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5–7) in James. Someone who presently disbelieves may still be watching and listening.

Historical transition: James led while Jewish believers were learning grace amid an operating temple system. Modern readers should not look down on them after inheriting Romans, Galatians, and Hebrews; these pioneers had to work out the transition from law to grace before most of the New Testament existed.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · September 8, 2025 · James : A Faith That Works
documents.excerpt: Josh answers the second question from James 1:1b: James writes “to the twelve tribes scattered among the nations.” The letter applies to all Christians, but its immediate recipients were Jewish Christians, written before Gentiles entered the church in large numbers: Scripture is not necessarily written to modern readers, but it is written for them.
excerpts: Josh answers the second question from James 1:1b: James writes “to the twelve tribes scattered among the nations.” The letter applies to all Christians, but its immediate recipients were Jewish Christians, written before Gentiles entered the church in large numbers: Scripture is not necessarily written to modern readers, but it is written for them.

Acts 11:19–21 supplies the historical picture. Persecution after Stephen’s death scattered believers to Phoenicia, Cyprus, and Antioch. Some preached only to Jews; others preached Jesus to Greeks, and many believed. Josh explains “scattered” as diaspora language that also evokes seed broadcast into soil. Persecution appeared to disperse and weaken the church but actually planted gospel seed across the Roman world. The displaced believers became the original church planters, and Jewish and Greek believers became one people of God by faith.
Those Christian Jews faced rejection from both sides: Gentiles rejected them as Jews, while unbelieving Jews rejected them as Christians. Many were poor, oppressed, and exploited by the rich.

Josh answers why James wrote: pressure exposed and amplified immaturity. Some kept Christianity private to preserve work, reputation, and security. That secrecy produced partiality: some courted the wealthy while poorer believers in the same church were mistreated (James 2:1–7). A leadership vacuum made many want to teach (James 3:1). Instead of speaking directly and building one another up, members used the tongue to campaign, demean rivals, and elevate themselves (James 3:2–12). Their competing desires erupted into fights in church (James 4:1–3). Genuine believers still loved the world and forgot Jesus under pressure (James 4:4). Pride, arrogant plans, disobedience, sickness, and wandering also marked the community (James 4:6–17; 5:14–20).

Josh turns the mirror toward the modern American church: suffering, dishonesty, professed faith without obedience, worship of money, power, and sex, pornography, and destructive speech remain recognizable.
Beneath the entire list is one issue: immaturity. James wants Christians to grow up because Christians who refuse to mature eventually tear others down.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · September 8, 2025 · James : A Faith That Works
documents.excerpt: Josh illustrates perseverance while describing a workout with his son Nolan. Nolan’s bench press has doubled, and after a difficult set Josh asks him to define perseverance: enduring through hardship. Because Romans 5:3–4 is a family memory passage, Nolan knows that perseverance produces character. Muscle grows by being torn, nourished, and rebuilt stronger; character develops the same way. Physical discipline is good, but Nolan must also “lift the Word.” Life will tear him, and spiritual milk cannot sustain maturity; he needs solid food (Hebrews 5:12–14).
excerpts: Josh illustrates perseverance while describing a workout with his son Nolan. Nolan’s bench press has doubled, and after a difficult set Josh asks him to define perseverance: enduring through hardship. Because Romans 5:3–4 is a family memory passage, Nolan knows that perseverance produces character. Muscle grows by being torn, nourished, and rebuilt stronger; character develops the same way. Physical discipline is good, but Nolan must also “lift the Word.” Life will tear him, and spiritual milk cannot sustain maturity; he needs solid food (Hebrews 5:12–14).

The first- and twenty-first-century church share the same immaturity problem. With the “packing” complete for a 10-week journey, Josh gives three ways to get the most from the series. Be born again. Spiritual maturity cannot exist without spiritual birth (John 3:3–8). The Spirit who hovered over the waters and brought light from God’s spoken Word (Genesis 1:2–3) uses the Word to create new life in a sinner who trusts Jesus. Josh calls this recreation or regeneration: whatever the delivery method—private reading, sermon, song, play, or film—the message remains the need for a new heart (Ezekiel 36:26–27). Salvation is God’s gift by grace through faith, not human works (Ephesians 2:8–9). Faith comes by hearing the message about Christ (Romans 10:17). Examine and obey. Hear each sermon for yourself, not for an absent cousin, spouse, in-law, child, or preacher. Pray for others, but examine your own life and obey what the Word teaches. Merely listening is easy; James says to do it (James 1:22, reapplied). Expect resistance. If believers begin walking more intentionally with Christ, the devil will try to trip them. Josh’s memorable counsel is to “kick the stick and keep stepping”: growing seriousness invites more serious schemes, but the church need not surrender.
Transition: After the lengthy series framework, Josh returns to James’s one-word greeting and begins the primary lesson on trials.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · September 8, 2025 · James : A Faith That Works
documents.excerpt: Josh reads James 1:2–3: believers should consider trials of many kinds pure joy because tested faith produces perseverance. A playful lemon/lemonade riff gives way to a sober correction of shallow teaching about suffering.
excerpts: Josh reads James 1:2–3: believers should consider trials of many kinds pure joy because tested faith produces perseverance. A playful lemon/lemonade riff gives way to a sober correction of shallow teaching about suffering.

Foundational claim: Anything that can happen to another human can happen to a Christian except the second death, eternal separation from God (Revelation 20:6, 14). Jesus promises both trouble and victory (John 16:33); trials are not hypothetical.

Josh argues that joy is unnatural because contemporary culture expects circumstances to go well and treats happiness as the measure of winning. He contrasts that expectation with earlier generations that assumed life could be unfair and difficult. In a pointed cultural application, he condemns prescribing hormone blockers or powerful medication to distressed adolescents rather than helping them endure, and he links that posture to high 2023 suicide statistics. His stated concern is a social narrative that losing what makes a person happy means life is irretrievably lost. He says the church has contributed by implying that God’s children are protected from major suffering. He rejects the distinction between “little” and “big” bad things: the issue is when, not if, trials come.

Joy is chosen by the Spirit, not performed for an audience. Believers are not merely to wear a cheerful face; because God commands joy, the Spirit enables them to set their minds on it (James 1:2, reapplied). Christians may need to pull one another back on course and ask how Jesus would view the situation.

Jesus supplies the pattern. For the joy ahead, Jesus endured the cross and its shame and sat at God’s right hand (Hebrews 12:2). He looked beyond the immediate trial to the completed work on the other side. Believers are likewise to consider the one who endured sinners’ opposition so they do not grow weary or lose heart (Hebrews 12:3). Jesus directed his mind toward joy rather than allowing suffering to define the horizon.

Josh then makes the teaching personal. His stepfather Dave, his mother’s husband, died the previous afternoon. Josh is hurting and will miss him, while believing Dave is with the Lord and better off. Joy does not mean pretending everything is fine. Joy can coexist with tears, misery, and loss; standing confidently before God while circumstances are not fine is where others see joy and God’s glory.

Jesus supplies the pattern. For the joy ahead, Jesus endured the cross and its shame and sat at God’s right hand (Hebrews 12:2). He looked beyond the immediate trial to the completed work on the other side. Believers are likewise to consider the one who endured sinners’ opposition so they do not grow weary or lose heart (Hebrews 12:3). Jesus directed his mind toward joy rather than allowing suffering to define the horizon.
Josh then makes the teaching personal. His stepfather Dave, his mother’s husband, died the previous afternoon. Josh is hurting and will miss him, while believing Dave is with the Lord and better off. Joy does not mean pretending everything is fine. Joy can coexist with tears, misery, and loss; standing confidently before God while circumstances are not fine is where others see joy and God’s glory.
documents.title: Count trials as joy by looking beyond present pain — Pressure That Produces

Society trains people to inventory what suffering took away, but Scripture says God can enrich believers through loss. excerpts: Josh reads James 1:4: perseverance must finish its work so believers become mature, complete, and lacking nothing. Society trains people to inventory what suffering took away, but Scripture says God can enrich believers through loss. If perseverance makes a person complete, then without perseverance that person remains incomplete. Josh names four “features that only come through fire.”

1. Christlikeness: Jesus was a “man of suffering” (Isaiah 53:3) without even a settled place to lay his head (Matthew 8:20). Sharing suffering can deepen fellowship with him. As Josh grieves Dave, he follows Jesus, who grieved Lazarus and wept (John 11:33–35). Tears do not erase the joy still set ahead (Hebrews 12:2, reapplied). Paul wanted to know both the power of Christ’s resurrection and participation in his sufferings, becoming like him in death and reaching resurrection (Philippians 3:10–11). Josh says Christians rarely speak this way because their minds are being conformed to the world rather than renewed by the Word (Romans 12:2).

2. Humility: Trials break pride. Paul’s brilliance, leadership, revelation, and capability could have fed self-exaltation, but the thorn in his flesh kept him dependent on Christ’s sufficient grace (2 Corinthians 12:7–9).

3. Compassion: Deep suffering equips believers to empathize with others. God, the Father of compassion and God of all comfort, comforts his people so they can pass that comfort to others in trouble (2 Corinthians 1:3–4). Josh warns against wasting suffering in self-pity when it can become a pathway to help someone else.
4. Faith: When other supports are stripped away, Christians learn to lean on God alone: “Though he slay me, yet will I hope in him” (Job 13:15).

Christlikeness, humility, compassion, and faith stand on the far side of the trial. That produced maturity is the promised joy; there is no alternate path to being complete. Josh repeats the command: “Consider it pure joy” (James 1:2, reapplied).

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · September 8, 2025 · James : A Faith That Works
documents.excerpt: Josh reads James 1:5–8: anyone lacking wisdom should ask God, who gives generously without fault-finding, but the asker must believe rather than doubt; the doubter is wave-tossed, double-minded, and unstable.
excerpts: Josh reads James 1:5–8: anyone lacking wisdom should ask God, who gives generously without fault-finding, but the asker must believe rather than doubt; the doubter is wave-tossed, double-minded, and unstable.

James observed that immature early believers struggled in prayer, just as Christians do now. Later James will say that some simply fail to ask (James 4:2). People claim to trust God but do not talk or walk with him.
Josh rejects prayer as a religious assignment. For the redeemed, it is unlimited access to the limitless God; refusing that access means refusing to walk in God’s offered power.

Why ask for wisdom rather than only strength, grace, or deliverance? Strength may carry someone through, grace may take someone over, and deliverance may pull someone out. Wisdom keeps the trial from being wasted by teaching the believer how to receive and use the moment.

Christians often consult a bestseller, preacher, podcast, spouse, parent, and friends before sitting quietly before God. If God gives generously, sparse prayer makes no sense. Josh does not forbid human counsel; his ordering point is that God must not be the backup plan or supporting role. The Creator is the lead. He invokes “Ask and you will receive” (Matthew 7:7) and challenges listeners to ask God for wisdom believing that he will answer.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · September 8, 2025 · James : A Faith That Works
documents.excerpt: Josh returns to James 1:6–8: doubt can kill the request before it is made, and James’s first major metaphor pictures the doubter as a wind-tossed wave.
excerpts: Josh returns to James 1:6–8: doubt can kill the request before it is made, and James’s first major metaphor pictures the doubter as a wind-tossed wave.

He illustrates the metaphor with a 2021 family trip to Big Beach, Hawaii. Josh and Madison eagerly swam through the large incoming waves because getting out seemed easy. Returning to shore was different: a rip current and repeated eight-foot waves battered them. Each time hope rose as they neared safety, another wave crashed, pulled them back, and forced them to begin again. Many Christians live the same way—up in one moment, crushed in the next, tossed between hope and despair.

Josh carefully says this instability is evidence of immaturity, not proof of lost salvation. The person has faith, or there would be no prayer at all; the same person also entertains unbelief, or there would be no doubt. Bouncing between the two makes the person double-minded and unstable.

Life may not match the desired plan or checklist, but Christ suffered for believers, and believers may now suffer for him. Pain, sickness, suffering, poverty, and death will be swallowed up in the coming reality with God (Revelation 21:4). Present sufferings cannot compare with the glory to be revealed (Romans 8:18).
Josh’s repeated pastoral command is: Hold on. Do not doubt God. Ask for wisdom. Persevere as Jesus did.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · September 8, 2025 · James : A Faith That Works
documents.excerpt: Josh closes the teaching with a direct question built from James 1:5–6, reapplying the passage: Do listeners believe God can give wisdom and will give it when they ask in faith? If so, why wait?
excerpts: Josh closes the teaching with a direct question built from James 1:5–6, reapplying the passage: Do listeners believe God can give wisdom and will give it when they ask in faith? If so, why wait?
He invites physically able listeners to kneel immediately. Pads are available for those who do not want “camel knees,” recalling James’s traditional life of prayer.

Josh supplies the substance of a candid prayer: Admit confusion over recurring hurt, loss, and suffering. Ask for understanding, but submit if explanation is not given. Ask for the wisdom needed to see a path through the tragedy toward God’s glory. Ask to become light to someone else in the middle of the tragedy. Confess trust in God regardless of the outcome.
He diagnoses frantic, prayerless living as a cause of much that is wrong in churches. Communion with God requires stopping, ceasing to fill every silence with words, sitting with him, and listening.

Josh directs the room into an integrated response of fellowship, prayer, the Lord’s Supper, singing, music, and access to elders at the tables. People need not fake emotion: the hurt may hurt and the sad may be sad, but they must talk to God.

In the closing prayer, Josh models his own appeal. He tells the Father that he is struggling, hurting, sad, and weary. He leans into God, asks comfort, presence, and peace for everyone mourning, and thanks Jesus for suffering so sinners can have peace with God. He offers to suffer faithfully to the end if that is his calling, thanks the Lord for loving him, and closes with “Amen.”

He is used to preparing whole series for the youth, or taking off, flying, or landing the plane as part of the Sunday teaching team, but this is a standalone message, so he is responsible for the open, the close, and everything in between.

Second, the church has just finished a study that took them into heavy and dark topics: how low people, even God’s people, can go when they wander into selfish desires, let sin reign unchecked, and live without a king. After Judges, talking about God’s promises might feel like sunshine after a storm or rainbows after a flood.

From 15 years in the high school math classroom, he likes to tell you what he’s going to tell you, then tell you, then tell you what he told you. documents.excerpt: The church just sang “Same God,” a youth favorite from summer camp, and it is easy to sing without noticing the lyrics: “I’m calling on the God of Jacob, whose love endures through generations. I know that you will keep your covenant.”
excerpts: The church just sang “Same God,” a youth favorite from summer camp, and it is easy to sing without noticing the lyrics: “I’m calling on the God of Jacob, whose love endures through generations. I know that you will keep your covenant.”

We can’t get to God’s promises without exploring covenants. A biblical covenant is a binding agreement initiated by God in which he makes promises and sets conditions for relationship with his people. He sets the terms, provides the promises, and, unlike human covenants, guarantees the fulfillment himself. A covenant is essentially a housing for one of God’s promises.

God covenanted with Noah never to flood the earth again, marked by a rainbow: a covenant of preservation. With Moses he declared Israel his treasured possession, a kingdom of priests and a holy nation if they obeyed: a covenant of law showing God’s holiness, Israel’s sin, and their need for a savior. With David he promised a descendant would reign forever: a covenant of kingship pointing to Jesus, the Son of David, whose kingdom will never end.

documents.context: Steve Coots · September 2, 2025 · God's Promises
documents.excerpt: Some of the more astute are thinking, “Steve, you missed one: what about Abraham?” God had already promised to bless Abram and make him a great nation, but God’s timeline was slower than Abram wanted, and he began to question the promise. Steve turns to Genesis 15 in three parts.
excerpts: Some of the more astute are thinking, “Steve, you missed one: what about Abraham?” God had already promised to bless Abram and make him a great nation, but God’s timeline was slower than Abram wanted, and he began to question the promise. Steve turns to Genesis 15 in three parts.

He reads Abram’s complaint that he remains childless, God’s command to count the stars, “So shall your offspring be,” Abram believing the Lord and it being credited to him as righteousness, and Abram asking how he can know, followed by God’s instruction to bring a heifer, goat, ram, dove, and pigeon, which Abram cuts in two.

This is how two men in that culture entered a covenant: they divided animals and walked through them, declaring, “Let it be done to me as was done to this animal if I should not keep my part.” It was a blood oath.

Picking up in verse 12, God tells the sleeping Abram his descendants will be strangers and slaves for 400 years before coming out with great possessions. Then the most important part: a smoking firepot and a blazing torch pass between the pieces, and the Lord makes a covenant with Abram.

Who walked through the pieces? Not Abraham. Only God. That is God saying, “I am taking full responsibility for this covenant. Even if you fail, I will bear the cost. The promise rests on me alone.” That is why Judges isn’t the last book in the Bible: even when the people were faithless, God remained faithful.
For extra study, the firepot represents what God indicated in verse 13, the dark, oppressive bondage of captivity, and the torch signifies that God would still be with them, a light in the darkness.

documents.excerpt: God is calling Jeremiah, a very young man, maybe 15 to 17, to be his voice and prophet. Steve reads Jeremiah 1:11: Jeremiah sees the branch of an almond tree, and the Lord says, “You have seen correctly, for I am watching to see that my word is fulfilled.” Then he sees a boiling pot tilting from the north.
excerpts: God is calling Jeremiah, a very young man, maybe 15 to 17, to be his voice and prophet. Steve reads Jeremiah 1:11: Jeremiah sees the branch of an almond tree, and the Lord says, “You have seen correctly, for I am watching to see that my word is fulfilled.” Then he sees a boiling pot tilting from the north.

Are we making plant-based milk here? Not quite. In Jerusalem the almond tree was the earliest to bloom, in February, a sign winter was ending, so biblically it represents anticipation, a promise of what is to come. The Hebrew word for almond is nearly identical to the word for watching, and God plays on it: he is watching over his word with care, like a shepherd who won’t let a single sheep wander or be lost.

Jeremiah needs that hope, because the boiling pot represents Babylon, the northern enemy that will take Judah captive. God’s will comes to pass, not just promises of blessing but promises of consequences and judgment. Like the almond blossoms, the people could anticipate good even in the mess.

documents.excerpt: We all know the sting of broken promises, and that is where 2 Corinthians 1 meets us. Paul had to explain why he broke a promise. His critics accused his character and thought him fickle and unreliable, because in 1 Corinthians 16 he had written, “I will come to you when I pass through Macedonia,” and he didn’t make that trip.
excerpts: We all know the sting of broken promises, and that is where 2 Corinthians 1 meets us. Paul had to explain why he broke a promise. His critics accused his character and thought him fickle and unreliable, because in 1 Corinthians 16 he had written, “I will come to you when I pass through Macedonia,” and he didn’t make that trip.

The Corinthians were used to manipulative, calculating ministers and assumed Paul was another shady preacher out for gain. But his first visit had been so difficult that he says in 2 Corinthians 2:1, “I made up my mind not to make another painful visit to you.” In verse 17 he asks, “When I was planning this, did I do it lightly?” He had the best intentions.

The good news is that we now have 2 Corinthians, with its teaching on comfort and affliction, strength and weakness, and servant leadership. If Paul had forced a return visit and taught in person, he would have had no reason to write it.

documents.excerpt: Has there been a time you had to go back on a promise? We scale our promises and how acceptable it is to break them: “Sorry, honey, we’ll go to the park tomorrow.” “But you promised.” “Sorry I broke curfew, Dad.” “We’re not going to make it home for Christmas.” “I just don’t think we can make this marriage work anymore.” “But you promised.”

documents.excerpt: Do you know God is faithful? When did you last look back and recount his faithfulness in big and little things, in easy and hard times, when joy came fast and when it had to be waited for?
excerpts: Do you know God is faithful? When did you last look back and recount his faithfulness in big and little things, in easy and hard times, when joy came fast and when it had to be waited for?

Steve’s family is approaching ten years since his middle son Josiah, at 8 months old, contracted bacterial meningitis, probably from a fungus at a pumpkin patch that October. Doctors at Phoenix Children’s said he was hours from permanent brain damage or death. Steve spent hours alone in the hospital chapel reading and praying, while hundreds prayed, many from this church.

documents.excerpt: How many promises has God made? Steve didn’t count them himself, but research tells him there are over 8,800 in the Bible, about 7,700 in the Old Testament before Jesus is on the scene. Unlike Paul or us, God has never had to explain why he didn’t keep one, because he has kept them all and will keep them all.
excerpts: How many promises has God made? Steve didn’t count them himself, but research tells him there are over 8,800 in the Bible, about 7,700 in the Old Testament before Jesus is on the scene. Unlike Paul or us, God has never had to explain why he didn’t keep one, because he has kept them all and will keep them all.

He jokes that they’ll now go through each one. But reading God’s word daily, you will come across many promises every day. The Bible is more than narrative, history, or poetry; it is a record of God’s character expressed through his promises, some for comfort, guidance, or warning, all trustworthy because they come from the mouth of God.

He reads a few and asks which one the Holy Spirit is calling each person’s attention to: I will be with you. I will protect you. I will keep my word. I will be your peace. I will always answer you. I will be your strength. I will fight for you. I will provide for you. I will prepare a place for you. I will come again. I will always love you. These aren’t greeting-card messages; they are God’s promises, and they are all yes in Jesus.

documents.context: Steve Coots · September 2, 2025 · God's Promises
documents.excerpt: Imagine having all the Old Testament promises with no Jesus. We might call the book good and well written, but not living, active, or life-changing. We would be asking, “God, if you are who you say you are, where are you?” But the cries of a baby in Matthew 1 pierced that silence. We have Jesus.
excerpts: Imagine having all the Old Testament promises with no Jesus. We might call the book good and well written, but not living, active, or life-changing. We would be asking, “God, if you are who you say you are, where are you?” But the cries of a baby in Matthew 1 pierced that silence. We have Jesus.

2 Peter 1:19 says we have the words of the prophets made more sure: fully affirmed and completely reliable, because we have Jesus, the Word himself, a lamp shining in a dark place until the day dawns. God’s promises were always there but dimly lit until Jesus, the light of the world, came to fulfill each one.

That is why we end every prayer “in Jesus’ name, amen.” They aren’t magical words; we acknowledge Jesus is our only access to the Father because of the finished work of the cross. We come not in our righteousness, since we have none, but in his. There is power in the name of Jesus.

excerpts: Steve returns to Jeremiah. In the mess of captivity, Jeremiah received a promise of hope that would not be fulfilled for generations. He reads Jeremiah 31: the days are coming when the Lord will make a new covenant, put his law in their minds and write it on their hearts, be their God, and forgive their wickedness and remember their sins no more.

This new covenant would be realized at the coming of Christ: a deeper, unbreakable, personal relationship with God that meets the needs the law covenant with Moses failed to meet, written on hearts, not stone. In Christ that promise is ours. God’s Spirit lives in us, his word is written in us, and his forgiveness is final, so we don’t just know or talk about the promises; we get to live them.

God has never broken a promise and never will. Every promise finds its yes in Jesus. So go live as his anointed, Spirit-filled, new covenant people in a world desperate for hope, declaring with our lives that God is faithful and his promises are true now and forever.

documents.excerpt: “In those days, there was no king in Israel. Everyone did what was right in his own eyes.” Elijah says that single sentence is the lens through which we must approach the final pages of Judges: the sound of a society untethered from the Lord.
excerpts: “In those days, there was no king in Israel. Everyone did what was right in his own eyes.” Elijah says that single sentence is the lens through which we must approach the final pages of Judges: the sound of a society untethered from the Lord.

Before reading, he issues a loving warning. Judges 19–21 is one of the darkest, most disturbing passages in all of Scripture: graphic, violent, and heartbreaking. God preserved these events for our instruction, not to entertain our curiosity but to expose our hearts. This is not a boogeyman story to fear-monger anyone toward belief; it shows the inevitable trajectory of sin and rebellion when it goes unchecked.

He asks the church to lean in with a sober heart and tells parents to use discretion with children. He refuses to censor what God has preserved: men not just walking apart from God but declaring themselves God and reaping the fruit of a rotting tree of disobedience.

We demand his favor while trampling his commands, but God will not underwrite our disobedience. He often lets us taste the bitter fruit of our choices, not because he has abandoned us but because he is disciplining us. His discipline is not rejection; it is mercy shaking us awake to what Paul says in Romans: the wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life.

Some have had to learn that the hard way, Elijah included, walking in outward disobedience and expecting inward peace. God loves us too much to let us live comfortably in our sin. When we wink at sexual sin, treat our marriage vows lightly, and entertain ourselves with the very filth Christ died to save us from, we prove that Gibeah isn’t just out there; it’s in here.

documents.excerpt: When we operate from outrage, chaos ensues. The tribes unite against Benjamin and demand the guilty men of Gibeah; Benjamin refuses, and now there is civil war. Elijah reads how Israel inquires of God, “Who of us is to go up first?”, and loses 22,000 on the first day.
excerpts: When we operate from outrage, chaos ensues. The tribes unite against Benjamin and demand the guilty men of Gibeah; Benjamin refuses, and now there is civil war. Elijah reads how Israel inquires of God, “Who of us is to go up first?”, and loses 22,000 on the first day.

The irony: Israel inquires of God when it is convenient. They want justice without accountability and repentance. It isn’t “Should we go up, Lord?” but “Who shall go up first?” They want God to bless their anger while keeping their idols hidden, and his guidance on a dark path he never sent them on.

Many Christians operate from the same place. We don’t seek God’s will; we seek confirmation of what we’ve already decided, then ask him to bless it. We want him as our consultant, not our king, our personal cheerleader rather than the one we seek. Before you ask God to fight for you, ask if you’re right with him.

If that’s you, you have nothing to run from. Our God is merciful and faithful, and as the apostle John reminds us, if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us. You can turn right now.

excerpts: The end is not much better than the beginning. Israel swore no one would give his daughter to a Benjamite, and after nearly wiping Benjamin out only 600 men are left. They weep at Bethel, crying, “Why has this happened to Israel?” Elijah’s answer: “Riddle me this, Batman.” They just don’t get it, and sometimes neither do we.

Their sorrow is not over their sin against God but over the consequences of their actions. That is guilt, not repentance, and there is a difference: you can feel guilty and still have no desire to right the wrong.

In the rest of the story Israel doubles down on its sin to fix the self-inflicted population problem, leading to more depravity, rebellion, idolatry, and death. The book ends not with a bang but a whimper: “In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did what was right in his own eyes.”

Think of the horror of Judges 19: a woman abused, abandoned, and butchered, a symbol of sin’s devastation in our lives and culture. In the gospel we find the opposite. documents.excerpt: Today the church encounters easily one of the best-known stories in Scripture. Jesus is the most popular figure in the Bible, but Samson has to be in the conversation for the top five; even people who have never opened a Bible have some idea who he was. Asked for the first word that comes to mind, many say Delilah.
excerpts: Today the church encounters easily one of the best-known stories in Scripture. Jesus is the most popular figure in the Bible, but Samson has to be in the conversation for the top five; even people who have never opened a Bible have some idea who he was. Asked for the first word that comes to mind, many say Delilah.

Josh thinks of Arnold, not the grumpy politician but the chiseled Mr. Universe. Scripture doesn’t indicate Samson was shredded, and that isn’t important. Samson wasn’t meant to picture peak male perfection, but God’s strength working through man by the power of his Holy Spirit; for all we know he looked like Captain America before the experiment.

Samson is the last judge mentioned by name in Judges, with three chapters, one devoted entirely to his birth story. Unusually for Josh, they will cover a ton of content: a ton of dysfunction, and then at the end something beautiful. He asks the church to hang in there.

documents.excerpt: Samson’s story is bigger than Judges; it reaches across all of God’s word as a divine demonstration of how God saves his people.
excerpts: Samson’s story is bigger than Judges; it reaches across all of God’s word as a divine demonstration of how God saves his people.

Israel isn’t just having a bad week. The cycle of disobedience, discipline, distress, and deliverance is inevitable: there is peace while a judge lives, then he dies, Israel forgets Yahweh, and it begins again. They were slaves to sin in desperate need of a Savior, and the symbolism in Samson’s story is remarkable.

documents.excerpt: Josh starts in Judges 13:1: again Israel did evil in the eyes of the Lord, so he delivered them to the Philistines for 40 years. He loves Judges because of what that phrase reminds us: the story never ends with our disobedience, though it seems like it should. Because of his great love, it always ends with his faithfulness, and that is why we praise him.
excerpts: Josh starts in Judges 13:1: again Israel did evil in the eyes of the Lord, so he delivered them to the Philistines for 40 years. He loves Judges because of what that phrase reminds us: the story never ends with our disobedience, though it seems like it should. Because of his great love, it always ends with his faithfulness, and that is why we praise him.

Forty years is the longest oppression yet; the number usually indicates finality and judgment. The Philistines were the world’s superpower, superior in military, infrastructure, and architecture, while Israel was still figuring out how to pitch a tent in a cave. They took what they wanted, castrated and impaled the men, kept the women and children, got drunk on beer and fat on bacon.

The text never says Israel cried out to God during those 40 years. Whether they were content or afraid to make things worse, it is frightening and humbling how easily God’s people accept the way things are instead of calling on him.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · August 18, 2025 · Without a King : The Book of Judges
documents.excerpt: In verse 3 the angel of the Lord says, “You are barren and childless, but you are going to become pregnant and give birth to a son.” Only God can have sentences like that. It is the first time in Judges a judge is promised before birth; Ehud, Deborah, Othniel, and Gideon were all alive. God refuses the assist from man and saves in the face of impossibility.
excerpts: In verse 3 the angel of the Lord says, “You are barren and childless, but you are going to become pregnant and give birth to a son.” Only God can have sentences like that. It is the first time in Judges a judge is promised before birth; Ehud, Deborah, Othniel, and Gideon were all alive. God refuses the assist from man and saves in the face of impossibility.

They didn’t cry out, had nothing to offer, and had not just given up but assimilated. Their future was hopeless, but God wasn’t done. His salvation doesn’t come from tears of desperation; you can’t earn, contribute to, or buy it. God creates salvation out of nothing, so you are never too far gone, whether you wandered four years or 40.

It isn’t 90% done for you to add the finishing touches; it is finished. And if he saved Josh without any help of his own, he will keep him too, because if it were up to Josh to keep his salvation, there is no doubt he would lose it.

excerpts: The angel tells her to drink no wine or fermented drink, eat nothing unclean, and never let a razor touch the boy’s head, because he will be a Nazirite dedicated to God from the womb and will begin to deliver Israel from the Philistines.

Numbers 6 describes the Nazirite vow: set apart, consecrated, and devoted to God, no cutting hair, nothing from the vine (not even Welch’s grape juice, so warm lumpy milk or water), and touching nothing dead. People normally took it for a period of time, like a fast. This one is unique because his mother kept it during pregnancy and Samson from birth; by age 12 Josh imagines serious male Rapunzel vibes.
The picture behind the vow is of a greater Samson who would one day be set apart, holy, and sinless.

Despite the odd couple, both display a timeless truth. Manoah was right in his fear of God, and the church needs more reverence, but all reverence and no comfort isn’t healthy, so his wife balances out the home: if Yahweh wanted us dead, we’d be dead. All fear and no joy is a nasty recipe for a Christian, and all joy and no fear is just as gross. Psalm 2 gives the balance: serve the Lord with fear and celebrate his rule with trembling. We can smile and tremble at the same time.

excerpts: The woman gives birth, names him Samson, the Lord blesses him, and the Spirit of the Lord begins to stir him in Mahaneh Dan between Zorah and Eshtaol.

Today we don’t care about names (“you just named your son Joab because that was the trend”), but names mattered in ancient cultures. Matthew 1 shows naming describes our Savior’s mission from birth: the angel tells Joseph to give him the name Jesus because he will save his people from their sins. With every Hebrew name to choose from, God chooses Yeshua, Joshua. What did Joshua do? He took down Jericho. And the Lord will take down the city of darkness. His name defines his mission to save.

excerpts: Who was Samson named after? The little-g god Shamash; his name compared his strength to the power of the sun. Ancient rabbis used it as a cautionary tale: the same sun that gives life and healing can scorch and burn. Samson’s God-given strength was a blessing to God’s people, but misused it could be destructive.

The sun imagery recalls the last prophet, Malachi: “But for you who revere my name, the sun of righteousness will rise with healing in its rays.” Samson is a type of Christ, a Nazirite savior who fought Israel’s enemies, but like the saviors before him he would fade and die: a temporary savior and a possibly dangerous light.

That takes Josh to Revelation 21 and the unceasing light of the New Jerusalem, which doesn’t need the sun or moon, for the glory of God gives it light and the Lamb is its lamp. See how much encouragement God’s people can gain from a name. This isn’t just a library of 66 books; it is the living, breathing word of God.

documents.excerpt: The next line may sound like a recent kitchen conversation: “I have seen a Philistine woman in Timnah; now get her for me as my wife.” His parents ask whether there isn’t an acceptable woman among their own people. Samson says, “Get her for me. She’s the right one for me.”
excerpts: The next line may sound like a recent kitchen conversation: “I have seen a Philistine woman in Timnah; now get her for me as my wife.” His parents ask whether there isn’t an acceptable woman among their own people. Samson says, “Get her for me. She’s the right one for me.”

Josh thinks the parents hit a home run here; the text never indicates they failed to uphold their vow. Despite being raised to honor the Lord, Samson ignores them and decides to marry a Philistine, a clear violation of God’s law. Living by sight, not by faith, he let lust lead him away from the law; he didn’t care about pleasing the Lord or his parents, only himself.
If believers are warning you about the path you are on, take notes on how things go for Samson. And don’t forget, God will accomplish his plans with or without us, the easy way or the hard way.

Samson scoops honey from a swarm of bees in it, eats as he goes, and gives some to his parents without telling them where it came from.

If you think Samson was chilling in vineyards without partaking, Josh thinks he was getting down on some wine; if so, he has now violated two-thirds of the Nazirite vow. His sin began with the lust of the flesh, “I want this,” then the lust of the eyes, “I want that,” and now the pride of life.

Breaking your vow and feeling bad is something we can all work with. It is another thing to drag down others, especially those who gave you your foundation, and then turn your disobedience into a joke. Samson didn’t take his broken vow seriously; he turned it into a riddle to entertain his wedding guests.

documents.excerpt: Unfortunately the story doesn’t end at Lehi. One day Samson goes to Gaza, sees a prostitute, and spends the night with her. Of course he does.
excerpts: Unfortunately the story doesn’t end at Lehi. One day Samson goes to Gaza, sees a prostitute, and spends the night with her. Of course he does.

Josh breaks our temptation to look down on him: Samson is not that different from modern Christians. He now only cares about appearing to be a Nazirite rather than keeping the vow; the only part left is the hair. By outward appearance he seems upright while he lies with a prostitute. Is the church different? We made it to church, memorized our doctrine, and sound Christian, while blatantly sinning against the one we say we love.

Just a few verses earlier a thirsty Samson whined in the desert that he would die, and the Lord provided water. To Samson and many Christians, they love his water but not his commands; they drink of the good but don’t care about the requirements. Grace is not a license to sin.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · August 18, 2025 · Without a King : The Book of Judges
documents.excerpt: Samson was in chains because he was prideful and arrogant, chased the lust of his flesh and eyes, and wanted vengeance. Unlike Samson, Jesus was not bound for his own sin, but for ours. That is good news, because many of us are like Samson: our past isn’t pretty, and we have lived to please ourselves with lust, power, sex, and money.
excerpts: Samson was in chains because he was prideful and arrogant, chased the lust of his flesh and eyes, and wanted vengeance. Unlike Samson, Jesus was not bound for his own sin, but for ours. That is good news, because many of us are like Samson: our past isn’t pretty, and we have lived to please ourselves with lust, power, sex, and money.

Jesus also tore something down when he died: the idea that God is behind a curtain, accessible only once a year. He replaced it with a new dwelling place, his people, and when he dwells in them they become strong where Samson was weak.

However far you have been from God, through a failed marriage, disobeying parents, broken promises, or sexual sin so deep you can’t see the light, don’t let shame, guilt, or pride keep you from the most amazing blessing there is: God answering a sinner’s prayer. Run to him now and borrow Samson’s plea: “Please, God, help me. I need you.” If he could turn Samson’s life around and use it for victory, he can turn your story around too.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · August 11, 2025 · Without a King : The Book of Judges
documents.excerpt: Josh opens week four of the Without a King series: remembering what life was like for God’s people in the period of Judges fills us with gratitude for our wonderful Savior, King Jesus.
excerpts: Josh opens week four of the Without a King series: remembering what life was like for God’s people in the period of Judges fills us with gratitude for our wonderful Savior, King Jesus.

He draws attention to Judges 17: “In those days Israel had no king; everyone did as they saw fit.” That is part of what makes our pursuit of Christ so valuable. Without a standard to reach for, we set our own. Jesus commands, “Be perfect, therefore, as your heavenly Father is perfect,” but without his words spurring us on, we would settle for being better than that guy, or better than our parents.

Josh opens week four of the Without a King series: remembering what life was like for God’s people in the period of Judges fills us with gratitude for our wonderful Savior, King Jesus.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · August 11, 2025 · Without a King : The Book of Judges
documents.excerpt: Scripture seems to disprove the character of everyone but one. Part of why God gave us the Old Testament is to show what happens when ordinary men do the work: here’s the law, but who can keep it? Here’s the priesthood, but who can keep it pure? Here are the judges, but who can live forever? Pick a king, until he becomes self-serving. Send prophets to guide the kings, until the people kill the prophets.
excerpts: Scripture seems to disprove the character of everyone but one. Part of why God gave us the Old Testament is to show what happens when ordinary men do the work: here’s the law, but who can keep it? Here’s the priesthood, but who can keep it pure? Here are the judges, but who can live forever? Pick a king, until he becomes self-serving. Send prophets to guide the kings, until the people kill the prophets.

God isn’t throwing things into history to see what sticks, like a chemist running an experiment. This is a gracious, intentional, patient demonstration of what won’t work, so his people see we need a greater lawkeeper, sacrifice, priest, judge, king, prophet, and Savior.

God uses man to disprove man and to prove God. Given the opportunity, you will go astray; we all, like sheep, have gone astray. In the worst circumstances and the best, you will fall short. But God loves us enough to teach us over and over that we need something we can’t obtain for ourselves.

Don’t lose track of the story: whose land is this? Israel’s, given by God. How humiliating, to go from conquerors to servant farmers. Why would God put them through this? Two reasons: God hates sin, and God loves his people.

Whenever they planted, the Midianites, Amalekites, and other eastern peoples came like swarms of locusts with their livestock and camels, ruined the crops all the way to Gaza, and spared no living thing, until Israel cried out to the Lord.
Don’t lose track of the story: whose land is this? Israel’s, given by God. How humiliating, to go from conquerors to servant farmers. Why would God put them through this? Two reasons: God hates sin, and God loves his people.

excerpts: “Pardon me, my lord,” Gideon replies (at least he uses his manners), “but if the Lord is with us, why has all this happened to us? Where are all his wonders that our ancestors told us about?… But now the Lord has abandoned us.”

Josh feels bad for Gideon. He knows what the Lord did in Egypt, but no one in his family thought to tell him about their disobedience. God didn’t abandon them; his parents abandoned God. This is what you get when a household isn’t dedicated to the Lord: kids who wrestle with God because they only have half the story. His ancestors explained what God did but not what God requires.
Gideon lacked faith and courage, but it isn’t as if his dad was walking around saying, “As for me and my house, we will serve the Lord.” His dad has an altar to a false god in the backyard.

Are you waiting for him to split the sea or send rain? The church declares he killed death. There is only one sign you need: God took on flesh, fulfilled the law, absorbed God’s wrath for sinners on the cross, lay in a tomb Friday and Saturday, and on Sunday walked out with an eternal victory over Satan, sin, and death.

documents.excerpt: They keep talking, and Gideon is so polite: “Pardon me, my lord, but how can I save Israel? My clan is the weakest in Manasseh, and I am the least in my family.” The Lord answers, “I will be with you, and you will strike down all the Midianites together.”
excerpts: They keep talking, and Gideon is so polite: “Pardon me, my lord, but how can I save Israel? My clan is the weakest in Manasseh, and I am the least in my family.” The Lord answers, “I will be with you, and you will strike down all the Midianites together.”

Josh loves Gideon’s humility, but can’t he see that it is because of his weakness that God chose him? God uses people who know they could never do it unless God did something miraculous: the lowly, the insignificant, the ordinary. That is good news for many of us; as for the self-appointed elite, you aren’t as great as you think you are.

Gideon knew he didn’t bring much to the table, and that is a good place to start. God goes out of his way to call the least expected so he receives all the glory, because the smart, the beautiful, and the talented end up confusing God’s wonders as their own. When God selects someone we never expected, we look at what was done and say, “Yep, that has to be the Lord.”

excerpts: Gideon wants assurance like we all do, but when he gets it, it isn’t comforting; it is frightening. Modern readers picture frolicking through the park holding hands with Jesus. We are friends with Jesus, but the romcom thing with you and Jesus is not a thing.

Many would want to reassure Gideon that God isn’t a big scary God. Josh says: is God loving? Yes. Should you fear him? Yes. Gideon’s reaction seems strange because of what side of the cross we are on. What makes grace so amazing is holiness, the distance between how awesome God is and how wicked we are, and how far he travels to come down to our level. That is what makes “I will be with you” so amazing.
When God asks you into something too big for you, don’t highlight your deficiencies but his proficiencies, because a timeless truth spans from BC to AD: with God all things are possible.

excerpts: Verse 25: that night the Lord tells Gideon to take his father’s second bull, tear down his father’s altar to Baal, cut down the Asherah pole, build a proper altar to the Lord, and offer the bull with the pole’s wood. Gideon takes ten servants and obeys, but at night, because he is afraid of his family and the townspeople.

Leave it to Christians to call him a coward for going at night. But by our Lord’s approach to judging rightly in Matthew 7, examine your own weak faith first. How much do you trust the Lord? Are you bold in the building but invisible in the wild? Being a Christian in here should be the easiest part of the week. Anyone can follow Jesus when it’s convenient and the crowd is cheering; will you follow him when it costs you, or when no one is looking?

documents.excerpt: They are coming up on the second anniversary of the death of Josh’s sister Jess, pictured holding Nolan. He and his family miss her so much; she left too soon, and his heart goes out to others grieving.
excerpts: They are coming up on the second anniversary of the death of Josh’s sister Jess, pictured holding Nolan. He and his family miss her so much; she left too soon, and his heart goes out to others grieving.

Months before she died she called while struggling through a divorce, and they dropped everything to help settle her into a new apartment and love on her. Weeks later his sister Andrea told him Jess said she had never experienced love and grace like that. Josh could have preached a whole series at Jess, but the greatest sermon could never have communicated half of what they said by serving her.

Sometimes the best witness isn’t a lecture in the spotlight but faithful obedience in the night. That night Gideon discovered that if you step out in obedience, even trembling, the Lord will cover you with his protection and ensure he alone gets the glory.
