Give him a crooked church, the word of God, and a few good men, and it can be straightened out; give him the most messed-up man and the gospel of Christ, and that can be fixed too.

The rebuilding continued because a couple of men started preaching the word. God speaks and creation begins and obeys, and so do his people. When God needs to wake his people from slumber, he sends preachers: Martin Luther and the Reformation, which transformed Germany and the whole Christian world; John Wesley in Great Britain, whose revival many historians credit with sparing England the bloodbath France experienced in its revolution. Don’t underestimate what God can do with a preacher who loves his word.

Josh couldn’t shake Spurgeon’s line that the man who preaches the word of God stands not on a mere platform but on a throne. Haggai launched his preaching ministry in 520 BC; five of his messages are recorded in his book, though not on YouTube like Crossroads’. The preaching led to the work continuing.

Once again the old-timers take us to school: how we deal with people matters, at work, on the freeway, even in the checkout line at Costco. Paul tells the Colossians to be wise in the way you act toward outsiders and make the most of every opportunity.

documents.context: Elijah Stanley · April 1, 2025 · Reclaim: The Book of Ezra
documents.excerpt: Elijah asks the church to imagine being an Israelite returning from exile: stepping over broken stones where houses stood, weeds growing through once-busy streets, dust blowing through the ruins. Then you see where the temple used to be, the house of the true and living God, now a pile of rubble with the altar, the very heart of worship, buried beneath debris and decades of neglect.
excerpts: Elijah asks the church to imagine being an Israelite returning from exile: stepping over broken stones where houses stood, weeds growing through once-busy streets, dust blowing through the ruins. Then you see where the temple used to be, the house of the true and living God, now a pile of rubble with the altar, the very heart of worship, buried beneath debris and decades of neglect.

You’d think the priority would be rebuilding the walls, securing the city, or laying the temple’s foundation. Instead the people do something that seems backwards: they rebuild the altar first. Having seen the destruction their pursuit of their own glory brought, they ground their efforts in a celebration of who God is and a repentant heart before laying a single brick.

Many of us are striving to rebuild things in our lives apart from God’s help, but the Lord wants us to submit to his way, his plan, and his timing. Are we sprinting toward our own ambition, or saying, “Lord, your will be done, not mine”? Elijah hopes the church learns from this passage that true revival isn’t emotionalism or signs and wonders but a return to the Lord, to worship and holiness. He then prays for the time together.

documents.context: Elijah Stanley · April 1, 2025 · Reclaim: The Book of Ezra
documents.excerpt: The first thing Elijah notices is the unity behind the decision. He loves how the ESV renders verse 1: the people gathered as one man to Jerusalem. The unity of God’s people has always mattered to God, which is part of why we still gather, for community, love, and encouragement, and to declare his praises with one voice as he commands.
excerpts: The first thing Elijah notices is the unity behind the decision. He loves how the ESV renders verse 1: the people gathered as one man to Jerusalem. The unity of God’s people has always mattered to God, which is part of why we still gather, for community, love, and encouragement, and to declare his praises with one voice as he commands.

Returning to Judah wasn’t enough; worship had to be resumed. The seventh month, Tishri, is the month of the Feast of Tabernacles, detailed in Leviticus 23, which commemorates Israel’s forty years wandering in the desert after slavery in Egypt. With the festival on the horizon, the people felt an urgency to rebuild the altar. What better way to celebrate a return from exile than to remember how faithful the Lord had been?

Elijah doesn’t believe in coincidences. Before a new foundation is laid, the Israelites get to submit their future plans to God and remember how faithful he has been to show them mercy and lead them toward restoration, though they didn’t deserve it. That should sound familiar: our God is the same yesterday, today, and forever, always good, kind, patient, and full of grace.

Worship is a posture of the heart first, and what we do is only worship when it flows from a thankful heart that seeks to honor him.

Worship is a posture of the heart first, and what we do is only worship when it flows from a thankful heart that seeks to honor him.
He recalls Jesus with the Samaritan woman in the Gospel of John: God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth.

Paul addresses this in Romans 12: offer your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God, your true and proper worship; don’t conform to the pattern of this world but be transformed by the renewing of your mind. And in 1 Thessalonians 5: rejoice always, pray continually, give thanks in all circumstances.

How often did the Israelites sacrifice? Daily. Paul’s language is intentional: true worship gives ourselves to God’s will instead of being wise in our own eyes, a daily decision to recognize our desperate need for Christ. You don’t sing on Sunday and live like the world on Monday; you lay your whole self, hands, feet, mind, desires, and ambitions, on the altar of obedience. Deny yourself, take up your cross, and follow him.

excerpts: Singing is often accompanied by clapping, shouting, lifting hands, and kneeling. Every expression in worship must come from Scripture, but Scripture gives much more freedom than we tend to use. He is good and his mercy endures forever, so let the world know.

Elijah doesn’t know how anyone can sing about the blood-bought mercy of Christ and stand like a statue, hands in pockets, lips barely moving. The gospel is not cold theology; it is the power of God unto salvation, and when that takes root something in you has to respond. David danced before the Lord with all his might; the psalmists shouted, clapped, and lifted their hands; Isaiah saw the throne room and came undone; the angels cry “holy, holy, holy” and never stop. Yet some think the right response to God’s glory is stoicism.

He gets the struggle: maybe you don’t like your voice, feel too dignified, or think it’s awkward. But this isn’t about you; it is about a God so glorious and worthy that the only right response is to sing back to him. If we can yell at a football game or belt out lyrics at a concert but go silent when the gospel is sung, something’s off.

The angels aren’t whispering in heaven, and the redeemed don’t mumble; they roar with joy. Sing when you feel it and when you don’t, in the storm and in victory, because worship isn’t about your personality but reality: Christ has won, death is defeated, and sinners have been adopted, washed, and set free. So where is your joy, your awe, your response to the infinite worth of Jesus? If the tomb is empty, and it is, our worship should look like people who actually believe it.

Don’t stand there like a statue
Singing is often accompanied by clapping, shouting, lifting hands, and kneeling. Every expression in worship must come from Scripture, but Scripture gives much more freedom than we tend to use. He is good and his mercy endures forever, so let the world know.
Elijah doesn’t know how anyone can sing about the blood-bought mercy of Christ and stand like a statue, hands in pockets, lips barely moving. The gospel is not cold theology; it is the power of God unto salvation, and when that takes root something in you has to respond. David danced before the Lord with all his might; the psalmists shouted, clapped, and lifted their hands; Isaiah saw the throne room and came undone; the angels cry “holy, holy, holy” and never stop. Yet some think the right response to God’s glory is stoicism.
He gets the struggle: maybe you don’t like your voice, feel too dignified, or think it’s awkward. But this isn’t about you; it is about a God so glorious and worthy that the only right response is to sing back to him. If we can yell at a football game or belt out lyrics at a concert but go silent when the gospel is sung, something’s off.
The angels aren’t whispering in heaven, and the redeemed don’t mumble; they roar with joy. Sing when you feel it and when you don’t, in the storm and in victory, because worship isn’t about your personality but reality: Christ has won, death is defeated, and sinners have been adopted, washed, and set free. So where is your joy, your awe, your response to the infinite worth of Jesus? If the tomb is empty, and it is, our worship should look like people who actually believe it.

excerpts: There’s more to this worship service. Elijah reads verses 12–13: older priests, Levites, and family heads who had seen the former temple wept aloud while many others shouted for joy, and no one could distinguish the shouts of joy from the weeping; the sound was heard far away.

The younger generation, who never saw the first temple’s glory, shouts at the beginning of something new. The older generation weeps because they remember the grandeur of Solomon’s temple. In that moment joy and sorrow meet in worship.

Isn’t that just like our lives, and like worship? True worship isn’t always neat and tidy; sometimes it mixes celebration and lament, “God, you are so good” and “God, we miss what was.” Both are lifted to the Lord, and both are part of the foundation of revival. Some are shouting because God is doing something new; some are weeping because things aren’t like they used to be. Either way, will we keep worshiping, because God is still faithful?

documents.excerpt: Josh is half wet from a baptism before the service. Last week the church launched Reclaim, a series on what God did for the Jews exiled to Babylon: in exile or in return, God remains faithful to his word, so when we fail, forget who we are, or sin, we can find comfort that through Jesus God has reclaimed us and nothing can change that.
excerpts: Josh is half wet from a baptism before the service. Last week the church launched Reclaim, a series on what God did for the Jews exiled to Babylon: in exile or in return, God remains faithful to his word, so when we fail, forget who we are, or sin, we can find comfort that through Jesus God has reclaimed us and nothing can change that.

We can also find comfort that the wicked will be dealt with. Josh wrestles with whether the wicked are getting away with it and when injustice will be dealt with. He knows the answers, but if you struggle there too, you aren’t alone: the psalmist asked, “How long, Lord, will the wicked be jubilant?”

Those who love God have long cried out, “How long?” We long to be in the garden with him again. In Egypt Israel was oppressed, but Babylon came in response to their disobedience. Whether we did the evil or it was done to us, we cry out to God to rise up and judge the earth.

Are the wicked getting away with it?
Josh is half wet from a baptism before the service. Last week the church launched Reclaim, a series on what God did for the Jews exiled to Babylon: in exile or in return, God remains faithful to his word, so when we fail, forget who we are, or sin, we can find comfort that through Jesus God has reclaimed us and nothing can change that.
We can also find comfort that the wicked will be dealt with. Josh wrestles with whether the wicked are getting away with it and when injustice will be dealt with. He knows the answers, but if you struggle there too, you aren’t alone: the psalmist asked, “How long, Lord, will the wicked be jubilant?”
Those who love God have long cried out, “How long?” We long to be in the garden with him again. In Egypt Israel was oppressed, but Babylon came in response to their disobedience. Whether we did the evil or it was done to us, we cry out to God to rise up and judge the earth.

In Revelation 7 an elder tells John that those who came out of the great tribulation have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.

So are your robes washed or soiled? Josh isn’t asking whether you sin; we all sin. He is asking whether you have gone to Jesus and asked him to wash your sins away. excerpts: Verse 6: all their neighbors assisted them with silver and gold, goods, livestock, and valuable gifts, besides the freewill offerings. Only about 50,000 returned; with the Jewish people having grown in exile, hundreds of thousands if not millions stayed in Babylon. Josh doesn’t assume those who stayed opposed the project; those moved to rebuild had tremendous support.

The timeless truth: God’s people give to God’s projects. Some give gold, some silver; some were led to rebuild and some to support financially. Whether money, time, or skill, Paul adds the way: not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.

Better still, Babylon kept changing hands, so some neighbors were probably Assyrian, Babylonian, or Persian. God was using false worshipers’ money to rebuild his temple. My God will meet all your needs according to the riches of his glory; he can use unexpected sources to provide for his church and mission.

All our resources belong to God, so when you give you are returning what he gave you. The sharp flip side: if you don’t give, you are keeping what isn’t yours, and there is a word for that: stealing from God. The neighbors gave because they believed God was doing what he said. We can see their faith in their giving; can we see yours? Crossroads wants to be a church that gives freely and joyfully, and invites people to join the work.

excerpts: Verse 7: Cyrus brought out the temple articles Nebuchadnezzar had carried off. It makes no sense unless you have seen God work in your own life. God moved Cyrus’s heart, and when God softens a heart you always see fruit.

Kings loved adding “the Great” to their names. But when God moves a heart, one of the first fruits is humility, which seeks to bring glory to God: God is great. Ambition says keep the gold and build your kingdom, with more buildings, statues, and treasures. Humility says, “I might be a great king, but I’m not the King of kings,” and values others above yourself.

What blows Josh away: as Isaiah 44 showed last week, Cyrus did not acknowledge God, yet a non-believer acts in obedience to God. There is more outpouring in a rebel king with a new heart than in most professing Christians today. That is proof of God at work, and you can’t fake it; you might fool the masses, but you cannot mock God.

documents.excerpt: Anyone can call themselves a Christian, but only true believers submit to God. Pride says my way is best; humility says, “God, your way, not mine.” Pride says, “I got this”; humility says, “God, I can’t do this, and even if I could, I don’t want to without you.”
excerpts: Anyone can call themselves a Christian, but only true believers submit to God. Pride says my way is best; humility says, “God, your way, not mine.” Pride says, “I got this”; humility says, “God, I can’t do this, and even if I could, I don’t want to without you.”

Pride says, “Listen to me; I’ve read the Bible cover to cover 18 times; I’m an expert.” Humility says, “The more I learn, the more I see how much I have to learn,” always at the feet of Jesus. Pride says, “This isn’t fair; I need more”; humility says, “Thank you; this is more than I deserve,” even in the red. Pride wants vengeance; humility says, “I might not trust you, but I forgive you.”

God humbles us not to break us but to bless us; he resists the proud and gives grace to the humble. Josh offers a dangerous prayer: ask God to reveal areas of pride, then walk away from them and walk in humility, and come tell him what happens. As Peter says, humble yourselves under God’s mighty hand: either you humble yourself and he lifts you up, or you lift yourself up and he humbles you.

A stewardship team of pastors, elders, and members, an elder team that approves the budget and reviews finances monthly, and an external audit every three years mean at least 14 people who aren’t his employees see the dollars every month, so givers can be confident their gifts go to God’s glory.

Money isn’t coming out of their ears: the $1.5 million budget ending April 1 is about $7,000 short, but expenses were managed well. Some churches in the Valley run multimillion-dollar operations with zero elders, which is how pastors end up in orange jumpsuits on CNN. No one is above accountability.

excerpts: It isn’t a random tangent: when God moves hearts, there is stewardship and accountability. The inventory lists gold and silver dishes, pans, and bowls, 5,400 articles in all, which Sheshbazzar brought with the exiles from Babylon to Jerusalem.

Ezra mentions Sheshbazzar four times and then never again. Most scholars agree it was another name for Zerubbabel, governor of Judah and grandson of King Jehoiachin. Exiles were often given Babylonian names, as Daniel was given Belteshazzar in Daniel 1.

For the numbers people with calculators out: the listed items add up to 2,499, yet verse 11 says 5,400 in total. Some cry contradiction, but slow down: Cyrus gave back what was stolen, and the neighbors gave as well, for a grand total of 5,400 articles to carry across the wilderness.

excerpts: Ezra 2 is a long list of family units and their numbers. Josh jokes he will read it, then doesn’t, but explains why it matters. Today we care about family history only if there is a trust fund; to Old Testament Jews it was very important to prove ancestry.

How would you prove you are an American citizen? Josh wouldn’t accept a driver’s license from a sketchy DMV employee, but a birth certificate or Social Security number would do (keep that to yourself). Should someone here illegally have the same rights and privileges? Josh’s opinion is no: they have human rights that should be upheld, but citizens are afforded rights noncitizens are not.

These genealogies were like ancient Social Security cards. Without proven ancestry you couldn’t receive the rights of the covenant people, who were set apart with a God-given task and couldn’t let outsiders lead them into idolatry. Returning Jews also couldn’t reclaim family land without proving lineage.

Josh’s favorite as a pastor: the lists kept non-Levites from serving in the temple and collecting a free pastoral check. Verse 62 shows some who searched for their family records and couldn’t find them, and they weren’t given a chance to be nice; they were excluded from the priesthood as unclean. Don’t leave Babylon without your ID.

These genealogies were like ancient Social Security cards. Without proven ancestry you couldn’t receive the rights of the covenant people, who were set apart with a God-given task and couldn’t let outsiders lead them into idolatry. Returning Jews also couldn’t reclaim family land without proving lineage.
Josh’s favorite as a pastor: the lists kept non-Levites from serving in the temple and collecting a free pastoral check. Verse 62 shows some who searched for their family records and couldn’t find them, and they weren’t given a chance to be nice; they were excluded from the priesthood as unclean. Don’t leave Babylon without your ID.

excerpts: Josh’s favorite verse in chapter 2: they also had 200 male and female singers. God is moving hearts, and they aren’t going on this journey without a decent playlist. Since the first Exodus the Jews composed songs to honor God; in captivity there weren’t many days for singing in the streets, but now they were heading home with a new song.

God loves music and loves your praise. We have a singing faith, and God loves to see his people’s joy in his faithfulness pour out in music. Psalm 150 says let everything that has breath praise the Lord, and over a dozen instruments are named in Scripture. Elijah preaches on worship next week and may be mad Josh let this play out.

Not only does God delight in the music; he joins in. Zephaniah says the Lord your God will rejoice over you with singing. With so much complaining about worship, Josh wonders whether there will be complaining in heaven, because heaven is filled with worship: in Revelation 5 the living creatures and elders fall before the Lamb with harps and golden bowls of incense and sing a new song. The elders have music and haze.

There was singing at creation: God asks Job who laid its cornerstone while the morning stars sang together and the angels shouted for joy. Heaven worshiped before man knew a single note. David plays and Saul is less of a jerk; Paul sings hymns and God shakes the prison doors open. How can we be lazy in worship when God delights in it, joins it, and responds with wonders? Worship isn’t just music; it is a divine expression of a changed heart. It is a miracle.

God used three pagan kings to help a small tribe of exiles go home and rebuild. documents.excerpt: Artaxerxes, a pagan king, granted Ezra authority to teach the law, which sparked revival. When God wants to punish a nation he sends a Nebuchadnezzar; when he wants to bless a nation he sends an Ezra.
excerpts: Artaxerxes, a pagan king, granted Ezra authority to teach the law, which sparked revival. When God wants to punish a nation he sends a Nebuchadnezzar; when he wants to bless a nation he sends an Ezra.

Ezra was born in Babylon yet cherished the Jewish Scriptures. With no temple, the priests and Levites were on something like a 70-year vacation, yet Ezra studied up. Verse 10 says he devoted himself to the study and observance of the law and to teaching it, and even the king noticed.

Maybe the author of Psalm 119 isn’t the mystery we think; some say David, Josh says why not Ezra: “Oh, how I love your law! I meditate on it all day long.” Ezra didn’t just study it; he obeyed it, like the next line: “Your commands are always with me and make me wiser than my enemies.”

God doesn’t want big brains; he wants humble hearts. James says those who look intently into the perfect law and do it will be blessed. If knowing the truth doesn’t result in obedience, the truth becomes a toy for entertainment instead of a tool for growth. Ezra fought that by teaching it to others.

excerpts: For some, studying God’s word hardly ever makes it onto the calendar, and you may need to clear things out to make space. Pray a dangerous prayer: ask God to reveal what in your life is less important than him, and fill it with him instead.

For others, study is no problem; you meet the Lord morning, afternoon, and evening. Your problem is a big head and no fire: you know stuff from your study, but you never kill stuff after it. You read about not forsaking the gathering but won’t come; about not sinning in anger but take no steps; you are impatient with your wife, hold grudges, watch porn constantly, know the Ten Commandments and the Beatitudes, and your theology is rock solid, but you don’t look anything like Jesus. You need a new heart, not a different study Bible.

Josh believes most of the church lands here: making time for the Lord, renewing their minds, seeking his ways, trying to act like Jesus, falling and getting back up to grab grace. The problem is you don’t have a single person you are willing to share it with. You are afraid they won’t like it, will ask a question you can’t answer, or will find out you don’t have all 800 proverbs memorized if you serve, launch a life group, or join a team.

documents.excerpt: Josh asks the church to call to mind the Christians who have had the greatest impact on their walk with Christ: celebrities, politicians, war heroes, athletes, or a less flashy list of Mom, Dad, Grandma, Grandpa. He was raised in a family of faith, flawed people who are a mess, but a mess that loves God and others.
excerpts: Josh asks the church to call to mind the Christians who have had the greatest impact on their walk with Christ: celebrities, politicians, war heroes, athletes, or a less flashy list of Mom, Dad, Grandma, Grandpa. He was raised in a family of faith, flawed people who are a mess, but a mess that loves God and others.

Outside his family he thinks of Eric Liddell, the 1920s Olympic gold medalist who refused to run on Sundays. Given the choice, Josh would trade the 2020s for the 1920s to pastor: a century ago athletes ditched their sport for church; now we ditch church for the sport.

Reggie White, the Packers’ “Minister of Defense,” was a pastor and a Super Bowl champion. Today there is Tim Tebow (Josh was once accused of flexing while preaching; it is involuntary), Steph Curry, Tony Dungy, and Kurt Warner.
Pastoral advice: Christian athletes often float side to side with culture instead of standing against it. Just because a Christian is visible doesn’t mean they are reliable. Test everything.

From left field: Amelia Earhart, the first woman to fly across the Atlantic. Josh isn’t sure where she stood with the Lord; her impact on him was social, cultural, and leadership. She didn’t care what the men of her generation said; she flew up and grabbed her dreams.

To the teenage girls in the room, and the way he speaks to his almost-19-year-old daughter: why care so much about how the world views you? If you have a dream, go get it. Don’t waste energy convincing people you are capable; just go do it.

documents.excerpt: Did anyone have Ezra? Of course not. He isn’t well known, but he was a faithful and courageous man of God: a priest, a scribe, and a gifted leader whose name means “help,” and he dedicated his life to serving God and helping God’s people. Tradition says he wrote most of 1 and 2 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, and Psalm 119, and helped lead a council of about 120 men who compiled the Old Testament canon.
excerpts: Did anyone have Ezra? Of course not. He isn’t well known, but he was a faithful and courageous man of God: a priest, a scribe, and a gifted leader whose name means “help,” and he dedicated his life to serving God and helping God’s people. Tradition says he wrote most of 1 and 2 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, and Psalm 119, and helped lead a council of about 120 men who compiled the Old Testament canon.

What Josh loves most is that Ezra not only knew God’s word but believed and obeyed it, with incredible reverence. God’s word humbled him and drove him to obedience and worship, unlike Christians who study the word to satisfy curiosity and boast in head knowledge. The word is meant to humble us, not puff us up.

documents.excerpt: Ezra is also known as the second Exodus. In the first, Israel grew into a massive people in Egypt, Pharaoh oppressed them, they cried out to God, and Moses, reluctantly, led them out to the promised land. Later Babylon conquered Judah and exiled many Jews, and Ezra focuses on God’s promise, prophesied by Jeremiah, that they would return.
excerpts: Ezra is also known as the second Exodus. In the first, Israel grew into a massive people in Egypt, Pharaoh oppressed them, they cried out to God, and Moses, reluctantly, led them out to the promised land. Later Babylon conquered Judah and exiled many Jews, and Ezra focuses on God’s promise, prophesied by Jeremiah, that they would return.

The second Exodus comes in three waves: first under Zerubbabel, a descendant of David and grandson of Judah’s last king before the exile; then Ezra 58 years later; then the third wave in Nehemiah, the subject of a series a couple of years ago.
For anyone who thinks God offers believers a cushy, comfortable life, tell that to Zerubbabel, Ezra, and Nehemiah. Many must have shaken their heads, but God’s hand is all over the second Exodus.

God isn’t interested in you just sounding like Jesus or regurgitating what he said; he wants to help you be like Jesus.

Josh is handling a Crossroads Cares need for a woman in Mayer, Arizona, who lost her son in September and learned right before the funeral that his widow was pregnant with a baby boy. He asks those who have met a need before to pray instead and leave this one for someone who has never met a need through Crossroads Cares; if it is taken, text him and he will find another way to help.

She was crying through her suffering, tears from her eyes and praise from her lips, preaching to Josh about God’s faithfulness. Our suffering is not meaningless or random; God uses it to refine, grow, build, and sanctify. Let Job preach: the Lord gave and the Lord has taken away; may the name of the Lord be praised. Or Joseph, sold by his family, who told his brothers, “You intended to harm me, but God intended it for good.”
Hard things are part of God’s plan. Christians pray for rain and get mad at the mud, pray for sunshine and get mad at the sunburn. Hard things shape us, like the potter using heat to keep the mold.

documents.excerpt: There is strong archaeological evidence for Cyrus’s edict: the Cyrus Cylinder, a football-shaped baked clay cylinder inscribed in Akkadian and found in the ruins of Babylon. It confirms two things in Ezra: Cyrus took Babylon without a fight and was welcomed as a hero (anything was better than Belshazzar), and his policy was to let peoples the Babylonians captured return home and rebuild their temples. Archaeology again confirms the Bible can be trusted.
excerpts: There is strong archaeological evidence for Cyrus’s edict: the Cyrus Cylinder, a football-shaped baked clay cylinder inscribed in Akkadian and found in the ruins of Babylon. It confirms two things in Ezra: Cyrus took Babylon without a fight and was welcomed as a hero (anything was better than Belshazzar), and his policy was to let peoples the Babylonians captured return home and rebuild their temples. Archaeology again confirms the Bible can be trusted.

Many call it the first declaration of human rights, and a replica sits at the UN. Critics once said no king would conquer territory and then send everyone home, and then the cylinder was uncovered. God keeps answering questions through findings over time, and Josh wonders what discoveries people will point to in a hundred years.

documents.excerpt: Josh thinks the burden of proof is on the non-believer, not the believer; historically the church has felt it had to prove this. There is so much evidence that the greater leap of faith, and a blind one, is to deny the resurrection.
excerpts: Josh thinks the burden of proof is on the non-believer, not the believer; historically the church has felt it had to prove this. There is so much evidence that the greater leap of faith, and a blind one, is to deny the resurrection.

In the first century there are over fifteen historical authors who claim Jesus was raised, more if you include non-Christian sources: Paul, Peter, James, Jude, Matthew, Mark, Luke, John, and others such as Clement, Ignatius, Polycarp, Justin Martyr, and Tacitus. They either witnessed it or had an immediate connection to an eyewitness.

Then the list of authors from that same time who denied the resurrection: there isn’t a slide, because there aren’t any. The critics show up much later, and the most credible objective ones not until the fifteenth century; the earliest were protecting an existing philosophy more than seeking truth. No one in the ancient world stood up with a conflicting eyewitness report. There is literally no contest.

documents.excerpt: The ancient world’s biggest pushback wasn’t against the reality of the resurrection. It was: why would you worship a God who lets people humiliate him? We see it in the Gospels: if you’re God, save yourself.
excerpts: The ancient world’s biggest pushback wasn’t against the reality of the resurrection. It was: why would you worship a God who lets people humiliate him? We see it in the Gospels: if you’re God, save yourself.

The modern Christian who was in Sunday school says, “Pick me”: Philippians 2. Christ Jesus, being in very nature God, made himself nothing by taking the very nature of a servant. What kind of God allows himself to be humiliated? A loving God. The one who made everything made himself nothing.

Why? The Christian who doesn’t forsake the gathering knows Romans 4: he was delivered over to death for our sins and raised to life for our justification. He humbled himself to bring us peace with God and reconciled us to God forever.

documents.excerpt: To the skeptic: all they keep uncovering is more evidence that the Bible can be trusted. A recently discovered underground church in Israel has a floor inscription saying, “Here we worship our God Jesus Christ.” First-century Christians always believed Jesus is God, and they believed it because of the resurrection; that is why they were willing to die and worship underground.
excerpts: To the skeptic: all they keep uncovering is more evidence that the Bible can be trusted. A recently discovered underground church in Israel has a floor inscription saying, “Here we worship our God Jesus Christ.” First-century Christians always believed Jesus is God, and they believed it because of the resurrection; that is why they were willing to die and worship underground.

One of Josh’s favorite discoveries is the Mount Ebal curse tablet (Eli called it the “cinnamon toast tablet”), found in December 2019 in a pile of dirt discarded from a 1980s excavation. Many believe it is the earliest written evidence of the name Yahweh, and it aligns with Deuteronomy 27:4–8, where Moses commands the Israelites to declare curses from Mount Ebal. They found it in a trash pile; God said, “You missed something.”

We have so much evidence we have to build museums. So, skeptic, one question: where is your museum disproving the resurrection? Ironically, the believer doesn’t even need the evidence, but it is amazing as it floods in. God reveals himself not only through oceans and mountains but through piles of dirt, history, science, and archaeology. If we treated creation like a crime scene, God wouldn’t get out of this one: he did what he said he would do.
Josh reads, “The heavens declare the glory of God… they have no speech, they use no words… yet their voice goes out into all the earth.”

excerpts: The resurrection proves Jesus Christ is who he claimed to be, the very Son of God. Some 99 percent of scholars, believers and non-believers, agree Jesus died on the cross under Pontius Pilate, and over 500 eyewitnesses claimed to see him alive.

He made incredible claims in the seven “I am” statements in John: the bread of life, the light of the world, the gate for the sheep, the good shepherd, the resurrection and the life, the way and the truth and the life, and the true vine. An empty tomb, multiple eyewitness accounts, ancient writings confirming the resurrection and none earlier refuting it, the transformed lives of the disciples, the birth of the church, the rapid spread of Christianity, and changed lives today: compelling isn’t a strong enough word. He has risen.

excerpts: For believers especially: your understanding of the evidence is not what pleases God. Without faith it is impossible to please God.

Josh never met Paul but believes he met Jesus on the way to Damascus; never met Mary but believes she found an empty tomb; never met Peter but believes he preached the first gospel message; never touched Jesus, but he is Josh’s best friend. He was never invited up a mountain by God, but he teaches his children the law as if God handed him the tablets. Mark wasn’t an eyewitness; he heard it from Peter, and Josh believes him.

When Thomas came to faith he said, “My Lord and my God,” and Jesus told him, “Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed.” How many actually saw the risen Jesus? Paul says 500. Far more Old Testament believers trusted in the coming Messiah without seeing; some generations saw the waters parted, others saw people dying in the wilderness. The pool of those who have not seen him is so much larger, yet the vast majority who have received salvation have never seen him. That is the faith that pleases God.

excerpts: Josh has been missing his sister. His wife has been using Jess’s quilt because he keeps the thermostat so low. Jess died at 39 and would have been 41 in January.

The last time he saw her was a Crossroads Cares need he will never forget: she was going through a divorce, and his family and his mom helped her settle into a new apartment. A member of the church bought security cameras through Crossroads Cares, and Josh installed them so she would feel safe.

They both professed faith and were baptized around age 10. High school was hysteria; Josh came back to the Lord, kicking and screaming, after about a decade, and lost connection with Jess. One night she handed him a beer and talked about how graduating from Harvard Law was the crowning achievement of her life. He had the chance to tell her that the crowning achievement of his life was conquering the shame of his sin through the Holy Spirit, but he was a coward and said nothing. He can preach to a stranger but was a coward with his sister, and he beat himself up for it.

Weeks later his older sister Andrea told him Jess had said: “When Josh and Kristen heard about my struggles they dropped everything and came running to help me, even though we hadn’t spoken in years. I’ve never experienced that kind of grace and love.” Josh wishes he had more time to show her that Jesus is the one to celebrate and rekindle with.

excerpts: Back to verse 1. Mark names these women three times in the last two chapters. He isn’t name-dropping; he is challenging readers to take his account as credible history. Richard Bauckham, a British scholar of ancient historiography, argues ancient historians gave more weight to oral accounts from living eyewitnesses than to written documents alone, because you could go ask them. Today we treat writing as ironclad, unless it is the Bible.
So the women’s names scream history, not myth. Mark is saying, “Go ask Mary; she’s right down the street.”

Celsus, a Greek pagan philosopher about 80 years after Jesus, wrote books to debunk Christianity, and his strongest argument was that it stood on the testimony of women, one “hysterical, half-frantic” woman who saw Jesus alive. Josh feels bad for his wife. The argument gained traction because women were so marginalized. But that means if Christians were making this up, they would never have made women the only eyewitnesses. The transparency is compelling: the women actually saw Jesus. The burden of proof is on the skeptic; show a lot of evidence that what the Bible says isn’t true.

The women named as witnesses
Back to verse 1. Mark names these women three times in the last two chapters. He isn’t name-dropping; he is challenging readers to take his account as credible history. Richard Bauckham, a British scholar of ancient historiography, argues ancient historians gave more weight to oral accounts from living eyewitnesses than to written documents alone, because you could go ask them. Today we treat writing as ironclad, unless it is the Bible.
So the women’s names scream history, not myth. Mark is saying, “Go ask Mary; she’s right down the street.”
Celsus, a Greek pagan philosopher about 80 years after Jesus, wrote books to debunk Christianity, and his strongest argument was that it stood on the testimony of women, one “hysterical, half-frantic” woman who saw Jesus alive. Josh feels bad for his wife. The argument gained traction because women were so marginalized. But that means if Christians were making this up, they would never have made women the only eyewitnesses. The transparency is compelling: the women actually saw Jesus. The burden of proof is on the skeptic; show a lot of evidence that what the Bible says isn’t true.

excerpts: The main benefit of the resurrection is justification. Remember Romans 4: he was raised to life for our justification, “just as if I’d never sinned.” Jesus bore our sins and satisfied God’s righteous requirements, and God credited Christ’s righteousness to us.

It was amazing if you were a Jew and annoying if you were a Roman. The population more than tripled, the military was on high alert, and a Roman soldier’s PTO request was always denied, to lower the chances that a Zealot would try to kill an official and incite a riot.

excerpts: If the triumphal entry doesn’t feel triumphant, Josh tells about the ascension and return. In Acts 1 Jesus ascended into heaven, and Paul told the Philippians he took his seat at the right hand of God and was given the name above every name, “Lord,” to which everyone who has ever existed will bow.

Jesus entered Jerusalem as a king and the religious elite crashed his party, but it came as no shock to heaven; it was the plan all along. This king wasn’t sent to conquer Rome but sin and death. God wove the gospel through Roman oppression and the leaders’ exploitation, and his providence demands our praise.

Jesus knew the donkey was waiting in that town, but he also knew the white horse waiting in heaven. Josh reads of the rider called Faithful and True, with many crowns and a robe dipped in blood, named King of kings and Lord of lords. If you are wondering where the victory parade is, there it is: the triumphal entry gets its name from a spiritual victory, not an earthly one.

Josh often thinks of the centurion in Matthew 27, who after the earth shook and the sun went dark said, “Truly this was the Son of God,” and wonders if he thought back to this parade. excerpts: What did the Romans think of this Passover parade? Probably mixed reviews. Josh often thinks of the centurion in Matthew 27, who after the earth shook and the sun went dark said, “Truly this was the Son of God,” and wonders if he thought back to this parade. At the start of the week it would have looked like a joke.

Romans were experts at victory parades: a returning general displayed trophies and captives, rode a golden chariot while priests burned incense, and ended at the arena where captives fought wild beasts.

Our Lord’s entry didn’t look like much, and spiritual victories are often hard to see in the moment. Josh says those being baptized today need to hear it most: victory looks different in the kingdom of God.

A Roman general had to kill 5,000 people to earn his parade. Peter preached to thousands who came to faith and received new hearts, and instead of a parade he got a custom crucifixion. What you don’t see is Peter’s victory parade in heaven. We are surrounded by a great cloud of witnesses, so let us run the race of faith with endurance.

Some worry Jesus is mistreating the tree, but he isn’t dealing with a tree at all. He is dealing with the nation of Israel, and with you and me. It is an object lesson: you have no fruit, and your temple is filled with corruption.
Jesus’ ministry isn’t marked by judgment, but at some point those who produce no fruit and invite corruption into the temple must be dealt with.

There are only two occasions where the Lord uses his divine power to destroy something in nature, and the series has seen both: the drowning of the pigs in Mark 5 and the fig tree in Mark 11. Two lessons surround the fig tree, fruit and faith, and Josh honors the way Mark splits the story around the temple.

documents.excerpt: Josh reads Mark 11:15–18: Jesus drives out the buyers and sellers, overturns the money changers’ tables, and says, “My house will be called a house of prayer for all nations, but you have made it a den of robbers,” and the chief priests look for a way to kill him.
excerpts: Josh reads Mark 11:15–18: Jesus drives out the buyers and sellers, overturns the money changers’ tables, and says, “My house will be called a house of prayer for all nations, but you have made it a den of robbers,” and the chief priests look for a way to kill him.

With the fig tree and the temple, Jesus is calling out shallow religion and exploitation. It isn’t the first time; in John 2 he made a whip and drove out the herds, saying stop making my Father’s house a market.

Josh loves that Mark mentions those selling doves. The dove was one of the few sacrifices poor people could afford. God didn’t price the poor out of making a sin offering, but the religious leaders tried to, and that angered the Lord. Josh thinks of Mark 9: better a millstone around the neck than causing a little one to stumble.

A place of prayer is where someone goes when they want to be changed; a den of thieves is where someone goes when they want to hide. Jeremiah faced the same in his day: steal, murder, and commit adultery, then stand in this house and say “We are safe.” “But I have been watching, declares the Lord.” The leaders were using the temple as a disguise, appearing holy while doing evil.

documents.excerpt: This is where the text hit Josh like a ton of bricks; he sat with it all week, and now it is the church’s turn. Jesus walked into a busy religious place: lots of events, noise, sign-ups, people, transactions, a whole day of entertainment for the family. What wasn’t happening? Prayer.
excerpts: This is where the text hit Josh like a ton of bricks; he sat with it all week, and now it is the church’s turn. Jesus walked into a busy religious place: lots of events, noise, sign-ups, people, transactions, a whole day of entertainment for the family. What wasn’t happening? Prayer.

Isaiah and Jeremiah both warned their people to stop bringing meaningless offerings; God said, “I cannot bear your worthless assemblies,” because he wants true heart reform. The greatest temple filled with wickedness is worthless; one man seeking God’s heart reform is priceless.

Before we point fingers at the religious leaders, we must examine this place to make sure we aren’t making merchandise of the gospel. Do outsiders think of this place as a house of prayer or a den of robbers? Do our neighbors know that no matter who they are or what they’ve done, they are welcome, that the doors slide open for everyone? Are Christians using the church as a disguise: appearing holy, then going home and doing evil?

If Jesus walked in here, or into your home, what reforms would he make? What would he remove, add, keep? “I have been watching, declares the Lord.” He isn’t impressed by how many life groups you attend or perfect attendance at events. Jesus didn’t die so you could fill your calendar with church stuff; he died so you could have a new heart.

“Josh, I just finished my Bible in a year.” That’s cool, but are you different? If you are smarter but not holier, go back, repent, and read again. Jesus doesn’t leave things how he finds them; he is always ripping stuff out, turning things over, making things new. Can others give testimony to Christ’s reform in your heart?

documents.excerpt: “Have faith in God,” Jesus answered. The call is for all of your faith, and it must be in God alone.
excerpts: “Have faith in God,” Jesus answered. The call is for all of your faith, and it must be in God alone.

We expect little faith in the culture; if God hasn’t given it to them, how can we expect it? What is shocking is walking in here and finding a lack of faith. It is by grace you have been saved through faith, and according to Paul this faith is the gift of God. Believers rarely struggle to believe what Jesus has already done; we lack faith in what he will continue to do, and we quickly doubt his presence in trials.

It sounds ridiculous: he saved me, how could I doubt him now? But some are afraid, ashamed, worried. Jesus says have faith in God. Have it holstered; don’t leave home without it; when you forget it, preach it to yourself.

We are saved by faith, but the second the rain pours we forget what we have. Jesus doesn’t say you can have too much, so give him all you’ve got: now, tomorrow, here, at home, at work, in the hurting marriage and the broken home, when you lie down and when you wake up. God gave it to you, so use it, and the more you use it the more it will grow.

We came to him weak, wandering, and defeated, and he sends us off powerful and ready for battle. Nothing can overcome your faith because the one who gave it already overcame everything. If you feel you don’t have enough faith, then have more. Could it be that simple?

documents.excerpt: Have crazy faith in God. Become like a child and have faith that makes no sense, that has people scratching their heads: “I don’t know, I just believe God’s going to do it.”
excerpts: Have crazy faith in God. Become like a child and have faith that makes no sense, that has people scratching their heads: “I don’t know, I just believe God’s going to do it.”

Josh reads Mark 11:23–25 about the mountain thrown into the sea, believing you have received what you ask in prayer, and forgiving anyone you hold something against. “That’s impossible.” No, nothing is impossible for God.

To pray effectively you need faith in God, not in what he may or may not give you. If your focus is on what you hope to receive and you don’t get it, you will be disappointed, but no one loved by God is ever left disappointed. If everything were taken and all Josh had left was faith, he would consider it net gain.

Jesus, our example, prayed, “Abba, Father, everything is possible for you. Take this cup from me. Yet not what I will, but what you will.” Our desires often lead us to prayer, but God’s desires need to finish our prayers.

excerpts: What is weighing on you? Is something in your life too much to bear? Have faith in God. Is it possible you have miscalculated your capacity for faith and have more storage than you ever thought?

Some are carrying health issues, praying for God’s will while afraid of what it might be: he will give you strength to endure. Some are fighting and praying for their marriage: lay it at his feet and have faith God will heal your marriage and home. Some lost a job: you are a believer, so have faith in God. Why spend one moment in worry when we can make requests?

Some think, “Josh, you have no idea what I’m going through.” He doesn’t, and they don’t know all the troubles he has had. But if someone told him in his darkest hour, “Josh, have faith in God,” he would thank them for being a good brother or sister and pointing him in the right direction.

documents.excerpt: To those who trust in Christ: forgiving others is tough. We love forgiveness when it is for us, not so much when it is for them. As you grow in Christ, your capacity for forgiveness will grow.
excerpts: To those who trust in Christ: forgiving others is tough. We love forgiveness when it is for us, not so much when it is for them. As you grow in Christ, your capacity for forgiveness will grow.

But if you pray while holding a grudge, you are no different than a tree without fruit or a temple without prayer. True faith changes the heart; real prayer breaks down pride and vengeance and replaces them with love. For powerful prayers and powerful ministry, the church has to show radical forgiveness.

Josh’s action step: if you aren’t right with someone here, go to them before you even think about communion. You cannot hold the body and blood of the Savior and your unforgiveness at the same time; drop one. If they aren’t here, let the plate pass, go outside and call them, then come back. Communion will be here all morning. It’s time to release our grudges and forgive. Have faith in God.

excerpts: The church continues through Mark in chapter 10, and it is loaded: Jesus discusses marriage and divorce, blesses the little children, speaks to a rich young man, predicts his death a third time, teaches the disciples about serving, and heals a blind beggar.

Josh didn’t launch this eight-week series to go verse by verse; the math doesn’t work. His goal is to show major themes about the kingdom of God and embrace Mark’s unique perspective. Over and over God’s kingdom has flipped social and cultural norms, and in chapter 10 power, position, importance, and influence are flipped too.

The reversal stands out in two sections. The first starts in verse 13, “The Little Children and Jesus,” where 95% of the message will be spent. The second, briefly, is in verse 35, which Josh affectionately calls “the ambitious anglers.”

excerpts: Two things stand out in chapter 10. First, today we look to influencers, scholars, and seminary graduates to guide our faith, but in Mark 10 Jesus says we should be more like children and slaves.

Josh suggests the church has a pandemic: so much content that professional Christians walk around with YouTube diplomas and no desire to sacrifice for others. Everyone wants to be a theologian and no one wants to wash feet. Christians have their AirPods jammed in so deep they will never hear the person screaming next to them. You watched an eight-hour podcast? You could learn more about following Jesus by asking a stranger if you can pray for them.

If people tune out the rest of the message, Josh asks them to get this: you will grow more in your faith through five minutes of obedience than in eight hours of observation. Take the YouTubers out of your head and you might hear from Yahweh. Listening has its place, but doing and sacrificing can’t begin until you stop listening. You don’t become a better Christian by hearing 18 sermons a week but by applying one. We have a content problem, 90% absorption and 10% action, and we need to flip it.

excerpts: Josh goes first: there is nothing good in him apart from Christ. He is naturally a selfish husband, and the Spirit nags him to love his wife, lead like a man of God, and lead like he would die for her. He would be a deadbeat dad if not for the Spirit nagging him to discipline his kids even when it is hard: you think you are loving them by being soft, but you are hating them.
The Christian with a superiority complex doesn’t part seas for others to see Jesus; they send people away. Anything superior in you is there by God’s grace alone, so stop pretending you built that.

We enter God’s kingdom by faith like little children, helpless and totally dependent on God’s mercy, and we enjoy it the same way, believing the Father loves us and will meet our every need. When a child is hurt, they run to Mama and Daddy. Many are settling for running to each other; run to him. Community has value, but not when it dismisses the community you need with him. “I’ll go first”: childlike, not childish
Josh goes first: there is nothing good in him apart from Christ. He is naturally a selfish husband, and the Spirit nags him to love his wife, lead like a man of God, and lead like he would die for her. He would be a deadbeat dad if not for the Spirit nagging him to discipline his kids even when it is hard: you think you are loving them by being soft, but you are hating them.
The Christian with a superiority complex doesn’t part seas for others to see Jesus; they send people away. Anything superior in you is there by God’s grace alone, so stop pretending you built that.
We enter God’s kingdom by faith like little children, helpless and totally dependent on God’s mercy, and we enjoy it the same way, believing the Father loves us and will meet our every need. When a child is hurt, they run to Mama and Daddy. Many are settling for running to each other; run to him. Community has value, but not when it dismisses the community you need with him. In our relationship with the Lord we learn from little children, but with one another we can’t afford to be childish.

Some say the gospel is simple; others say it is complicated. Josh says it is both. He had to die because the wages of sin is death; he absorbed God’s wrath, was raised for our justification, ascended, and sits at the Father’s right hand as our heavenly Advocate and only mediator. Every tongue will confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, he will return and make all things new, and Jesus reversed the curse, for it is by grace you have been saved through faith.

Faith without works is dead, but works without faith is filthy; phony faith is just as bad as empty religion. You need to run to the feet of Jesus and confess your sins to him every day, and he will forgive you. If he died for you, you can kill your sin for him. The gospel doesn’t just touch lives; it changes them forever.

Children are dependent. The gospel needs a helpless response: not just knowing Jesus paid your debt, but depending on him completely to earn what you couldn’t. Children don’t come in with their own part to play. Your child won’t walk in like Boss Baby with a briefcase and offer to get a job because raising him is expensive; parents of 26-year-olds at home know they need everything from you.

documents.excerpt: The world condemns the church when it speaks out; heaven condemns her when she stays silent. Who are you playing for?
excerpts: The world condemns the church when it speaks out; heaven condemns her when she stays silent. Who are you playing for?

It is scary, but have your testimony loaded and ready; it is your weapon, so don’t leave home without it. Share what God has done, let people ask questions, let them hate you for it if they want, and invite friends and neighbors to church. You are never alone; he promised to be with you to the very end. Pray for strength and wisdom, write your testimony out, be vulnerable about your struggles, and don’t worry about the outcome; just be faithful.

Peter says: who will harm you if you are eager to do good? Even if you suffer for what is right, you are blessed. Revere Christ as Lord and always be prepared to give the reason for your hope, with gentleness and respect. However it goes, pray for them and keep sharing the word. Spurgeon said it best: if sinners be damned, at least let them leap to hell over our dead bodies, and if they perish, let them perish with our arms wrapped around their knees, begging them to stay.

excerpts: Secondary issues are incredibly important but don’t affect salvation, though they lead to denominational differences. Josh firmly believes Christians can differ greatly here and still celebrate one another’s faith, take communion together, and worship together. The On Mission class covers these more fully.

Examples: baptism by immersion or sprinkling, and infant or believer’s baptism (the church practices believer’s baptism by immersion, but Josh would welcome someone sprinkled as a brother); church governance (Crossroads is elder-run, and Josh is the only staff member who is also an elder, so they are his peers and his boss, which is awkward, but they make it work); cessationism versus continuationism; end-times views, premillennial, amillennial, postmillennial, which many in this church need to hear are secondary; and the role of women in ministry, complementarian versus egalitarian.

These may lead you to another church, but they don’t have to. If we disagree on women elders, Josh isn’t wondering whether you’re saved; he is questioning your view of the authority of Scripture, and you can work through it together. The closer you look, the more a non-essential can start to feel essential, but even then be charitable and show grace and mercy.

Worship style: hymns or contemporary. The church likes both, and if you came from a church that hates instruments, they rather like them; Eli the worship guy claps. In the hands of God’s servants they make music that pleases the Lord, so they will sing and play until their throats hurt. Bible translations: there are bad ones, but someone once left the church because Josh said he preferred the NIV over the ESV. He likes the ESV too, just not that much. Christian liberty demands a different approach. Views on creation, young earth or old earth; Josh jokes that he thinks the earth is flat.

The last two tertiary issues cause the most division: dietary and lifestyle choices, and politics. That includes alcohol and whether to burn the Easter Bunny at the stake. Go back far enough and everything is pagan; that doesn’t mean it can’t be robbed for God’s glory. On drinking, ask before you order. Josh and his wife enjoy wine together, but he won’t pop champagne with someone holding a 90-day recovery token. Use common sense and don’t cause your brothers and sisters to stumble.

documents.context: Steve Coots · February 16, 2025 · Mark : Come Follow Me
documents.excerpt: Studying the text this week, Steve was haunted by words he spoke as a ninth grader to his youth leader, Mr. Landis, who had asked, “How about you, Steve? Who do you say that Jesus is? How’s your relationship with him?” Steve answered that he had led a boys’ small group for two years, his family was Christian, and his grandparents were missionaries. What started slow and hesitant ended with pride and confidence: surely that was what Mr. Landis wanted to hear, so he could focus on the guys who lacked Steve’s upbringing.
excerpts: Studying the text this week, Steve was haunted by words he spoke as a ninth grader to his youth leader, Mr. Landis, who had asked, “How about you, Steve? Who do you say that Jesus is? How’s your relationship with him?” Steve answered that he had led a boys’ small group for two years, his family was Christian, and his grandparents were missionaries. What started slow and hesitant ended with pride and confidence: surely that was what Mr. Landis wanted to hear, so he could focus on the guys who lacked Steve’s upbringing.

He had never been more wrong. It was the late ’90s and he was sporting at least three “What Would Jesus Do” bracelets, but his thoughts betrayed him: “That was close; you’ve got to do better next time.” Better at what? The game, the show, the image, keeping everyone thinking all is good.
Steve opens with that memory because it is a clear example of how poorly he answered a question about Jesus, and because the text takes us to the most important question anyone will ever be asked.

excerpts: Steve reads from verse 22: at Bethsaida some people bring a blind man and beg Jesus to touch him. Jesus leads him by the hand outside the village, spits on his eyes, puts his hands on him, and asks, “Do you see anything?”

All along Jesus has been showing how the in-breaking kingdom flips assumptions on their heads. You might expect him to do the miracle in front of everyone so more would believe and follow, but that isn’t his concern. He shows personal, intimate care for the sick, the disenfranchised, and now the blind. With the disciples likely present, the way he heals is intentional: he asks the man, “Do you see anything?” and very soon he will ask the disciples what they can see spiritually. This run-of-the-mill miracle sends ripples of truth that become waves of meaning in the next section.

documents.context: Steve Coots · February 16, 2025 · Mark : Come Follow Me
documents.excerpt: In verse 24 the man says, “I see people; they look like trees walking around.” Jesus puts his hands on his eyes again, his sight is restored, and he sees everything clearly. Steve loves “on the way.” It recalls the Shema in Deuteronomy 6, Hebrew for “hear”: love the Lord your God with all your heart, soul, and strength; impress these commandments on your children; talk about them when you sit at home and when you walk along the road, when you lie down and when you get up. It is an expectation for parents, grandparents, and anyone who cares for the spiritual growth of those younger: make the things of God part of your regular rhythms. Jesus models it; he doesn’t travel silently saving his teaching for the next town (and a mic check, Philip). He redeems every opportunity.

To help parents, the youth ministry sends out a family discipleship guide every Thursday with a summary of what students are learning and questions to open discussion at the dinner table, on the drive to soccer practice, in the doctor’s waiting room, or in the school drop-off line, which is the longest.

excerpts: Jesus starts this conversation with a question. Steve didn’t count them himself, but Jesus is recorded asking 307 questions in the gospels, from “Do you want to be made well?” to “Why are you so afraid?”, to last week’s “Who touched me?”, to this chapter’s “Do you see anything?”

After 15 years in public education and four in youth ministry, Steve has learned the value of a good question; every Wednesday he carefully writes small group questions for students. We are an answer-driven society; some data shows the average person asks a search engine or AI 20 to 30 questions a week. But Jesus knows that letting people wrestle with a question is the best tool to transform hearts and minds.

Jesus isn’t interested in the answer to “Who do people say I am?”; he already knows it. It is a tool to get the disciples thinking, like asking students why most teens struggle with Bible reading, which takes the pressure off. The next question is the one that does the heart work: “What keeps you from God’s word?”

Herod perpetuated the first idea; having had John beheaded over a twisted promise to his stepdaughter, he heard of Jesus’ ministry, recorded in Mark 6, and said, “John, whom I beheaded, has been raised from the dead.” That wasn’t possible, since Jesus and his cousin John had overlapping ministries and John baptized him.
excerpts: Verse 28: some say John the Baptist, others Elijah, others one of the prophets. Herod perpetuated the first idea; having had John beheaded over a twisted promise to his stepdaughter, he heard of Jesus’ ministry, recorded in Mark 6, and said, “John, whom I beheaded, has been raised from the dead.” That wasn’t possible, since Jesus and his cousin John had overlapping ministries and John baptized him.

Elijah never died but went up in a chariot of fire, and the scripturally well versed held this view because Malachi 4 says Elijah must first appear to announce the Messiah. Steve finds it interesting that this is why those at the cross thought Jesus was crying for Elijah, possibly mocking him further as though Malachi’s prophecy had failed. But Jesus identified John the Baptist as a type of Elijah who would prepare the way of the Lord, in John 1.

The last rumor, one of the prophets, shows the people’s desire for a political reformer to set the wrongs right and bring Israel back to justice and peace. Something Steve noticed this week: Old Testament prophets began with “Thus says the Lord,” but Jesus began, “Truly I say unto you.” Jesus was much more than a prophet of old.

excerpts: This answer is crucial because our salvation rests on it. As Peter said, there is salvation in no other name, so you’ve got to get this identity right. Salvation is by grace through faith in Christ alone.

The clearest description Steve knows is Romans 10:9: if you declare with your mouth “Jesus is Lord” and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved. Two things: you declare that Jesus is something, and you believe he did something, and the “and” means both are required.

Steve used to think that sounded too easy; couldn’t any Joe Schmo off the street do that and be saved? Yes, and that is the beauty, simplicity, and power of the gospel. But honestly declaring Jesus is Lord means releasing the throne of your life to him, and believing God raised him means proclaiming that God was pleased with his Son’s sacrifice as sufficient to cover your sin and the sin of the whole world.
So the question cuts deeper: salvation depends on it, and a proper personal answer yields a further response. Knowing who I am, will you truly come follow me?

documents.excerpt: Why such an intense response? Satan had already shown his hand in the wilderness. After 40 days without food, Satan tempted Jesus three times, including Matthew 4:8–10: showing him all the kingdoms of the world, “All this I will give you if you will bow down and worship me.” Jesus said, “Away from me, Satan!”
excerpts: Why such an intense response? Satan had already shown his hand in the wilderness. After 40 days without food, Satan tempted Jesus three times, including Matthew 4:8–10: showing him all the kingdoms of the world, “All this I will give you if you will bow down and worship me.” Jesus said, “Away from me, Satan!”

Satan was offering a shortcut. Jesus knew his mission to seek and save the lost would walk the narrow road; he knew he was the promised Messiah, the reason for all his “musts.” He knew Isaiah said he must be despised and rejected, a man of suffering, pierced for our transgressions, crushed for our iniquities, and by his wounds we are healed. He had to fulfill every word to bear the sins of mankind, suffering and dying on the way to becoming king of the kingdom of God, not of the world.

So Satan offered the glory without the suffering for a little worship; Satan always wanted to be God, which is why he fell. But Jesus knew there were no shortcuts to the will of God. The Father had already promised him the real kingdom; the price would cost him everything, but the power was greater, the goal higher, and the victory sweeter.

Steve is so glad Jesus wasn’t tempted by momentary fame and glory, but followed God’s plan for three more years and gave it all up to endure the cross of shame, so that we could enter his joy and have unshakable hope.

excerpts: What does the way of the cross look like for those who follow him? Verse 34: Jesus calls the crowd and the disciples: whoever wants to be my disciple must deny themselves, take up their cross, and follow me; whoever wants to save their life will lose it, but whoever loses their life for me and the gospel will save it.

The disciples likely imagined lives of favor and popularity once Jesus took control, with privileges and honor along the way. But he had been showing them an upside-down kingdom: the first shall be last, the weak strong, the poor truly rich, the persecuted blessed, to be free is to be a servant, and now, to save one’s life it must be counted as loss. This passage flies in the face of the “live your best life now” mentality in American churches: we want Jesus, but a lot of other things too, and will follow him as long as he contributes to our success and happiness.

Christians often hear “deny yourself” as denying sin and temptation, which we must do. But Jesus simply said, “Deny yourself”: you will be called to lay down your rights on the narrow road. What idols give you value and security? They can’t come with you. It isn’t settling for a mid house, car, and job and calling that self-denial.

Denying yourself is so much more: sometimes not saying what you want to say, sometimes saying what needs to be said despite the consequences; laying down your rights to control, perfection, calling the shots, and being right; letting go of your pride, dreams, and desires simply because they are yours. excerpts: “Take up your cross” shows the extent of self-denial, even to death. If you were literally carrying your cross to crucifixion, your deal was sealed; there was no turning back, and nothing held back, just as Jesus held nothing back for us.

The same idea appears with the rich young ruler in Matthew 19, whose list of laws kept since youth reminds Steve of his answer to his leader. Jesus answered, “If you want to be perfect, go, sell your possessions and give to the poor,” implying all of them, “then come, follow me,” and the young man went away sad because he had great wealth.

True faith requires a willingness to surrender all at Christ’s bidding. Our struggle is wanting to hold on to something rather than surrender fully, but the only way to full joy and a grasp of Jesus is to release every other possession, physical, mental, or emotional, that would hinder the pursuit.

excerpts: The youth group just finished a four-week series called Gospel Culture on how the good news should transform us individually and together. Steve realized we can get so close to the gospel that we lose sight of its beauty, form, and function.

Many students have memorized this definition: the gospel is all your sins, past, present, future, fully, freely, forever forgiven in the person and work of Jesus Christ. It shows why denying self is to our eternal advantage even if not our earthly one: it matters who Jesus is and what he has done, and what the cross accomplished for those willing to take up theirs. Remove any one word, all, past, present, future, fully, freely, forever, and the good news becomes just news.

documents.context: Steve Coots · February 16, 2025 · Mark : Come Follow Me
documents.excerpt: We need our sight restored, each of us has a question to answer personally, and there is a cross to be taken up by anyone who would truly come follow Jesus.
excerpts: We need our sight restored, each of us has a question to answer personally, and there is a cross to be taken up by anyone who would truly come follow Jesus.

As many suspected, Mr. Landis wasn’t thrilled with Steve’s freshman answer. Hebrews 13:7 tells us to remember our leaders who spoke the word of God to us, and Mr. Landis is one; Steve owes much of his spiritual growth to his faithfulness. He let Steve off the hook that night, but pushed and pursued him for the next four years until Steve could honestly declare who Jesus is, and his answer shifted from facts and other people’s relationships to firsthand experience. Following Jesus means discovering more on the way, and there is joy in the journey.

So how about you, Steve, who is Jesus to you? He is Lord, Savior, Redeemer, friend, the Son of God, the only one worthy of praise, time, and full pursuit, the one Steve will follow with all his life, who gives access with confidence before the throne, the bearer of his sin, remover of his shame, and lifter of his head.
Steve leaves two questions everyone must answer: Who do you say Jesus is? And just as important, what are you going to do about it?

This is part four of an eight-part series through Mark, investigating major themes, especially the kingdom of God and its upside-down values. Again and again this reverse kingdom loves the marginalized instead of lording it over them, notices the vulnerable even as the powerful scream accusations, and calls the worst of us to follow a new king.

documents.excerpt: Now there are generations of God’s people who don’t live like everyone else. The world trains us to acquire wealth, build a name, and worry about our legacy: what will they say about you when you’re gone? This upside-down kingdom isn’t worried about wealth or reputation on earth but about whom it will bring to heaven. Forget what they think when I’m gone; what will heaven say when I arrive?
excerpts: Now there are generations of God’s people who don’t live like everyone else. The world trains us to acquire wealth, build a name, and worry about our legacy: what will they say about you when you’re gone? This upside-down kingdom isn’t worried about wealth or reputation on earth but about whom it will bring to heaven. Forget what they think when I’m gone; what will heaven say when I arrive?

When people flip their mindset from the temporary to the eternal, a fork develops in the road, and no one is without excuse. The wide road to the left looks familiar: no leaving your comfort zone, free to “do you.” The narrow road to the right looks very different: where you chased success you embrace sacrifice, where you aimed for notoriety you grow in humility, and instead of your own glory you are trained and convinced to focus on God’s glory and making great the name of Jesus.

documents.excerpt: Josh just finished a big, thick book called We Believe, a collection of creeds, catechisms, and confessions from the second to the late 16th century; he admits he nerded out. Among his favorites was the Scots Confession. He warns readers that “Kirk” is the Scottish word for church; the first time he ran into it he had a mini identity crisis wondering whether it meant Kirk Cousins or Captain Kirk. Others in his top three are the Westminster Confession of Faith and the Apostles’ Creed.

We don’t pause enough to appreciate how blessed we are to pull all these up on a phone and see the core of the Christian faith preserved over centuries. Josh can’t even get “empty the dishwasher, Madison” communicated to his kids, yet the faith has been preserved for thousands of years. He is encouraged that his views of God and salvation align with some dude from Scotland in the 1600s, maybe a Christian Viking; if Josh had to live in any other era, he would want to be a Viking and train a dragon.

documents.excerpt: The battle cry of the Protestant Reformation was sola scriptura. The Holy Spirit convicted God’s people to return to Scripture and shed many unbiblical traditions the Roman Catholic Church had imposed, returning to divine revelation as the final, only infallible rule of faith. But the Reformers didn’t throw the baby out with the bathwater; they kept these statements of faith for a reason, and Josh thinks more Christians should occasionally take a second-century theology class.

excerpts: Our beliefs about God are rooted in Scripture, but that doesn’t mean the creeds lose value. Deuteronomy 6:4: “Hear, O Israel: the Lord our God, the Lord is one.” Paul references this to the church in Corinth: there is but one God, the Father, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom all things came.

When the fullness of time came, God sent his Son into the world, the promised Messiah we call Immanuel, truly God and truly man in one person. Born under the law, he met its every demand where we couldn’t, and instead of taking the victory for himself he made a way for us to wear a crown too. He absorbed God’s wrath toward sinners; he was pierced for our transgressions, and as Isaiah would say, by his wounds we are healed.
Jesus wasn’t done: he rose again for our justification and destroyed the author of death. His enemies tried to cover it up, but eyewitnesses testified, and many gave their lives to protect the truth.

Josh goes on: he believes in the Holy Spirit, whom he sees working in his life and theirs; in the church, not a call out to the Roman Catholic Church but to the universal church, the Lord’s church, whose brothers and sisters are his; in the forgiveness of sins; and in the promise of eternity.

excerpts: Josh wants to introduce the wideness of Christ’s love and mercy. In Mark 5 there are two very different people in need, and he reads the whole text before breaking it down, starting in verse 21.

Jairus, a synagogue leader, falls at Jesus’ feet pleading for his dying little daughter, and Jesus goes with him. In the pressing crowd a woman who had bled for 12 years, spent all she had on doctors, and grown worse touches his cloak, thinking, “If I just touch his clothes, I will be healed.” Her bleeding stops. Jesus asks, “Who touched my clothes?” She falls trembling at his feet and tells the whole truth, and he says, “Daughter, your faith has healed you. Go in peace.”

Messengers arrive: your daughter is dead, why bother the teacher? Jesus says, “Don’t be afraid; just believe.” At the house, to the wailing mourners, he says the child is not dead but asleep, and they laugh. He takes her by the hand and says, “Talitha koum,” which means, “Little girl, I say to you, get up!” She stands and walks around; she was 12. They are completely astonished.

documents.excerpt: Before that, Josh points to where the text lies. Chapter 5 begins with Jesus sending demons into a herd of pigs, and then the people began to plead with Jesus to leave their region. Jesus had just saved a man’s life; why would they want him gone? Two reasons. First, they were afraid of his power: their pagan gods were easy to manipulate with a gift, but Jesus saw through the gift to the heart of the giver, and that freaked people out. Mostly, though, they saw dollar signs as the pigs drowned; they cared more about their livelihood than the man’s needs.
